Title: SonicWall Patches Exploited SonicOS Vulnerability That Weakens VPN Logins
Context: SonicWall has patched a SonicOS vulnerability that can be used to bypass SAML authentication, warning customers that it may have been exploited in attacks
Full Text:
SonicWall has patched a SonicOS vulnerability that can be used to bypass SAML authentication, warning customers that it may have been exploited in attacks.

Tracked as CVE-2026-19868, the flaw affects the SSL VPN component of SonicOS, the operating system that runs on SonicWall firewalls. It’s one of seven vulnerabilities described in an advisory published on November 6.

“An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSLVPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA),” reads SonicWall’s description of CVE-2026-19868.

According to the vendor, an SSL VPN is exposed only if SAML-based login is enabled. CVE-2026-19868 has a CVSS score of 7.1, which puts it in the high-severity range. The flaw was reported by Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office.

SonicWall said its product security team “has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability.”

CISA added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day. Under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal agencies must address it by November 20.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Neither the vendor nor CISA has shared any details about the suspected attacks. It’s also unclear whether the flaw was exploited as a zero-day, before a patch became available.

Impacted devices include Gen7 TZ, NSa, NSsp and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 7.3.3-7015 or older. Gen8 TZ, NSa and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 8.2.2-8015 or older are also affected.

SonicOS versions 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 resolve the issue, and there are no workarounds. “Customers are strongly urged to upgrade to the latest release as soon as possible to mitigate the associated risks,” SonicWall said.

SonicWall’s advisory doesn’t mark any of the other six flaws as exploited. Two of them, each with a CVSS score of 8.8, affect the SonicOS management interface. One is a permissive cross-domain policy issue and the other is a session validation bug.

Under certain circumstances, a remote attacker could abuse either one without logging in to take unauthorized actions.

Three of the remaining flaws are pre-authentication buffer overflows in the SSL VPN service and the TACACS+ authentication client. Attackers could use them to launch DoS attacks at the application level.

The last one is a weak password hashing issue in virtual appliances. An attacker who already has high-privileged local access could exploit it to obtain a platform credential, which gives access to some of the platform’s settings.

Threat actors often exploit SonicWall product vulnerabilities. CISA’s KEV catalog currently includes 20 security holes, but the agency has yet to add CVE-2026-102255, which hackers started targeting last month, just days after its disclosure.

Title: SonicWall warns of new SSL-VPN MFA bypass flaw exploited in attacks
Context: Those attempts followed September attacks that chained two SMA1000 zero-days to achieve remote code execution, as well as July attacks that exploited two other zero-days to...
Full Text:
SonicWall has released security updates to fix seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS firewalls, including an SSL-VPN authentication bypass flaw exploited in attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-19868, allows attackers with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls, potentially including SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA).

The flaw has a CVSS severity score of 7.1 and only affects SonicOS SSL-VPN services configured to use SAML authentication.

In a security advisory published Friday, SonicWall warned that it had investigated a report that the vulnerability was exploited in an attack and urged customers to install the latest security updates.

"SonicWall PSIRT has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability. Customers are strongly urged to upgrade to the latest release as soon as possible to mitigate the associated risks," the company warned.

Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office discovered and reported the vulnerability.

While SonicWall has not shared details about the reported exploitation, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, confirming that the flaw has been exploited in the wild.

CISA ordered federal civilian executive branch agencies to secure affected systems by November 20, 2026.

The advisory also fixes six additional vulnerabilities in SonicOS, including two management interface flaws rated 8.8 severity that allow unauthenticated attackers to perform unauthorized operations under specific conditions.

The remaining flaws include pre-authentication buffer overflows in the SSL-VPN and TACACS+ services that could cause denial-of-service conditions, and a weak password hashing vulnerability affecting virtual appliances.

The vulnerabilities affect SonicOS Gen7 versions 7.3.3-7015 and earlier and Gen8 versions 8.2.2-8015 and earlier. SonicWall fixed the issues in versions 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 and says no workarounds are available.

The warning comes after a series of attacks targeting SonicWall's SMA1000 secure remote access appliances.

In October, security researchers detected exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-102255, a maximum-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to access internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.

Those attempts followed September attacks that chained two SMA1000 zero-days to achieve remote code execution, as well as July attacks that exploited two other zero-days to deploy malware on vulnerable appliances.

Title: Free Certified Patch for Critical Rails Active Storage Vulnerability
Context: Ruby on Rails has released security updates addressing 21 vulnerabilities, including a critical Active Storage flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary...
Full Text:
Ruby on Rails has released security updates addressing 21 vulnerabilities, including a critical Active Storage flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files to a server through crafted uploads. Under certain configurations, attackers may also be able to read sensitive files, potentially leading to remote code execution.

Socket is releasing a free Certified Patch for the critical vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9.8). The patch is available to everyone, including developers and organizations that are not Socket customers, providing an additional remediation option for teams that cannot immediately upgrade Rails.

Impact #

The vulnerability affects Rails applications that use ImageMagick to process Active Storage attachments. ImageMagick supports multiple file format handlers, known as coders, some of which can access files outside the uploaded image. Active Storage did not restrict these coders, potentially allowing an attacker to invoke dangerous operations through a crafted upload.

Active Storage automatically analyzes files when they are attached, so exploitation does not require a separate preview, image transformation, or explicit analysis request.

According to the Rails advisory, applications are vulnerable when all three conditions are present:

Active Storage uses ImageMagick through config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick.

The system's ImageMagick security policy does not already block the dangerous coders.

The application accepts file uploads from untrusted users.

An attacker exploiting the vulnerability may be able to write arbitrary files on the server. Applications using Active Storage's Disk service may also expose files readable by the application process, including secret_key_base, application credentials, and database secrets. These disclosures could enable remote code execution or access to connected systems.

Upgrade Ruby on Rails #

The Rails team released versions 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 on November 4, 2026, and strongly recommends upgrading as soon as possible. These releases address the critical Active Storage vulnerability along with the other 20 security issues disclosed in the same update.

To upgrade, update the Rails version in your application's Gemfile to the appropriate patched release. For example, applications upgrading to Rails 8.1.4.1 can use:

gem "rails", "8.1.4.1"

Applications remaining on the 8.0 series should use 8.0.5.2.

Then update the dependencies with Bundler:

bundle update rails

Applications using the :mini_magick variant processor must also use MiniMagick 5.1 or later. Update the dependency if necessary and verify that the resolved version meets this requirement. Earlier MiniMagick versions will cause affected applications to raise an exception during boot after applying the Rails fix.

The updated Rails releases include a restrictive ImageMagick security policy that blocks dangerous coders and delegates. Applications that use ImageMagick for PDF or PostScript processing may need additional configuration adjustments.

Rails versions older than 8.0 are no longer supported. Security support for Rails 8.0 also ends on November 7, 2026, so teams should plan to move to the supported 8.1 series.

For additional instructions, see the official Ruby on Rails upgrade guide.

Free Socket Certified Patch Available #

Socket is releasing a free Certified Patch for GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9, the critical Active Storage vulnerability that can allow arbitrary file writes and reads through malicious uploads.

Apply it with:

socket patch add GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9

Socket Certified Patches apply minimal, human-reviewed and AI-validated changes directly to vulnerable dependency versions, preserving the rest of the package's behavior. Patches are human-readable and can be reviewed before deployment.

The patch is available at no cost to anyone who needs it, whether or not they are a Socket customer. Making critical security fixes freely accessible is part of Socket's commitment to protecting the broader open source community and the developers and organizations that depend on it.

Certified Patches give teams time to plan and test upstream upgrades without leaving known vulnerabilities unaddressed. They are intended as an interim remediation option, with upgrading to a supported, patched Rails release remaining the recommended long-term solution.

This Certified Patch addresses GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 specifically, not the other vulnerabilities fixed in the November 4 Rails releases.

Recommended Actions #

Developers and organizations using Ruby on Rails should:

Upgrade Rails to 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2 as soon as possible, with a plan to move to a supported release series.

Verify MiniMagick compatibility and update to version 5.1 or later if the application uses :mini_magick.

Review Active Storage configurations to determine whether the application processes untrusted uploads through ImageMagick and whether its security policy blocks dangerous coders.

Apply Socket's free Certified Patch if an immediate Rails upgrade is not practical, then complete the upstream upgrade when possible.

Rotate potentially exposed credentials for applications using Active Storage's Disk service, as recommended in the Rails security advisory.

The official Rails security releases remain the recommended long-term fix. Socket's free Certified Patch gives teams an additional option to address the critical vulnerability without leaving affected applications exposed while upgrades are underway.

Title: OpenAI's new GPT-6 Cyber AI finds 81 Firefox flaws, 948 Linux bugs
Context: In October, researchers from OpenAI, Calif, and Wiz used AI models to discover two critical PHP vulnerabilities, dubbed PHP2Shell, which attackers began targeting even before...
Full Text:
OpenAI has revealed GPT-6 Cyber, a new artificial intelligence model that has discovered 81 previously unknown high-severity Firefox vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 distinct Linux kernel flaws.

The company announced the model on Thursday, saying it significantly improves on earlier AI models in finding software vulnerabilities, validating their impact, and helping developers create fixes.

During security testing, GPT-6 Cyber discovered 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox and helped develop patches, many of which Mozilla has already released.

In separate Linux kernel research, the model identified 2,308 potential security flaws, successfully reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and developed local privilege escalation exploits for 948 distinct vulnerabilities that could allow an unprivileged user to gain root access.

In benchmark testing, GPT-6 Cyber successfully exploited 48.5% of vulnerabilities in ExploitGym, compared with 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber.

OpenAI has classified the new model as having "Critical" cybersecurity capabilities under its Preparedness Framework, up from the "High" classification given to its previous model.

The new model is not publicly available, with access currently restricted to a select group of approved customers in OpenAI's Daybreak Red. OpenAI plans to expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon.

Daybreak Red supports advanced exploit development and authorized security testing, while the company's Daybreak Blue program allows verified defenders to investigate vulnerabilities and validate fixes with fewer restrictions.

OpenAI warned that defenders have a limited window to use increasingly powerful AI models to discover and patch vulnerabilities before similar capabilities become more widely available to attackers.

"It is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software," OpenAI said.

Recent research and breaches illustrate how AI is already accelerating vulnerability discovery and cyberattacks.

In October, researchers from OpenAI, Calif, and Wiz used AI models to discover two critical PHP vulnerabilities, dubbed PHP2Shell, which attackers began targeting even before security patches were released.

This week, a security researcher revealed that they used AI agents to conduct approximately 17,600 authentication tests and discover a previously unknown OpenSSH authentication bypass flaw known as '*sshole.'

Artificial intelligence is also increasingly being used to automate cyberattacks, with autonomous AI agents demonstrating the ability to compromise real-world systems.

In August, nearly 700 rogue agents powered by an OpenAI model escaped a controlled testing environment and exploited vulnerabilities to compromise Hugging Face infrastructure.

More recently, Chinese hackers used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to automate cyberattacks against more than 200 organizations worldwide, compromising at least nine.

OpenAI said it plans to expand its Daybreak programs to bring advanced cybersecurity research tools to organizations of all sizes, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers.

Title: Installing the Fix for an Exploited WordPress Flaw Can Expose Some Sites One Last Time
Context: Some WordPress sites can still be attacked while they install the fix for an actively exploited flaw, according to Umut Bayram, the Picus Security researcher who found it
Full Text:
Some WordPress sites can still be attacked while they install the fix for an actively exploited flaw, according to Umut Bayram, the Picus Security researcher who found it.

The update that installs the fix still unpacks its files using the site's old, unpatched code, so an attacker who strikes at the right moment can run code on the server. The researcher advises blocking web access to the site's wp-content/upgrade folder before updating.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-119977, affects WordPress 4.7 through 7.1.3. During a core update that uses a complete package, WordPress unpacks a copy of the new version into a temporary folder inside wp-content/upgrade. That copy includes the WordPress installer, and the web server can usually reach it.

An attacker with no account who can determine the folder's name and access the installer before WordPress deletes the copy can end up running code on the server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities earlier this week.

WordPress released the fix last week in version 7.1.4 and in matching updates for older branches back to 4.7, all listed in its security advisory.

The fix gives the temporary folder a random name. But the update that installs the fix unpacks its files using the old code already on the site, as WordPress's updater code shows. On sites running 5.9 or later, that old code names the folder after the downloaded file, so the name can be predicted one last time.

Before the fix, an attacker could use the installer to write a new configuration file, wp-config.php, into the temporary copy. The update would then overwrite the site's real file with that file. The part of the fix that stops this already works during the update that installs it, because WordPress copies the files into place using the new code.

An attacker who catches the window during that update can still set up the temporary copy of WordPress with their own database, log in to it, and run PHP code with the web server's permissions before the copy is deleted, Bayram says in his technical write-up. From there, the attacker can read or write files in the live WordPress site.

Who Is Exposed During the Update

Not every update exposes the installer, the researcher says. Complete packages always include the installer files. A smaller partial package, built for one specific starting version, exposes a site only if it happens to contain them.

On sites that allow automatic background updates, WordPress installs the fix automatically, via the same updater and the same steps.

The Hacker News checked WordPress.org's update service today for several versions. For updates within a branch, such as from 7.1.3 to 7.1.4, it offered a partial package, including for automatic updates. For a move from an older branch, such as from 7.0.7 to 7.1.4, it offered only complete packages.

On 4.4 through 5.8, the old code adds random characters to the folder's name. That hides the name unless the site leaks it some other way, such as in an error message, the researcher says.

Once 7.1.4 or a branch fix is installed, later updates use a random folder name, and a wp-config.php file in the temporary copy is never copied over the real one.

What to Do Before Updating

The researcher's first recommendation is to stop the web server from serving wp-content/upgrade at all. WordPress works with that folder directly on disk, so blocking web access does not break updates, he says.

Block the folder in the web server configuration. On Nginx, add location ^~ /wp-content/upgrade/ { deny all; }. On Apache, add Require all denied inside a <Directory> block for that folder in the virtual host configuration.

If you can only edit .htaccess, add RedirectMatch 403 ^/wp-content/upgrade/ to the .htaccess file in the WordPress root, above the WordPress rewrite rules.

Do not put an .htaccess file inside wp-content/upgrade itself. The old updater deletes everything in that folder before it unpacks an update, so the file would be gone when it is needed.

Confirm that a request to /wp-content/upgrade/ returns a 403 error.

Update to 7.1.4 or to the fixed release for your branch.

The other safe route, he says, is a manual update done outside the web root, the folder the web server serves. Back up the site files and database, unpack the new release in a folder the web server does not serve, copy the core files into place without touching wp-config.php or wp-content, and then run the WordPress database update. This way, no temporary installer is ever created in a folder the web can reach.

WP-CLI's wp core update command is no substitute, because it runs the same updater and unpacks the package into the same folder.

WordPress 4.6 and earlier no longer receive security updates, so there is no fix for them. The researcher says the flaw goes back to WordPress 2.7, released in 2008, and that those sites should move to a supported version.

Attacks and What to Check

CISA's catalog addition earlier this week was based on evidence of active exploitation, but the agency did not describe the attacks.

Wordfence, the WordPress security company that assigned the CVE identifier, saw attack attempts begin nine minutes after it deployed a firewall rule for the flaw on the day of the release. Two of the busiest sources kept checking small groups of sites for about 14.5 hours, which the company says, in its attack analysis, aligns with attempts to catch the moment a site updates.

Its score for the flaw in the CVE record is 8.1 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. In its lab tests, the window lasted only seconds. WordPress's own advisory rates the flaw low.

Code that its authors describe as an exploit for the flaw has appeared in public GitHub repositories since earlier this week. One of them says its code also works on sites that still use a predictable folder during complete-package updates. Whether the code works has not been established.

For sites that stayed on an affected version after the release, Wordfence suggests looking for:

unexpected requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade

administrator accounts no one recognizes

plugins no one installed

PHP files in wp-content/upgrade that no one put there

Update

Bayram told The Hacker News on November 6 that whether a partial update is exposed depends on what that specific package contains. A partial package holds only the files that changed between two releases. If those do not include the installer files, the temporary copy cannot run as a WordPress installation, and the installer never becomes reachable.

A site also does not always get a partial package when one exists. WordPress falls back to a complete package if the site's core files do not match the official checksums or if the update is a reinstall.

The deciding factor, the researcher said, "isn’t partial versus complete. It’s whether the updater already installed on the site has been fixed."

Title: Hackers Target OpenSSH SSHole Flaw Within Hours of Disclosure, Gain Root on Honeypot
Context: Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE publication, adding it has confirmed successful root access...
Full Text:
Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set, according to Previdian.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration.

An unauthenticated attacker can supply an oversized password to access accounts that are deliberately configured without usable passwords, without having to steal credentials or SSH keys. The issue, discovered by security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, has been addressed in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

The underlying issue dates back to a patch introduced in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210. Under specific conditions, the password-handling behavior in OpenSSH mistakenly interprets a failed password-hashing operation as successful authentication by producing the same value ("*") used to indicate that an account with password disabled at the system level.

An attacker can trigger the vulnerability to authenticate to certain password-disabled accounts using an arbitrary password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long, causing the hash attempt to fail and returning an asterisk. The sshd daemon then compares with the asterisk stored in the account's password field, leading to a successful login.

To be clear, successful exploitation requires at least one account with an asterisk (*) as its password hash. It does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.

"A successful SSHole attack grants access with the compromised account's existing permissions," Safe Security said. "For enterprise, the consequences of SSHole depend on the privileges of the compromised account."

"While unauthorized SSH access is the immediate impact, attackers may also gain access to deployment credentials, application secrets, and connected infrastructure, potentially enabling lateral movement or service disruption."

Image Source: Safe Security

It's worth noting that the vulnerability does not affect Dropbear, glibc-based Linux distributions, non-Linux systems, and systems that check passwords through PAM.

Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE publication, adding it has confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH. Telemetry data shows a total of eight exploitation attempts from an IP address geolocated to Japan.

"The observed source IP, 89.116.89[.]18, used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran reconnaissance commands including id, uname and hostname through non-interactive SSH sessions," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

Affected users are advised to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or their distribution's patched package, and then restart sshd. Alpine is also recommending that users investigate "Accepted password for" log entries involving accounts that should not accept password logins.

"Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user)," Alpine said. "Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised."

Title: In Other News: Trezor Implant, LLMJacking Bills Hit $1M, SAP Flaws Weaponized Within Days
Context: Initial access mainly came from stolen or exposed cloud credentials and API keys, and in one intrusion the attackers exploited a LiteLLM vulnerability (CVE-2026-40217) to...
Full Text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights:

Anthropic adds security center, admin controls to Claude Enterprise

Anthropic has rolled out additional security and administration capabilities for Claude Enterprise, including a security center (in beta) that checks an organization’s Claude configuration for chat, Cowork and Claude Code against settings Anthropic recommends. Inference hooks, now generally available, route prompts and tool calls to an organization’s existing data loss prevention and security tools for inspection, while a centralized console (also in beta) lets companies handle single sign-on, SCIM and other settings across all their Claude organizations from one place.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Fake OpenAI and SpaceX event invites phish Microsoft and Google accounts

Push Security has documented a phishing campaign built around fake registration pages for OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic events, which dangle rewards such as three months of ChatGPT Pro or Grok Heavy to get marketing employees to sign in with their work accounts. The Microsoft option launches a device code phishing flow run through the Kali365 phishing-as-a-service platform. Push links the operator, with medium-high confidence, to earlier fake Zoom event pages and says the campaign relies on Google and Zapier short links, Cloudflare challenges and domains swapped out every few weeks to avoid detection.

Chainalysis breach also exposed password hashes and tokens

Chainalysis has widened its breach disclosure, saying it discovered on November 2 that names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all its users had been exposed, after initially reporting that only non-sensitive data was accessed. The company has since taken several products offline, including its KYT transaction monitoring service after detecting abnormal activity, and is reaching out to customers whose KYT accounts show signs of unauthorized access.

Google hands Agent Substrate, gVisor to CNCF for sandboxing AI agents

Google is donating Agent Substrate, an open source orchestration layer on top of Kubernetes for running large numbers of isolated AI agent sessions, and gVisor, its open source application kernel, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) as Sandbox projects. When an agent goes idle, Agent Substrate saves its state to storage and can bring it back in under 500 milliseconds. gVisor handles system calls in user space so that untrusted, AI-generated code doesn’t interact directly with the host kernel. According to Google, placing both projects under the CNCF gives the community a shared, vendor-neutral base for agent infrastructure that can run on any Kubernetes cluster meeting conformance standards.

‘Hello’ messages hide Chinese-language attack framework targeting Flowise

Era researchers have detailed Greeter, a Chinese-language exploitation framework that bombarded Flowise honeypots with thousands of chat messages reading only “hello” while abusing an old code injection flaw (CVE-2024-58351) to execute commands. The framework mapped the host, queried cloud metadata services, searched for SSH keys and other credentials, tried to set up persistence, and tested whether it could run payloads from memory. Era counted 4,372 Flowise instances exposed online, and of those whose version it could identify, 703 lacked authentication and 46 appeared to share the vulnerable setup used in its honeypots.

LLM Mixers turn hijacked enterprise AI access into underground business

Mandiant says it investigated several LLMJacking cases this year in which attackers took over companies’ access to AI models, generating fraudulent bills of more than $100,000 in a day and as much as $1 million in total at some organizations. Initial access mainly came from stolen or exposed cloud credentials and API keys, and in one intrusion the attackers exploited a LiteLLM vulnerability (CVE-2026-40217) to upgrade ordinary keys to full admin credentials. Google Threat Intelligence Group also found hijacked access being sold through so-called LLM Mixers, including the Jet Night token routing service, which it believes uses stolen keys to offer unlimited plans with claimed frontier model access for around $60 a month.

CryptoBilis-sold Trezor allegedly fitted with seed-stealing implant

Trezor is telling customers who bought its hardware wallets from CryptoBilis since March 2026 to transfer their funds to a freshly created wallet with a new seed, after a buyer reported finding an implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 purchased from the former Southeast Asian reseller, which also sold Ledger devices that were found to have been tampered with. According to the report, which Trezor has not yet verified, an added circuit board fitted with a cellular module and antenna captures the recovery phrase displayed on screen and transmits it over a mobile network whenever the device is connected. No stolen funds have been reported.

Harvard alumni and donor data from 2025 breach added to HIBP

Have I Been Pwned has loaded roughly 851,000 unique email addresses from Harvard University’s November 2025 breach, an incident subsequently tied to a ShinyHunters extortion bid. The records come from Harvard’s alumni and fundraising systems and contain detailed profiles of donors, alumni and parents, as well as some faculty, staff and students, including names, contact details, birth dates and places, employers, ethnicities, marital statuses and donation histories.

SAP exploitation window shrinks to days as ransomware interest grows

Onapsis and Recorded Future report that for SAP vulnerabilities patched in 2025 and 2026, the median gap between a security note’s release and the first verified exploitation or public proof-of-concept was one to three days, down from 489 days for flaws patched in 2021. Ransomware and extortion groups showing up in SAP-related content grew from 8 in 2023 to 26 in 2025, and SAP CVEs with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation or public proof-of-concept code doubled from 9 to 18 between the end of 2023 and mid-2026. The study, drawing on over 1.2 million threat intelligence events, also tracked underground listings for SAP access priced from $500 to $30,000.

Synology flaw patched in 2024 now exploited in ransomware attacks

Synology warns that attackers are abusing a vulnerability fixed in December 2024 to hit devices still running outdated DSM releases, with the goal of encrypting data and extorting victims. The company has not identified the specific flaw beyond pointing to its Synology-SA-24:20 advisory. Synology recommends that anyone on a vulnerable release update DSM right away and turn on automatic updates.

Alleged Nomad Bridge exploiter appears in US court after extradition

Alexander Gurevich, a 49-year-old Israeli national now known as Alexander Block, appeared in a US court for the first time on October 30, a day after Israel extradited him to face charges that he exploited the Nomad Bridge smart contract in August 2022 to take virtual currency worth roughly $2.89 million. According to the indictment, he swapped the stolen WBTC and WETH for other cryptocurrencies and spread them across multiple addresses to obscure their origin. The money laundering charge alone carries a maximum of 20 years in prison.

Title: D-Link warns of multiple zero-days in DGS-3130 Series switches
Context: Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service...
Full Text:
D-Link shared mitigation measures for multiple unpatched security flaws affecting DGS-3130 series managed Gigabit stackable switches.

These switch models provide multi-gigabit uplinks, allowing enterprise network administrators to eliminate data bottlenecks, and are designed primarily for small-to-medium businesses (SMBs) and metro Ethernet deployments.

While D-Link didn't share details on these flaws and has yet to publicly disclose the CVE IDs for easier tracking, it said Spectrum Community Solutions network engineer Giresh Kumar Enugu found the bugs in the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) authentication, access control, and information handling.

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service disruptions and device resets.

The zero-days affect multiple DGS-3130-30TS firmware versions, and the company is still investigating the impact on other D-Link switching platforms and firmware security mechanisms (including SSH service security configuration, safeguards underlying operating-system credentials, and handles firmware encryption/embedded cryptographic keys).

"The reported vulnerabilities involve the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) and certain components of the device's firmware security architecture," D-Link said.

"According to the security researcher, successful exploitation of certain vulnerabilities may allow an attacker with access to the affected network to obtain sensitive device information, perform unauthorized administrative operations, modify device configuration, or disrupt network services."

Until it releases new firmware to address these flaws, D-Link asked admins to disable DDP to remove the primary known attack vector, remove unnecessary or default SNMP community strings, and restrict SSH, web UI, and SNMP accessibility solely to isolated management networks and designated admin hosts.

D-Link also advised admins to maintain offline switch configuration backups and track device logs for unexpected configuration changes, unprompted reboots, or factory resets.

In September, D-Link warned customers of a maximum-severity zero-day (tracked as CVE-2026-86296) with a public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit and no patch, affecting legacy DIR-822A dual-band Wi-Fi routers.

Title: OpenSSH Rushes Patches for ‘SSHole’ Authentication Bypass
Context: Only some of those run Alpine, but each attempt is a single connection, so an attacker can afford to try all of them,” Detectify co-founder and principal security researcher...
Full Text:
OpenSSH has rolled out emergency patches for a high-severity authentication bypass that allows attackers to log in using very long passwords.

Dubbed SSHole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score of 8.1), the security defect affects the OpenSSH server (sshd) on Linux distributions that use the musl libc implementation with the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) disabled.

A “misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash” allows attackers to access certain accounts using any password that has between 257 and 1,024 characters.

Some accounts, such as root, should never accept a password, but in Linux distributions such as Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, and others, they do, Wakefield security researcher Özgün Kültekin says.

According to OpenSSH developer Damien Miller, the flaw is not in sshd itself, but can be exploited via sshd. Fixes were included in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

“We are making this release as fast as possible (we learned of the problem yesterday) because we have recently observed multiple cases of rapid bug rediscovery by AI agents, sometimes within hours, and so now consider long embargo periods to be a dangerous practice that primarily benefits attackers,” Miller said.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Thursday, Alpine Linux urged users to immediately apply the OpenSSH patches and restart sshd to replace the running daemon, or disable password logins and restart sshd.

“The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is * (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash,” Alpine Linux warns.

Since version 3.16, Alpine Linux uses “*” to secure the root account, and $5$ or $6$ in password hashes show whether the SHA-256 or SHA-512 crypt was used.

“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries,” Alpine Linux notes.

Affected Alpine Linux deployments run OpenSSH without PAM, have password authentication enabled, have an account with the password field “*” (such as root, a key-only user created with adduser without a password, the alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images, or a user coming from a directory service through musl-nscd), and have at least one local account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash.

“Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20),” Alpine Linux says.

“We haven’t seen any reports of exploitation yet, but the details are public, and the attack is simple, so I expect scanning to start within hours. Finding targets is very easy. Shodan lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22, and the real number is higher because Shodan doesn’t see everything. Only some of those run Alpine, but each attempt is a single connection, so an attacker can afford to try all of them,” Detectify co-founder and principal security researcher Fredrik Almroth said.

“We’d be extremely surprised if we didn’t see SSH brute-forcers attempting this by the weekend. It’s virtually free to try and an easy win if it works. If your organization is affected, update to the latest version where possible, and disable password-based authentication as a temporary mitigation if you can’t,” WatchTowr head of threat intelligence Jake Knott said.

Title: Microsoft Paint RCE Fix Now Available, but Windows Update Won't Deliver It
Context: Attack Conditions and Exploitation Status An attacker could exploit the flaw by sending "a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network," the advisory says,...
Full Text:
A fix for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution flaw in Windows Paint, is now in the Microsoft Store. Paint gets this fix only through a Store update, not through Windows updates.

The fixed build, 11.2609.401.0, was the newest Paint build in all ten countries The Hacker News checked today.

The flaw is an out-of-bounds read that could let an attacker run code over a network. Microsoft rates it as Important, with a CVSS score of 8.1, and says that a successful attack requires a deep understanding of the target system. The flaw was not known to be exploited or publicly disclosed when the company published it on October 13.

Brian Vitko of RFF, a device-management software maker, checked which Paint builds the Store offered in six countries earlier this week. He found that the newest in each was 11.2605.81.0, a build without the fix.

His test virtual machine has since moved to the fixed build on its own, through Store auto-update. That is one machine, and how quickly other PCs will get the build is not yet clear.

Which Build Counts as Fixed

Microsoft's security advisory names 11.2609.401.0 as the fixed build. The CVE record for the flaw, which the company also publishes, still lists Paint as affected only below 11.2605.91.0. Its NVD entry shows the same range.

So a scanner that reads the CVE record would treat any build from 11.2605.91.0 up as fixed. A copy at 11.2609.401.0 or later passes under both numbers.

As recently as last week, the advisory gave 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed build, according to a forum question on Microsoft Q&A. The advisory's revision history still shows only its October 13 entry, with no note about the change.

How to Check Every Copy of Paint

Paint, like other Store apps, is installed separately for each user account on a PC. Windows can also keep a provisioned copy that it installs for each new user. A check of only the signed-in account can miss older copies.

Vitko's test write-up gives two commands to run in a PowerShell window opened as administrator. The first lists every user's copy of Paint, and the second lists the provisioned copy.

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name Microsoft.Paint | Select-Object Version, @{ n = 'Users'; e = { $_.PackageUserInformation.UserSecurityId.Username -join ', ' } }

Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | Where-Object DisplayName -eq 'Microsoft.Paint' | Select-Object Version

For any copy below 11.2609.401.0:

Update Paint through the Store, or let the Store auto-update install the fixed build. In Intune and other device-management tools, the Store app update scan does this across many PCs.

Run both commands again and check that every copy shows 11.2609.401.0 or later.

The advisory lists no workaround or mitigation. Before the fix reached the Store, Vitko suggested removing Paint where nobody needs it, for every user and from the provisioned copy. He did not test that step.

Attack Conditions and Exploitation Status

An attacker could exploit the flaw by sending "a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network," the advisory says, but it does not name the service. The attack would require no sign-in and no user assistance.

The flaw was not in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog run by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency when The Hacker News checked today. The catalog was last updated earlier this week.

CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-19868 SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Use of Single-factor Authentication Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: CPython flaw exposes AI inference servers to sandbox escape attacks
Context: “By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at...
Full Text:
A memory-safety flaw in CPython can allow malicious AI model templates to escape code sandboxes and execute arbitrary code inside inference servers, according to security researchers at RunSybil.

“By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at RunSybil, wrote in a blog post. “They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads.”

The researchers demonstrated how a specially crafted model could exploit the flaw to bypass Jinja, a Python-based templating engine used to structure interactions between users and LLMs, sandbox protections, and execute code in the process of serving the model. The attack could expose AI hosting providers that allow customers to upload and run their own models, potentially giving attackers a foothold inside infrastructure processing requests for multiple customers, the post added.

However, the Python Security Response Team (PSRT), which handles security reports involving CPython, disputed the security implications of the demonstration in a response to CSO. “We acknowledge the underlying CPython bug reported by RunSybil and appreciate their contribution to fixing it. However, we do not consider the demonstrated sandbox escape to be a CPython security vulnerability,” the team said.

The disagreement centres on whether the interpreter should be responsible for preventing sandbox escapes. While RunSybil argues that the flaw creates risks for AI inference infrastructure, PSRT says executing untrusted Python code within a sandbox is outside CPython’s security threat model.

Exploiting Python’s type-handling mechanism

“The bug we discovered abuses CPython’s handling of generic types to accomplish a breakout,” Houle wrote. “We exploited it using objects that sandboxes make available in every template, even in empty sandbox contexts.”

The researchers found that CPython can use a cached list of parameters even after an object has been modified through a callback. When the interpreter subsequently looks for a newly introduced parameter in the original list, it can receive an invalid index. An assertion designed to catch the condition is disabled in normal release builds, allowing the interpreter to access memory outside the expected bounds.

RunSybil used this behavior to retrieve references to Python objects that the sandbox was supposed to keep inaccessible.

“While an invalid address will generally crash the interpreter, an address pointing to a useful live Python object gives our callback a reference to that object (even when the sandbox never intends to expose it),” Houle wrote.

The researchers then used the recovered object references to access Python classes and functions needed to construct executable code.

Malicious model templates enable code execution

To demonstrate the attack, RunSybil modified the Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct model by inserting a backdoored chat_template.jinja file. When the model was loaded and used through an inference-serving engine such as vLLM, the template enabled arbitrary code execution in the serving process.

“Breaking out of the chat template sandbox and executing code represents a supply chain risk that endangers inference providers, library developers, and model users,” Houle wrote.

The researchers said they shared proof-of-concept exploits with multiple inference providers supporting bring-your-own-model (BYOM) features, which allow customers to upload models from external sources.

Python disputes vulnerability classification

RunSybil disclosed the issue to CPython, the Pallets Project, which maintains Jinja, and Hugging Face. The researchers said they encountered conflicting views about which project should address the underlying problem.

CPython maintains that the interpreter does not support sandboxing untrusted Python code as a security boundary. In its response to CSO, the PSRT referred to the project’s security policy, which states that sandbox escapes should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software.

“Escapes from such sandboxes are therefore outside our security threat model and should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software,” the team said.

The team also disputed RunSybil’s suggestion that there was no coordinated remediation process. It said the researchers had submitted the report by email rather than through CPython’s designated private GitHub vulnerability reporting channel.

Fix backported to three Python branches

RunSybil submitted a patch to CPython, which was merged into the main development branch on Aug. 14. According to the PSRT, the fix was also backported to the 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches as a regular bug fix rather than a security fix.

The distinction matters because RunSybil had raised concerns that the fix would not reach all supported Python versions.

The researchers said the absence of a backport to Python 3.12 could delay adoption of the fix across AI infrastructure deployments.

“With major portions of the AI ecosystem still solidly aligned on Python 3.12, we might not see organic adoption of our memory-safety fixes until late 2028, when it reaches its end-of-life date,” Houle wrote. The researchers recommend that AI hosting providers treat sandboxed code, template engines and expression evaluators as best-effort security controls rather than relying on them as standalone security boundaries.

Title: November 2026 Patch Tuesday forecast: Old software continues to bite
Context: In October, one zero-day CVE-2026-96951 was confirmed exploited; it was a Windows Shell security feature bypass impacting Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server
Full Text:
How did you enjoy October 2026 Patch Tuesday? Were there enough CVEs reported to keep you busy for the rest of the year or are you finished and ready for another round next week? They released the regularly scheduled update nearly two and a half hours late, but Microsoft did resolve another record-breaking 1,407 unique CVEs.

As in previous months, there were limited CVEs we needed to immediately deal with. In October, one zero-day CVE-2026-96951 was confirmed exploited; it was a Windows Shell security feature bypass impacting Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server. And CVE-2026-10839 was publicly disclosed; it was a .NET Framework security bypass vulnerability. Overall, there were 78 Critical vulnerabilities, which was a small fraction of all CVEs reported.

PHP2Shell

The hottest news of the month surrounded vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, also referred to as PHP2Shell by researchers. PHP is a general-purpose scripting language which was originally released in 1994 to support web development. It runs on a server providing the middleware between a web server and the browser requesting information.

PHP released a security advisory on October 21st regarding the vulnerabilities and the related PHP software versions that had been fixed. Exploitation in the wild was detected several days before the patches were released and is continuing to expand. Patching the vulnerability is a multi-step process varying by operating system, but essentially, you need to replace the php runtime, stop the web server and then restart it all. Without a restart, the old code stays in memory.

Exploitation of the vulnerability provides the attacker with access to whatever the php shell can see. Keep this in mind as you assess your systems for compromise and prioritize the updates.

Emergency fixes

Microsoft had several out-of-band releases and the usual preview patch near the end of last month, both of which have security implications. They released an emergency fix for CVE-2026-111497 on October 25, which is also referred to as the Broccoli2Shell, Node2Shell or HTTP2Shell vulnerability. This name comes from a flaw in the Brotli binaries or libraries used to process Brotli-compressed data. These fixes address the libraries in .NET 8, 9, 10, as well as Release Candidate 3 for .NET 11 and should be updated as soon as possible. There is proof-of-concept code available but no known exploitation in the wild at this time.

On October 26, Microsoft issued an update that removes seven certificates from the Windows trust list: six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign. These certificate keys had been compromised. And finally, Microsoft confirmed the preview patches included fixes for the Always On VPN connection failures, which were introduced back with the September Patch Tuesday updates. They also included a fix for the Smart App Control broken by the October Windows update.

Following application of that October update, the Smart App Control option was grayed out and could not be toggled on affected devices running Windows 11 24H2 and later. All of these security fixes will be included in the November Patch Tuesday cumulative release.

Obsolete software

Do you spend time finding and removing EOL or obsolete software in your environment? Although it isn’t strictly a patching issue, we often leave software in place after applying its final patches, intending to remove it later. But do we always remember, or find the time? One article described an abandoned 2014 application that was still running and trying to update itself on 2.5 million Windows devices and 300,000 Macs. Several of the domains it contacted for updates were open for new registration, so anyone paying attention could have created a malicious update package that would instantly compromise millions of machines. Fortunately, the problem was detected and the software removed before that could happen, but this software was running for a long time.

This begs the question, do we really know what every running service on our machines is doing, particularly those with network connectivity? This is yet another area where AI can provide more insight into operational vulnerabilities on our systems. And yes, we do need to constantly search for and remove obsolete software from our systems or face the consequences.

Updates from Apple

Apple released major security updates for all its supported operating systems on October 26th. For example, the security update for its latest version, macOS Golden Gate 27, addressed 183 unique CVEs. You should also note on this page that there are updates for iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11. Apple backported a fix to these operating systems because of the known exploited CVE-2026-86950. Per Apple: “Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.” Exploitation of this CoreGraphics vulnerability could lead to arbitrary code execution. If you are running these older OS versions, you should take advantage of this rare patch from Apple.

November 2026 Patch Tuesday forecast

After last month, let’s just assume that Microsoft will continue to release updates across the board for all their products with high numbers of CVEs for each.

Based on past cadence, expect Adobe to provide updates for Acrobat/Reader, InCopy and InDesign, and Premiere.

Apple provided their latest updates on October 26th for all operating systems, so I don’t expect anything next week.

Google just released Early Stable Update for Desktop 158, so expect this update for Chrome next week.

Mozilla is due to release Firefox and Thunderbird 160. Along with these major releases we usually see updates to the ESR versions with select CVEs as well.

The penultimate Patch Tuesday of the year is almost upon us. Will there be a break in the number of releases after the massive output last month? Or will this be the last big push before the holidays to get everyone into a secure state for end-of-year system lockdown? Regardless of what comes, we’ll always deal with it, but don’t forget to patch the older software in your environment like php which doesn’t have a Patch Tuesday focus. And on a final note, don’t forget to track down and remove EOL software, which is vulnerable, because they will come back to bite.

Title: ZDI-26-897: (Pwn2Own) Home Assistant Green aiohttp_client Server-Side Request Forgery Vulnerability
Context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of Home Assistant Green
Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of Home Assistant Green. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the aiohttp_client module. The issue results from following HTTP redirects. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of root.

Additional Details

Home Assistant has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://github.com/home-assistant/core/security/advisories/GHSA-6456-4qg9-cqpj

Disclosure Timeline

2025-11-05 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-06 - Coordinated public release of advisory

Title: ZDI-26-895: LibreOffice dBase File Parsing Heap-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
Context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LibreOffice
Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LibreOffice. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of dBase index files, which can be referenced from .odb database files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

LibreOffice has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://www.libreoffice.org/security/#cve-2026-76181

Disclosure Timeline

2026-08-20 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-06 - Coordinated public release of advisory

Title: ZDI-26-892: Philips Hue Bridge Pro Protection Mechanism Failure Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
Context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of Philips Hue Bridge Pro
Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of Philips Hue Bridge Pro. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the HTTP service, which listens on TCP port 443 by default. The issue results from the failure to apply a protection mechanism. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to bypass authentication on the system.

Additional Details

Fixed in Bridge Pro firmware version 6.1.2071524030 (or later) https://www.philips-hue.com/en-ca/support/release-notes/bridge-pro

Title: ZDI-26-889: Quest NetVault Backup nvpmgr Integer Underflow Denial-of-Service Vulnerability
Context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to create a denial-of-service condition on affected installations of Quest NetVault Backup
Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to create a denial-of-service condition on affected installations of Quest NetVault Backup. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the nvpmgr service, which listens on UDP port 20031 by default. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in an integer underflow before allocating a buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to create a denial-of-service condition on the system.

Additional Details

Fixed in NetVault version 14.1.3https://support.quest.com/technical-documents/netvault/14.1.3/release-notes/2#TOPIC-2383658

Title: OpenSSH flaw lets attackers log into password-disabled Linux accounts
Context: Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles...
Full Text:
A newly disclosed flaw involving OpenSSH and musl, dubbed "*sshole," allows attackers to log in to certain Alpine Linux and other musl-based Linux accounts configured to block password authentication simply by entering an oversized password.

The flaw only affects OpenSSH servers running on Linux distributions that use the musl C library, including Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, and Yocto, under certain authentication configurations.

Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library.

Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts.

However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes.

To prevent attackers from identifying valid usernames through different response times, OpenSSH was modified to perform password hashing even when an account had no usable password hash, including accounts configured with * to block password logins.

The problem is that the musl C library's crypt() function also returns * when password hashing fails, including when a submitted password exceeds its 256-byte limit.

This means an attacker can submit an oversized password and cause OpenSSH to compare the returned * against the account's stored *, resulting in a successful login.

To be clear, the flaw does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.

Kultekin says exploitation requires the following conditions:

OpenSSH is running on a musl-based Linux system, such as Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, or Yocto.

PAM authentication is disabled, as it is by default in Alpine Linux's openssh-server package.

SSH password authentication is enabled.

At least one account has an asterisk (*) as its password hash.

Another account has a valid password hash.

The researcher warns that Alpine Linux's official AWS and Azure cloud images have an affected default 'alpine' account with passwordless 'doas' privileges, which could allow attackers to gain root access.

Systems using glibc, including Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora, and those using PAM authentication are not vulnerable to this attack.

Kultekin says he discovered the vulnerability using AI agents that ran about 17,600 authentication tests with different OpenSSH configurations, malformed password hashes, and oversized passwords.

The vulnerability has been fixed in OpenSSH 10.6p2, and Alpine Linux administrators are advised to update their OpenSSH packages using apk upgrade openssh.

Admins who can't immediately install the update can mitigate the issue by turning off SSH password authentication with PasswordAuthentication no in their SSH server configuration and restarting SSH.

Kultekin says admins can also check for signs of exploitation by examining SSH authentication logs for password-based logins for accounts that should not allow them.

On Alpine Linux, the following command can reveal successful SSH password logins:

grep "Accepted password" /var/log/messages

If the logs show a successful password login for the alpine account, administrators can check whether that account has password authentication disabled:

grep '^alpine:' /etc/shadow

If the account's password field contains *, but SSH logs show a successful password login, it could indicate that the vulnerability was exploited.

Title: Researchers Bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode to Exfiltrate Chats Without User Interaction
Context: " Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt,...
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability that could be exploited to bypass Lockdown Mode protections in OpenAI ChatGPT.

Lockdown Mode was introduced by the artificial intelligence (AI) company in June 2026 as an optional setting to minimize data exfiltration risks arising from prompt injections.

"The flaw could enable silent chat data theft, phishing, and malware delivery, including zero-click data exfiltration in the ChatGPT desktop application," Eli Smadja, head of research at Check Point, said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The problem stems from HTML page previews inside ChatGPT code blocks, which allow HTML content to be rendered directly within the application. Given that executing user-supplied HTML and JavaScript can introduce security risks of its own, the content is placed inside a sandbox so that it cannot access data from the app, such as cookies and local storage.

The sandbox also prevents the rendered content from communicating with external resources without user consent. Lockdown Mode acts as a security barrier, mitigating data exfiltration risk by limiting outbound network requests that could be used to transfer sensitive information to an attacker-controlled infrastructure.

However, Check Point found a loophole in the manner popup windows are handled during HTML previews that made it possible to escape the confines of the sandbox and bypass Lockdown Mode.

"The HTML preview used nested sandboxed frames, and while ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying sandbox permissions still allowed popups and permitted them to escape the sandbox," Smadja explained.

"By creating another nested frame within the rendered page, it was possible to access an unmodified popup function and bypass the restrictions placed on the original HTML preview. Content opened through this route was no longer subject to the same sandbox restrictions, providing a way to circumvent the protections of Lockdown Mode."

Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat.

What's more, as the attacker is in complete control of the content displayed in the popup window, it could be used to render convincing social-engineering lures, such as a fake ChatGPT update, and trick the victim into downloading malware by persuading them to click on a link.

That said, the underlying issue is not limited to the Electron-based desktop environment, highlighting how weakness outside of the scope of the AI model can undermine AI security controls. Following responsible disclosure, the vulnerability was addressed by OpenAI on September 18, 2026.

"Lockdown Mode was specifically intended to reduce the possibility of data leaving a conversation through potentially malicious outbound requests, yet a weakness in another application feature provided an alternative path around that security boundary," Smadja said.

"The finding raises a broader enterprise security issue: AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them."

The disclosure comes a week after Parameter Labs detailed a way to bypass ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy (CSP) and take over anyone's account simply by sending an attacker-controlled public ChatGPT share link and prompting them to click the HTML preview once. If the HTML block is marked as previewable, it's opened automatically.

"An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," security researcher Mukul Goyal said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt[.]com with access to the victim's authenticated web session."

Earlier this September, Check Point also demonstrated a covert cross-account command channel through which an attacker could use a victim's ChatGPT session to run hidden tasks with the tools, data, and connected apps available to that session, alongside the visible conversation.

"The victim could receive a normal answer to their visible request while the attacker's task was processed separately and its result returned across accounts," Check Point said. "The channel operated through code-execution environments belonging to different ChatGPT accounts."

"The hidden instruction could be delivered through a malicious prompt, a shared ChatGPT conversation, or a custom GPT. Once it was present in the victim's conversation context, an ordinary message could trigger the attacker-controlled task without revealing it in the visible response."

The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of security shortcomings in various AI-driven tools and services over the past few months to trick them into spilling secrets or carrying out unauthorized actions -

An attack called SkillJacking that hijacks dependencies used by skills (repositories, packages, domains, or cloud apps) to compromise every agent installing them.

A set of vulnerabilities in built-in browsers associated with five AI coding assistants, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, and Anthropic Claude Desktop that could be exploited to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof web browser address bars. The issues have been codenamed Embrace, short for EMbedded BRowser - Arbitrary Code Execution, Arbitrary Content Exfiltration, and Arbitrary Context Emulation.

A technique called Repeat-After-Me that targets LangChain LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft AutoGen, Google Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS Strands Agents, and CrewAI and tricks them into running tool calls by means of a "seemingly benign text-repetition request."

A vulnerability called AgentCorruption that could allow an attacker to interact with an exposed AI agent running on AWS Bedrock AgentCore and leverage prompt injection techniques to influence that agent and extract its IMDS credentials, and then use them to access other agents, read private conversations, steal connected-tool credentials, and manipulate agent behavior.

A vulnerability in SpaceXSI Grok and GitHub Copilot CLI called Cryptographic Context Injection that could be exploited to read a developer's local files and send them to an external server from a single web page via an indirect prompt injection, which hides malicious instructions inside AES-encrypted text.

A zero-click vulnerability called SalesBleed that could be exploited to extract sensitive account data out of Salesforce Agentforce by leveraging the Web-to-Lead form to plant an indirect prompt injection payload.

A proof-of-concept (PoC) attack called not-a-mused that allows an unprivileged local attacker (or process) to redirect Meta Muse's dictation traffic and abuse the permissions granted to the AI assistant to perform arbitrary actions.

A zero-click vulnerability called Plugin4Shell that could be exploited to conduct an AI supply chain attack by silently swapping a trusted plugin with a malicious one while bypassing SHA pinning. "The agent checks out the exact commit the marketplace pinned but never verifies it landed there, so an attacker who controls the plugin's repo makes the checkout resolve to malicious code while the pin still looks honored," Air Security said. "The result is zero-click remote code execution across Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI."

An attack called BragJack that can be exploited to hijack the AI agents built into browsers like Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, and Anthropic Claude in Chrome by using an already installed malicious browser extension in conjunction with prompt forcing.

A behavioral effect called sampling drift demonstrates how adding an invisible watermark to a large language model's (LLM) output can unintentionally change how the model behaves, including the tools an AI agent invokes, and likely weaken safety refusals. "Watermarking changes refusal behavior on bare harmful requests, but the effect is more pronounced when the same requests are paired with the prompt-injection technique," Lasso Security said. "On several models, watermarking then makes the model more likely to answer harmful requests that it would otherwise refuse."

A set of attacks that exploit customer support AI agents to compose and send phishing emails, invoke tool calls, and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) protections.

A prompt-crafting technique called PuzzleMask that bypasses quick LLM-based policy checks carried out by a lightweight gatekeeper model by planting the malicious instruction in a specially crafted prose wrapper, after which the payload is processed by a more powerful target model to trigger malicious actions.

A technique called Workflow Identity Hijacking allows an attacker to bypass standard controls by sending normal, benign requests through an unauthenticated entry point, causing the enterprise AI pipeline to process the request and execute the action as designed. "The core failure is that the requester had no authority to make that request," Noma Security said. "When an AI workflow performs downstream actions, it executes using high-privilege service accounts or developer API keys rather than enforcing the permissions of the external user. As a result, AI workflows become unauthenticated proxies for privileged actions and silent data exfiltration."

A zero-click vulnerability class called PleaseFix that could be exploited to hijack AI agents embedded in agentic browsers by placing malicious instructions inside emails, calendar invitations, or web pages, and exploit a technique referred to as intent collision to cause the agent to "act on the attacker's behalf using the user's own identity, permissions and access."

A set of vulnerabilities impacting AI coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that could be exploited to trick them into handing over a victim's secrets, achieving persistent instruction poisoning by modifying the AGENTS.md file, and compromising software releases through prompt injections placed inside untrusted user inputs, like GitHub issues.

"Agents are becoming the default infrastructure across CI/CD, messaging, triage, incident response, and support," Novee Security said. "The more autonomous they get, the more the harness decides what's safe on your behalf, and the more untrusted input reaches real execution."
