Indicators of compromise (IOCs)

Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected approximately 7.3 billion email-based phishing threats from July through September, including a sharp increase to nearly 3 billion in September alone, up 41% from August. Yet the increase did not extend across the techniques that had driven threat actor activity earlier in the year. QR code phishing remained far below its early-year peak, while CAPTCHA-gated phishing reversed several months of decline, driven in part by renewed use of SVG attachments.

Q2 in review

Shifting tactics and other trends ›

Figure 1. Monthly detected email threat volume (January – September 2026)

The quarter also highlighted how sender identity and security exceptions can shape the outcome of detected threats. Microsoft detected approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services. Many were delivered because organization- or user-configured exceptions overrode security protections, even after the messages failed authentication checks and were identified as malicious, showing how overly broad exceptions intended to preserve legitimate workflows can also expose them to impersonation. In Microsoft Teams, attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names rather than explicit help desk identities while continuing to use live interactions for social engineering. Across malicious attachment activity more broadly, credential theft remained the dominant objective in Q3.

Two campaigns observed during the quarter illustrate the range of activity behind these trends. An August campaign targeting legal organizations used personalized salary review documents and QR codes to lead recipients into device code phishing, despite the broader decline in QR code attacks. In September, purchase order and payroll lures used disguised archives to deliver Agent Tesla, malware commonly used to collect credentials and other information. Together, the campaigns show how familiar business requests remained effective lures across distinct attack paths.

TYCOON2FA

Inside the PhaaS platform ›

The effects of the March disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform also remained evident. By July, Microsoft detected approximately 21,000 phishing messages linked to the platform, down 99.8% from 8.9 million in February, the last full month before the operation.

Figure 2. Tycoon2FA-linked phishing email volume (January 2026 – July 2026)

This blog provides a view of email threat activity across Q3 2026, examining shifts in phishing techniques, malicious payloads, business contact impersonation (BCI), and Teams-based threats. We also highlight spoofed business-service sender domains and two campaigns that show how attackers used familiar work requests to make malicious messages appear credible. Together with recommendations, Microsoft Defender detections, and hunting queries, these findings can help defenders assess where existing protections may be weakened and investigate activity across email and collaboration platforms.

Spoofed sender domains

Requests to sign a document, review an invoice, or respond to a survey are routine business communications. Attackers exploit that familiarity by spoofing the sender domains of the legitimate services that deliver them. Rather than relying only on a misleading display name or a lookalike domain, these messages claim the service’s actual domain as their sender identity.

Microsoft detected approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the business-service domains tracked in this analysis during Q3. Activity had remained consistently high since at least May, at roughly 41 million to 46 million messages a month. DocuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of that month’s total. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also saw increases toward the end of the quarter, even as overall spoofing volume remained broadly steady.

Figure 3. Malicious messages spoofing tracked business-service sender domains (May – September 2026)

The more consequential finding was how security exceptions affected these messages after detection. Despite failing email authentication checks and being identified as malicious, many were associated with tenant- or user-level overrides. In September, overrides applied to 63% of messages with a recorded security outcome, with tenant-level overrides accounting for most of them.

The figures do not establish that recipients opened the messages or that accounts were compromised. They do show why exception policies deserve attention alongside detection coverage. An organization may create an exception to avoid interrupting a legitimate business workflow, but an overly broad exception can also weaken protection against messages impersonating that workflow. Familiar branding is not a substitute for an authenticated sender.

QR code phishing attacks

QR code phishing ended Q3 far below the levels seen during its early-year surge. Microsoft detected approximately 12.1 million attacks over the quarter, down 67% from Q2. The decline continued through September despite the broader increase in email threats, leaving monthly QR code volume 86% below its March peak.

Figure 4. Monthly QR code phishing volume (January – September 2026)

Much of the volume reduction came from the attachments that had supported that earlier growth:

PDF attachments remained the most common delivery format in Q3, accounting for 78% of QR code attacks in July and August before dropping to 61% in September. Nonetheless, the volume of PDFs carrying malicious QR codes fell by roughly 65% by the end of the quarter.

DOC/DOCX attachments accounted for 14% of QR code attacks in July and August before rising to 20% in September. Word document delivery volume similarly contracted in Q3, falling 39% between July and September following a sharp drop at the start of the quarter.

Email-embedded QR codes increased from 5% of attacks in July to 12% in September. After dropping to near-zero in Q2, the volume of malicious QR codes embedded in email bodies more than tripled by the end of Q3, although the method remained a smaller delivery category than attachments.

Figure 5. QR code phishing delivery method share by month (January – September 2026)

The distinction between delivery methods matters for inspection coverage, but not for the recipient’s experience: either attachment or embedded formats can move a user from a message on a managed device to a phishing page on a personal phone. The reduction in volume has not changed that underlying challenge.

CAPTCHA-gated phishing tactics

CAPTCHA-gated phishing began to recover while QR code attacks continued to fall. By September, Microsoft detected 3.1 million CAPTCHA-gated attacks, nearly twice the volume seen at July’s low. Activity remained well below its March peak, but the recovery ended several months of sustained decline.

Figure 6. CAPTCHA-gated phishing volume (January – September 2026)

The increase in CAPTCHA-gated phishing attacks was not confined to a single attachment format as delivery methods shifted throughout Q3, though SVG attachments were central to the initial recovery.

SVG attachment volume increased sixfold in August, accounting for almost half of September’s total CAPTCHA-gated phishing attacks. Up from 17% of attacks in July, SVGs represented 65% of CAPTCHA-gated phishing attacks in August, remained elevated at 49% in September, and were the leading delivery method at the quarter end.

Email-embedded URLs accounted for 49% of attacks in July before falling to 19% in August as SVG activity surged. URL-delivered attacks more than doubled in September, reclaiming 30% of attacks.

PDF attachments declined from 22% of attacks in July to 12% in August, remaining at 12% in September.

HTML attachments declined from 9% of attacks in July to 2% in August, then more than tripled in volume in September to account for 6% of attacks.

DOC/DOCX attachments remained comparatively uncommon throughout Q3, representing only 1% of attacks each month.

Figure 7. CAPTCHA-gated phishing distribution method share by month (April – September 2026)

Malicious payloads

The dominant risk from malicious attachments continued to be credential theft, not malware installation. Approximately 94-96% of payload-based attacks during Q3 directed recipients toward a phishing site or presented a fraudulent sign-in page locally. An attachment did not need to install software to put an account at risk.

HTML and PDF attachments remained the two most common malicious payload types during Q3, together accounting for approximately 56–62% of payload-based attacks each month, while the more significant change was the return of SVG files:

Figure 8. Malicious payloads by type

HTML attachments accounted for nearly two-thirds of malicious payloads and remained relatively steady across the quarter. HTML files ranked first in July at 32% of attacks before declining to 26% in August and recovering to 29% in September.

PDF attachments accounted for 27–30% of attacks and were the leading payload type in August and September. Volume remained comparatively stable, declining only 2% between July and September.

SVG attachments increased from 13% of attacks in July to 20% in August, when volume reached 10.1 million—the highest monthly volume in more than a year. Volume then fell 34% in September, although SVGs still represented 13% of attacks and remained roughly 50% higher than the monthly average for the first half of 2026.

DOC/DOCX attachments declined from approximately 5% of attacks in July and August to less than 3% in September, falling 76% below its monthly average volume for the first half of 2026.

ZIP/GZIP attachments declined from 5% of attacks in July to 3% in August before recovering slightly to 4% in September. Raw volume remained 24% below July.

The reduced use of Word documents alongside the renewed use of SVG files left a different mix of attachment threats, though credential theft remained the dominant objective.

Figure 9. Malicious payload file type distribution by month (June – September 2026)

CAPTCHA-gated phishing accounted for only part of the malicious SVG activity. The resurgence was therefore broader than the use of SVG files to deliver that particular technique.

Business contact impersonation

Microsoft defines business contact impersonation (BCI) as a text-based attack targeting enterprise users that impersonates a trusted entity for the purpose of persuading a recipient into initiating a fraudulent financial transaction or sending the attacker sensitive documents.

BCI volume declined throughout Q3, totaling approximately 6.2 million attacks. That was substantially below Q2, although the comparison is influenced by the unusually large spike in April. By September, monthly activity had fallen to its lowest level since at least July 2025.

Figure 10. Monthly BCI attack volume (January – September 2026)

The reduction in overall volume also concealed differences among financial lures. Generic messages continued to dominate initial BCI contact during Q3, but explicit task and financial requests gained share as overall attack volume declined:

Generic outreach messages, such as “Are you at your desk?”, accounted for 82% of attacks in July and August before declining to 79% in September. Raw volume fell 14% across the quarter, reinforcing that operators still overwhelmingly favored establishing contact before introducing a fraudulent request.

Generic task requests represented 8–10% of attacks during Q3, increasing from 9% in July to 10% in September despite a 9% decline in raw volume.

Within the smaller subset of explicit financial requests:

Payroll update requests were the most common financial lure, accounting for 6% of attacks in July and August and 7% in September. Raw volume remained broadly stable at approximately 126,000–130,000 attacks per month.

Invoice payment requests recovered from June’s low. Volume increased 34% in July, 25% in August, and 89% in September, more than tripling between June and September. Their share reached 3% in September, its highest level since March.

Gift card requests remained at 2% of attacks each month, while raw volume declined 9% from July to September.

Figure 11. Initial BCI email content by type (Q3 2026)

The decline in BCI overall did not extend equally to the requests reaching payment and payroll staff.

Microsoft Teams threats

Microsoft observed approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3. Activity peaked in July before declining 31% by September, although September volume remained 38% above the monthly average for the first half of 2026. Teams-based attacks continued to use live interactions across chat, voice, screen sharing, and remote-support tools to facilitate remote access, credential theft, and hands-on-keyboard compromise.

Figure 12. Monthly observed malicious Microsoft Teams calls (January – September 2026)

Attackers increasingly moved away from display names that explicitly announced an IT- or tech-related support role. Ordinary personal-name display names rose from 46% of the observed July sample to 88% in September, while explicit help desk identities fell from 17% to 2%.

Figure 13. Malicious Teams call impersonation comparison (Q3 2026)

This shift does not necessarily mean attackers abandoned IT support stories. A personal name can accompany a claim to work for the help desk, while the underlying account address retains technical or service-related wording. More targeted attempts also used domains resembling the intended victim organization’s domain, emphasizing that the visible name is only one part of the impersonation.

Voice phishing attempts peaked in July and then receded, but September volume remained above the levels observed early in 2026. Calls were concentrated during recipients’ weekday working hours, when a live response was more likely. These attempts included unanswered, rejected, and short-lived calls, partly reflecting Microsoft’s expanding visibility and ongoing efforts to strengthen protective measures against social engineering abuse. Attemps should not be interpreted as successful attacker interactions.

Notable phishing campaigns

The following campaigns were observed during the quarter and highlight notable credential phishing, BCI, and malware delivery activity. For analysis of a separate Teams-based IT-support impersonation campaign observed in August, see Impersonating IT support: Threat actors turn remote session into enterprise-wide access.

Salary review lure delivers personalized QR code attachment for device code credential capture targeting legal organizations

On August 19, 2026, Microsoft Defender Research observed a phishing campaign targeting more than 10,000 users across more than 4,800 organizations, almost exclusively located in the United States. While most phishing attacks typically don’t focus on a single vertical, this campaign targeted the professional services sector, specifically law firms and legal organizations. Messages in this campaign were sent out over a 13-hour period between 13:27 UTC on August 19, 2026, and 2:59 UTC on August 20, 2026.

Figure 14. Intended campaign targets by industry

Emails in this campaign were sent with the subject line “Salary Review” from smtp[@]wekash[.]net via Amazon Simple Email Service. The email body carried no visible text and the sole payload was a Word document attachment named Your-Q3-Compensation-Summary.docx.

Figure 15. Sample of the campaign document attachment

The Word document impersonated the recipient’s own organization, displaying company branding and addressing the recipient by name. The message claimed that the recipient’s compensation had been revised following a Q2 performance review and that updated details were ready for review. A QR code in the document carried an instruction to scan it to access the revised details. This approach moved the phishing URL out of the email body and into an image, bypassing email gateway controls that scan text-based links but do not decode QR code images.

Scanning the QR code would have directed users to an attacker-controlled phishing page impersonating a Microsoft OneDrive sign-in portal hosted on the domain splace[.]co[.]za. The page presented an alphanumeric code and instructed recipients to copy it and proceed to the Microsoft sign-in portal.

Figure 16. Sample phishing landing page

The phishing page used a device code phishing technique, which works by making an authentication request to Microsoft’s device authentication service before the recipient arrived, receiving a user code in return, and embedding that code into the page. When a recipient copied the code and proceeded, the page redirected them to the legitimate Microsoft device authentication portal at microsoft.com/devicelogin, where they entered the code and signed in. Completing that sign in would have transferred a valid session token to the attacker. The token granted persistent access to the recipient’s Microsoft 365 account without ever exposing the password and without re-triggering multifactor authentication (MFA). A countdown timer on the page signaled that each code had a limited validity window, pressing recipients to act quickly.

Spanish-language purchase order and payroll campaign leads to Agent Tesla malware

On September 21, 2026, Microsoft Defender Research observed a phishing campaign targeting more than 56,000 users across more than 8,100 organizations. The campaign primarily targeted users in Spanish-speaking countries, with Colombia accounting for the largest share of intended recipients (15%), followed by the United States (12%), Mexico (12%), Chile (11%), and Spain (8%). Like most large-scale phishing attacks, this campaign did not focus on a single vertical, but instead targeted a broad range of industries, most notably retail and consumer goods (27%), manufacturing and agriculture (19%), and financial services (13%). Messages in this campaign were sent out over an almost nine-hour period between 14:57 UTC and 23:35 UTC on September 21, 2026.

Figure 17. Timeline of campaign message volume

Two lure variations were observed throughout the duration of the campaign: a purchase order theme, which was used in 63% of messages, and a payroll theme, which was used in the remaining 37%. Both variations were sent from the address contacto06[@]carloxmextos[.]org. Sender Policy Framework (SPF), DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) all passed for that domain, so the messages did not depend on simple address forgery. The actor changed the display name to resemble a sales or human resources identity associated with the recipient’s organization. That combination gave the messages technically valid authentication while using the visible sender identity and familiar business context to support the impersonation.

The purchase order lure variation used the reply-style subject “Re: solicitud de cotización”. Its body said, “Buen Dia”, claimed that a purchase order was attached, and asked the recipient to confirm receipt before closing with the lowercase “saludos”. The abrupt wording, inconsistent capitalization, and copied professional signature made the message look like a short continuation of an existing commercial exchange while avoiding details that a recipient could easily challenge.

The attached file, Nuevo orden de compra – 21092026.pdf.uu, was a RAR archive despite its uncommon .uu ending and PDF-like name. Inside it was Nuevo orden de compra – 21092026.pdf.js, a JavaScript downloader whose second extension exposed the executable script type only after extraction. If run, the script fetched a file named Lincoln.ps1 from a campaign-controlled object in Firebase Storage, and that PowerShell payload led to Agent Tesla malware. The nested archive and misleading extensions separated the visible business document theme from the code that executed, while the cloud-hosted download gave the actor a remotely accessible staging point.

Figure 18. Redacted rendering of the purchase order lure email

The payroll-themed lure used the subject “Nomina 21.09.2026”. It addressed the recipient by name, said the September 21 payroll list was attached, and signed off as a human resources manager. The date-specific payroll pretext created an immediate work-related reason to open the file, while the personalized greeting made a bulk message appear locally relevant.

The payroll lure’s attachment, Nomina 21.09.2026.xml.001, was also a RAR archive. Extraction produced Nomina 21.09.2026.xml.exe, an Agent Tesla executable disguised with an XML-themed double extension. Unlike the purchase order delivery chain, this branch did not require a separate downloader in the supplied evidence, but both paths used the same sender infrastructure, attachment camouflage, date, and malware family. Agent Tesla is commonly used to collect credentials and other information from an infected host, so the shared final payload suggested that credential and information theft were the campaign’s likely objective.

Figure 19. Redacted rendering of the payroll lure email

Defending against email and collaboration threats

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

Microsoft helps organizations reduce the risk of phishing and social engineering in Teams through user awareness and layered, built-in protections. Users should exercise caution with external connection requests and messages, including verifying a sender’s identity and requests before acting on them. Administrators can also block external Teams users and specify which users in their organization are permitted to chat or meet with people outside the enterprise. These flexible controls help organizations manage risk for employees in sensitive roles and departments. Teams will also be introducing AI-powered phishing detection that uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users. Together, these measures help organizations collaborate more securely in Teams.

Review the recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to ensure your organization has established essential defenses and knows how to monitor and respond to threat activity.

Invest in user awareness training and phishing simulations. Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender for Office 365, which also includes simulating phishing messages in Microsoft Teams, is one approach to running realistic attack scenarios in your organization.

Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.

Responders can also manually check for and purge unwanted emails containing URLs and/or Subject fields that are similar, but not identical, to those of known bad messages. Investigate malicious email that was delivered in Microsoft 365 and use Threat Explorer to find and delete phishing emails.

Turn on Safe Links and Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.

Enable network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support Microsoft Defender SmartScreen, which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.

Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. Refer to this article for the different authentication methods and features.

Conditional access policies can also be scoped to strengthen privileged accounts with phishing-resistant MFA.

Configure automatic attack disruption in Microsoft Defender XDR. Automatic attack disruption is designed to contain attacks in progress, limit the impact on an organization’s assets, and provide more time for security teams to remediate the attack fully.

Title: India Warns of New AI-Driven Cyber-Attacks Targeting Financial and Crypto Businesses
Context: Financial companies are being targeted in successive attacks by a newly identified cyber threat actor known as ‘Crafty Falcon’ using AI and agentic AI tools, including some...
Full Text:
Financial companies are being targeted in successive attacks by a newly identified cyber threat actor known as ‘Crafty Falcon’ using AI and agentic AI tools, including some previously attributed to Chinese hacking groups.

In a new security advisory published on November 4, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned that non-banking financial companies, including digital lending platforms, fintech firms, payment aggregators, payment services providers and cryptocurrency exchanges, have reported falling victim to repeated cyber-attacks.

Some of them received a restricted-distribution advisory in early October warning them of cyber threat actors exploiting application programmable interfaces (APIs) traditionally used for payment and disbursement transactions to make unauthorized transfers.

Despite undertaking remediation after receiving this previous warning, these financial organizations were attacked again, with CERT-In noting “incomplete remediation” on their part.

Attacks were typically observed during holiday periods, on weekends and “other low-monitoring windows” to delay detection and response, CERT-In added.

Crafty Falcon’s Attack Lifecycle

According to CERT-In’s Finance branch (CERT-Fin), Crafty Falcon is a previously undocumented threat actor that uses a range of AI and agentic AI penetration testing tools to breach the systems of its victims.

Typically, Crafty Falcon gains initial access through internet-exposed non-production environments, such as user acceptance testing (UAT), staging and testing environments.

Once inside, the threat actor moves from non-production environments into production systems by exploiting shared credentials, authentication tokens or network paths between the environments.

The actor reverse-engineers the organization's application codebases to develop tailored exploits. They then use altered or modified application packages to initiate unauthorized API calls, bypassing security controls that assume only the legitimate client application will communicate with the APIs.

The actor also bypasses IP allow-listing restrictions by routing traffic through whitelisted third-party fetcher IP pools, such as content-acceleration services and app-store review fetchers. These shared services can be instructed by any internet user to fetch arbitrary URLs, allowing the actor to originate traffic from IP addresses already trusted by the organization.

Another Crafty Falcon characteristic move is to target the victim’s cloud infrastructure, including compute, serverless and management services. Cloud management services, such as AWS Systems Manager and Lambda, are abused to execute commands and deploy malicious files, allowing malicious activity to blend into legitimate cloud management operations.

Before executing large-value transfers, the actor performs micro-value test transactions, such as transactions of Rs. 1, to validate that unauthorized fund flows are possible. They exploit or abuse merchant settlement APIs belonging to payment aggregators to move funds.

The actor targets cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual digital asset service providers, stealing wallet keys and siphoning funds from cryptocurrency wallets.

CERT-In noted that Crafty Flacon also exploits newly published vulnerabilities as soon as they become publicly available. These include file-upload and deserialization exploit chains, leading to the deployment of web shells in PHP and Node.js applications.

Throughout these activities, Crafty Falcon creates large numbers of custom, tailored scripts on the fly. Functionally identical variants are refined in rapid succession, a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development.

Notably, CERT-In and CERT-Fin observed the use – and combination – of several AI-powered offensive security tools against affected entities. These include:

Penetration testing tool ARTEX, based on PentAGI, an autonomous, multi-agent framework that can be plugged to large language models (LLMs)

Penetration testing framework CyberStrikeAI

Attack search engine Cairn

These tools allow attackers to “execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession and adapt their payloads based on target responses,” CERT-IN indicated.

While these tools are publicly available and could be used by many threat actors, most previous malicious campaigns where they were deployed were linked to China-based actors.

Read now: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants

CERT-In Provides Crafty Falcon Threat Mitigation Recommendations

In its latest advisory, CERT-In provided a long list of recommended security measures organizations can take to mitigate the threat. These include:

Maintaining heightened 24/7 security monitoring, increased staffing and lower alert thresholds during holidays, weekends and periods of reduced monitoring

Centralizing real-time monitoring of cloud audit logs and alert on high-risk events, including remote command execution, serverless function code updates and creation of roles, users or access keys

Restricting cloud management and serverless execution to approved principals and accounts

Implementing instance metadata service protections, least-privilege roles, restrictions on wildcard egress and default-deny internet egress for serverless functions

Separating UAT, staging and testing environments from production, ensuring no shared credentials, tokens, API keys, databases or direct network paths

Making application deployment directories read-only for application runtime users and implement file-integrity monitoring to detect web shells

Treating client applications and packages as untrusted and enforcing server-side transaction validation, API request signing using nonces and timestamps, application attestation and certificate pinning

Establish rapid patching SLAs for Internet-facing applications, prioritizing file-upload and deserialization vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js. Use WAF virtual patching as an interim measure

Extending real-time transaction monitoring to identify small-value test transactions to new beneficiaries followed by high-value transfers. Treat these as strong indicators of potentially unauthorized fund transfers and hold or review such transactions

Storing cryptocurrency wallet keys in hardware security modules or cold custody

Prohibiting unauthorized security and attack tools, including publicly available AI-driven offensive frameworks, on corporate infrastructure

Monitoring and governing LLM API usage and keys. LLM API traffic originating from servers or non-development hosts may indicate an attack infrastructure or planted operator console

Adjusting SIEM correlation to identify machine-speed, multi-technique attacks, parallel attack threads, adaptive payload changes and continuous activity outside business hours. Implement automated SOAR-based containment

Adopting zero-trust principles, micro-segmentation, identity-based access controls for every user and service and inspection of east-west traffic

The agency also urged organizations to report any suspicious activity that could be related to Crafty Falcon to incident@cert-in.org.in with all relevant logs and to contact the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C) and its Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS).

Title: UNM Health Shuts Clinics and Diverts Patients During Security Incident
Context: The hospital also warned people to watch out for phishing and fraud attempts by attackers exploiting the incident
Full Text:
A cybersecurity incident forced UNM Health to divert ambulances, cancel appointments, and pause care while it contained the threat.

On Monday, October 26, the University of New Mexico Health System (UNM Health) faced the kind of security incident that healthcare leaders dread: one serious enough to change how patients could receive emergency care.

A major hospital network in New Mexico worked urgently on Monday to fix a cybersecurity problem. The issue forced it to send ambulances to other hospitals and left the state without a hospital emergency department able to treat the most serious injuries.

UNM Health operates New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center. These centers treat the most serious and complex injuries. Even a temporary closure can put extra pressure on other hospitals.

UNM Health runs New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center. That matters because a Level 1 center handles the most complex injuries, and losing even temporary access to it puts pressure on every nearby hospital.

The organization told patients not to come to its main Albuquerque hospital and canceled appointments across more than 30 clinics.

“The University of New Mexico Health System is experiencing a cybersecurity issue at this time. UNM Health officials are actively working to resolve this issue. Currently, all ambulance traffic is being diverted to other hospitals and all appointments at all clinics today have been cancelled. UNM Health patients should not show up to UNM Health facilities on October 26. Emergencies should be handled by 911 and non-emergencies should be delayed until further notice.” reads the update published by the organization on October 26, 2026. “The cybersecurity threat is affecting the entire University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center. “

UNM said its IT security teams identified the threat around 11 a.m. and began containment work. They later said the event affected some end-user devices but did not reach core systems or servers.

Leadership activated an Emergency Operations Center, brought in outside support, and notified state and federal law enforcement. That is the right sequence: isolate first, investigate second, communicate continuously.

From 12:30 to 2:30 p.m., UN Health temporarily stopped accepting new patients while teams protected the network. “System outages also required the suspension of outpatient surgeries and appointments for the remainder of the day.”

This was not an abstract IT problem. Patients arrived for care and were told to reschedule. Staff had to explain, repeatedly, why a hospital visit could not proceed as planned.

UNM also canceled classes at its Health Sciences Center and sent nonessential employees home. Medical, nursing, pharmacy, and population health students lost a day of instruction because the institution had to protect its network.

Other providers stepped in. Presbyterian Healthcare Services and Lovelace Health System coordinated with UNM and took additional patients, which is exactly what a functioning regional healthcare system should do.

UNM Health began restoring its systems on Monday afternoon. By the following day, hospitals, ambulance services and clinics were back to normal.

The incident is still under criminal investigation. Employees reported messages claiming that patient, student and staff data had been stolen, but UNM has not confirmed this. The hospital also warned people to watch out for phishing and fraud attempts by attackers exploiting the incident.

Title: Is Your Exposure Management Platform Leaving You Exposed? Five Tests to Find Out
Context: Threat activity: Whether attackers are targeting the vulnerability or technology
Full Text:
A critical finding can move through several security tools and still leave the organization exposed.

The vulnerability has a severity score, and a ticket has reached the queue. Progress then depends on information the finding may lack: who owns the system, whether attackers can reach it, what protection exists, and how a change could affect the business.

Each missing detail creates another investigation, another handoff, and another delay.

An exposure management platform should connect discovery with a clear priority, an appropriate response, and evidence that protection has improved.

Continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) connects this work through scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation, and mobilization. These five tests establish whether a platform can support that process across infrastructure, identities, sensitive data, and external threats.

Security teams often have several records of the same asset. A cloud platform identifies an instance, an endpoint tool records its hostname, and an inventory lists an owner who has changed roles.

Cyber asset attack surface management (CAASM) connects those records, helping reveal stale information, missing ownership, and protection gaps.

The resulting view needs enough detail to support action: the asset’s owner, business purpose, assessment history, and security coverage. A system with no reported vulnerabilities should be distinguishable from one never assessed.

Disagreements between sources also need to remain visible. If an endpoint tool reports an active server while the inventory marks it retired, source records and update times help teams resolve the conflict.

Figure 1. CAASM connects source records with asset ownership, security coverage, and exposure context.

External discovery adds another perspective. External attack surface management (EASM) helps uncover what assets make accessible from the outside, including shadow IT, forgotten subdomains, and exposed services that internal tools never see.

EASM and CAASM work best together: CAASM maps what you know you own, while EASM validates that picture from the attacker’s point of view and surfaces what’s missing. Every unmanaged asset EASM finds can be fed back into CAASM, closing coverage gaps and giving each asset an owner. EASM also covers brand exposure, extending discovery to phishing sites, fraudulent profiles, and brand impersonation, so the same external view that finds your unknown assets also finds the lookalikes attackers build to target your customers and employees.

Read CAASM Was Never Meant to Stand Alone to see how asset intelligence supports the decisions and actions that follow discovery.

2. Explain Which Exposures Require Action First

Prioritization depends on understanding what an exposure actually puts at risk. A customer-facing application may carry the same severity score as an isolated development system while presenting very different business risk.

Prioritization should connect:

Reachability and exploitability: Whether attackers have a usable path to exploit the weakness.

Threat activity: Whether attackers are targeting the vulnerability or technology.

Business impact: What the system supports and what compromise could affect.

Existing protection: Whether relevant controls cover the system and are enforced.

Those conditions change. New exploitation activity may accelerate a response, while a disabled protection may invalidate an earlier assessment.

External threats need similarly specific reasoning. A fraudulent support account approaching customers may require rapid disruption; an abandoned company profile may first need ownership review.

See what the 2026 Exposure Gap Report reveals about prioritization and remediation performance.

3. Validate the Exposure and the Proposed Response

A clear priority can still stall when the system owner lacks confidence in the proposed change.

Validation needs to establish what the exposure allows and how the response could affect operations.

Identifying vulnerable software, confirming reachability, and demonstrating exploitability establish different things. A platform should distinguish observed evidence from analysis and untested assumptions. Attack-path relationships also need supporting evidence and clear limitations.

The proposed response requires separate assessment. A patch may depend on application testing and a maintenance window. An intrusion prevention system protection may require observation in Detect mode before enforcement.

Evidence should address the action’s scope, dependencies, false positives, performance impact, and recovery options. Following a proposed change through this assessment reveals what the platform establishes and what teams must investigate themselves.

4. Carry Safe Remediation Through Existing Workflows

Knowing what to fix first is great, but only if the fix happens quickly. The permanent patch often waits on testing, approval, and a maintenance window, and the exposure stays open the whole time. That’s true whether the weakness is on an internet-facing server or a phishing site targeting your customers.

Speed comes from confidence. Teams hesitate when they can’t say what an action will touch. When the platform already knows the asset, its owner, the active threat, and the controls in place, that hesitation disappears. Many Check Point Exposure Management customers remediate safely within one hour, because the context is complete and the safety checks are built in.

To test this, take one real finding and follow it from priority to protection:

Owner: Is the right person assigned automatically?

Safety: Is the action validated before it runs, including its impact and a way back?

Execution: Does it run through the controls you already have, whether a virtual patch, a configuration change, or a takedown?

Confirmation: Is the result verified, with the permanent fix still tracked?

Interim protection buys time, but it shouldn’t replace the long term fix.

Figure 2. Safe remediation connects observation, validation, action, and confirmation.

Speed holds up at scale. Between January 1 and October 26, 2026, an airline group completed more than 1,500 takedowns of profiles impersonating its airlines and support teams, combining analyst review with automated remediation.

And when an action fails, the exposure should stay visible with a clear next step.

Read Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production to see how validation, execution, and confirmation work together.

5. Show What Changed and What Remains

A completed action needs evidence of the resulting state.

A patch may miss unavailable systems. A policy update may exclude an intended asset. A takedown request may be accepted before the account disappears.

Verification should establish whether the vulnerability remains, protection is enforced, or malicious content has been removed. Monitoring should identify recurrence.

Reporting must distinguish removed vulnerabilities, interim mitigations, completed takedowns, and accepted risk. Each leaves different responsibilities outstanding.

Mean time to remediate (MTTR) requires agreed starting points, completion criteria, and treatment of temporary protection.

Tracking assignment, approval, execution, and verification separately reveals delays.

Recurring findings, failed actions, and aging mitigations can expose operational problems another scan will not resolve.

In this article

Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) sends viewing data from your smart TV to third parties.

Vizio and Samsung TVs both appeared to send this data even when researchers opted out of ACR.

Only four out of eight smart TVs appeared to completely honor ACR opt-out.

If you thought that opting out of surveillance on your smart TV would give you your privacy back, think again.

A study by researchers at Northeastern University found that some smart TVs still seem to send information about what you’re watching to third parties, even after you pressed the opt-out button.

The study, ‘Watching the watchers‘, tested twelve smart TVs from ten manufacturers to find out how well they respected opt-outs from automatic content recognition (ACR). ACR is a TV feature that captures audio and/or video content from smart TVs and uploads it to a third party (typically the TV manufacturer).

The third party converts this content into digital fingerprints to understand what you’re watching, and can then use it to send targeted advertising or allow others to do the same. It’s on most if not all smart TVs, and 82% of US households had a smart TV as of last year.

The test took in the eight operating systems behind roughly 95% of US smart TVs, and ran ten viewing scenarios on each of them. These ranged from viewing antenna TV through to viewing via screen mirroring from another device. The researchers tested viewing the first-party streaming services provided free with the manufacturers’ operating systems, along with sessions using third-party streaming apps. And they tested sessions where the TV was connected to another device via its HDMI port.

The study ran all of its tests both with ACR left on, and with the opt-out setting selected. The whole test involved over 5,000 automated sessions.

Vizio continued to send 100% of what looked like traffic when viewing its first-party streaming services and antenna-based TV services, even after people had opted out, the study said. It also sent the same amount of traffic when idle. However it didn’t send any ACR traffic for third-party streaming data, according to the report.

Samsung did appear to leak some traffic from third-party streaming services after the researchers opted out of its ACR function. They tested 30 runs of Samsung’s built-in streaming service after opting out of ACR, and found that it still showed traffic “consistent with ACR”.

After opt-out, the Samsung TV’s Tizen OS seemed to send ACR-related traffic about Netflix in 7% of runs, YouTube in 10% of runs, and Tubi TV in 20%. It sent ACR 60% of the time from HDMI sessions. Like the Vizio TV, it also sent ACR traffic for all of its first-party streaming sessions.

Late last month, a researcher reverse-engineered a Samsung Smart TV and cast doubt on whether disabling ACR worked on the device.

There was good news, though. Four smart TV operating systems went completely silent after the researchers turned off ACR: LG’s WebOS, Sony’s Google TV OS, Amazon’s FireTV OS, and Supersonic’s VIDAA OS.

Encryption is a research challenge

Vizio agreed to pay $2.2 million in a 2017 FTC settlement over charges that it collected viewing histories on eleven million smart TVs without user consent. At the time, it agreed to allow people to opt out of ACR.

The Vizio TV that the researchers tested sent traffic to Kinesis, an Amazon-run data ingestion service that the manufacturer uses to analyze data from its smart TVs. The researchers noticed no dip in traffic to this domain when they opted out of ACR on a Vizio TV. They said:

“The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint. However, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement.”

That’s a challenge to this research because most smart TVs encrypt their ACR traffic, including Samsung. So the researchers had to infer that this was ACR traffic based on signals such as where it was being sent, along with timing, volume, and protocol details.

One exception was Supersonic’s VIDAA OS, which sent ACR data to servers unencrypted. The servers responded unencrypted with a genre for what they recognized. Anyone watching the network could see it all, they warned. And because the servers didn’t require a login at the time of the test, over 57 million ACR detection results from other people’s TVs were accessible.

Vizio’s first-party streaming service WatchFree+ also dropped unencrypted titles of any show or channel being watched into online communications with the free TV service provider. There’s no way to turn that off, the researchers warned.

Walmart acquired Vizio for $2.3 billion in 2024, partly to help “advertisers to meaningfully connect with customers at scale and boost product discovery”.

The retailer also runs Walmart Connect, a retail media business that uses its customers’ data to help other businesses target them with ads.

Walmart was particularly interested in Vizio’s advertising business it, said at the time:

“Pairing it with Walmart Connect will be impactful and allow us to invest in our business even further on behalf of our customers.”

What smart TV owners can do

What can you do to protect yourself from a smart TV that might be sending your viewing data elsewhere? The researchers have some suggestions:

WebOS (LG), Fire TV OS, Google TV on Sony, and VIDAA OS on Supersonic all appeared to honor ACR opt-out, so selecting it on these TVs should be safe.

Disconnect the TV from the internet and use an external streaming device. That way the TV can’t send back data, even if it picks it up from the HDMI connection.

Use a blocklist. This takes a little more technical knowledge. If you run an internet router that can accept blocklists, then you can add a list of known ACR endpoints that will stop your TV’s traffic reaching them. The researchers provide one here.

Title: New York's Queens Public Library battles ransomware crims: Wi-Fi, checkouts, and website go dark
Context: New York City's Queens Public Library (QPL) is battling a ransomware attack, it confirmed on Wednesday evening via social media and to patrons directly
Full Text: New York City's Queens Public Library (QPL) is battling a ransomware attack, it confirmed on Wednesday evening via social media and to patrons directly. The disruption has downed QPL's website, on-site computers, check-out and return machines, its public Wi-Fi, mobile app, and its digital media services. Renewals are also unavailable, although library users are not charged fines for returning materials late. (Since 2021, In October 2021, QPL, Brooklyn Public Library, and New York Public Library - in an effort to help lower income users from being put off borrowing - permanently killed daily late fines on books and circulating materials.) Each of the library system's 66 locations remains open, including the central library in the Jamaica neighborhood in Queens, but QPL warned: "it will take some time before the library's network and systems are restored." QPL said "certain virtual and in-person programs may be impacted," advising visitors to check availability with their local branch via phone, and check the library's social media channels for official updates. "Our IT department is working to resolve the issue, and we will keep you informed,” it said in the statement. It added: "We apologize for any inconvenience and appreciate your patience." No established ransomware group has yet claimed responsibility for the disruption, although attacks on publicly funded institutions rarely lead to lucrative payouts. The British Library's infamous ransomware attack in 2023 at the hands of Rhysida saw the organization refuse to pay the criminals' 20 Bitcoin ransom demand, opting instead to drain its cash reserves and fork out millions for an IT rebuild. Although the library's response to the attack drew widespread praise, few institutions of its kind are in a financial position to follow its lead. Other libraries might not be willing or able to commit to a recovery period as lengthy as that of the British Library. In its 2025/26 annual report, published in July, the institution said its recovery is still incomplete, and work to fully restore customers' ability to purchase electronic resources, such as journals and research databases, and reopen access to electronic legal deposit content is ongoing. This is likely to be completed by the end of 2026, the British Library added. ®

Title: Chinese Nation-State Threat Activity Falls Sharply in Q2 and Q3 2026
Context: The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state...
Full Text:
Despite the sharp fall in China-aligned detections, observed PRC cyber activity remained “substantially higher” than nation-state cyber activity from Russia and Iran during the period, the researchers noted.

“The decline may reflect changes in targeting, infrastructure or detection visibility rather than a reduction in activity. The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state actors,” they wrote.

A number of Chinese nation-state espionage campaigns have gone undetected for long periods in recent years. For example, in 2025, the Chinese-nexus actor Weaver Ant was found to have infiltrated the network of an Asian telecommunications service provider and remained undetected for more than four years.

Such cases highlight that there may be significant ongoing Chinese nation-state activity occurring that has not yet been detected.

US and Turkey Primary Targets for Nation-State Actors

The Trellix report, published on November 4, found that nation-state targeting primarily focused on two countries, the US (38%) and Turkey (37.1%), which collectively represented over three-quarters of all detections from April to September.

The researchers noted that the US represents a valuable target due its status as the world’s largest economy and the concentration of high-value technology, defense and government infrastructure. Meanwhile, Turkey also represents a key strategic target given its location at the intersection of Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia, as well as its NATO membership.

The third most targeted country by nation-state actors was Germany, representing 4.4% of such activity.

Title: Norway's aid agency pwned and all users' data is stolen
Context: " The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations
Full Text: Norway's national aid agency, Norad, has confirmed that cyber criminals broke into its systems, stealing information about each and every registered user of its grant portal. Norad, which coordinates Norway's assistance for foreign development, said that 20,614 registered individuals had their names and email addresses swiped, and information from at least three organizations' applications was "misdirected." The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations. In addition, the grant applications for at least three organizations are confirmed to be involved, though Norad said it may discover more as its investigation continues. Torger Kjeldstad, director of digitalization at Norad, said "the attack is complex," and confirmed the agency has initiated a crisis team to manage it. "We know a lot about what has happened, but to ensure that we have a complete overview of the attack, we are working to engage external experts in cybersecurity," he said. "They will give us a detailed description of what information those who attacked the solution have gained access to." Kjeldstad added that "it should be safe" to continue using Norad's services while it continues to probe what happened, and who was behind it. Norad did not reveal many details about how the attack unfolded, other than saying that 27 accounts were compromised and were then used to gain access to the portal and the data in question. The agency said the intrusion was detected on October 30, but did not offer any indication as to how long the attackers retained access to the grant portal. It also refused to rule out that names of applicants in "conflict areas and authoritarian states" may have been included in the stolen data – it is not known if recipients would have also been registered users – and said it is approaching the matter "very seriously." The grant portal, managed by Norad, which itself is part of Norway's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is responsible for handling applications from organizations across the world. Recent case studies include support for independent, investigative journalism in Moldova, a country which routinely battles Russian propaganda and election interference, and backing for Ukrainian children and prisoners of war. The issues Norad and the Norwegian government support, however, are wide-ranging – from access to healthcare for transgender people worldwide and Kenyan incubators for innovative transport solutions, to delivering aid to war-torn Gaza. ®

Title: New Lindnor Backdoor and Glut of Security Killers Used in Ransomware Attack on U.S. Org
Context: The first indicator of the intrusion was the detection of the new Lindnor backdoor, which was found on two machines that were also the only two Microsoft SQL Servers among those...
Full Text:
Key findings

Attackers using the Anubis ransomware targeted a U.S. organization in October 2026 using a new custom backdoor that Symantec has called Backdoor.Lindnor.

The backdoor masqueraded as a Chrome component and as a VMware file, and was found on two Microsoft SQL Server machines.

Within roughly an hour, the attackers dropped at least 13 executables to help terminate security services, along with five publicly known vulnerable drivers.

The attackers also installed the legitimate remote access tool AnyDesk and a separate tool to run it in Safe Mode, likely to maintain access when security software was not fully running.

The file encryption payload was blocked from execution, and there’s no evidence that any files were encrypted.

Anubis has claimed approximately 96 victims in the past 12 months, and 52% of those victims are in the U.S.

Overview

Attackers using the Anubis ransomware, which is developed by a group Symantec tracks as Hawkmoth, deployed a previously undocumented custom backdoor and an unusually large number of security software-disabling tools in an October 2026 attack on an organization in the U.S.

Hawkmoth runs a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that emerged in December 2024 as a rebrand of the Sphinx ransomware. Its payload appears to be largely unchanged from the Sphinx version, with only the branding updated. As Hawkmoth operates an affiliate program, Anubis attacks may be carried out by different groups of affiliates. Attackers using it seem to be particularly tenacious. In a July 2026 Anubis attack documented by Symantec, we noted that the threat actor used four different exfiltration tools (Megasync, WinSCP, Filezilla, S3browser) to steal data from the affected network and that it was unusual to see that many of the same type of tool deployed in a single attack.

The group has claimed approximately 96 victims in the past 12 months, and the majority of them (52%) are located in the U.S., which aligns with previous targeting patterns by the group.

We did not identify how the attackers gained initial access. The first indicator of the intrusion was the detection of the new Lindnor backdoor, which was found on two machines that were also the only two Microsoft SQL Servers among those affected.

Tooling and tradecraft

Custom backdoor

The backdoor, called Backdoor.Lindnor, was installed with the filename healthcontroller64.exe in a folder made to resemble a Chrome component unpacker directory on one machine, and as svchelper.exe in a VMware folder on the other. In both cases, the backdoor appears to have run as a service.

The backdoor sent the process ID, operating system version, its own file path, computer name, user name, domain and logon server to a command-and-control (C&C) server. It was configured with a primary C&C server and a fallback, which are both accessed via port 443.

The presence of this backdoor is notable as custom backdoors remain relatively uncommon in ransomware attacks. Ransomware attackers generally rely on publicly available, dual-use and living-off-the-land tools to carry out the majority of pre-ransomware activity in their attacks. This backdoor was also spotted on the networks of two other unrelated organizations, though in those cases no ransomware activity was identified on the networks.

Security evasion tools

A notable aspect of this attack was that the threat actors dropped at least 13 executables in quick succession, for the purpose of terminating security products. They clearly favored the Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) approach, as demonstrated by their dropping of five signed but vulnerable drivers for the purpose of abusing them to gain kernel-level access. Two of the executables, gbbsym.exe and symgooq.exe, masqueraded as Symantec software. Both accepted the switch (-l) to list kernel callbacks through a loaded vulnerable driver and a second switch (-d) to list and remove them. The observed command lines show the second switch (-d) was used. Eleven of the 13 executables appear to have been previously unpublished. The vulnerable drivers were all publicly known.

All the dropped executables were blocked except huntreagent.exe and s1.exe. These files were not available for analysis so their exact purpose is unknown, but it is possible they may have been used to run one or more of the vulnerable drivers. Both tools are the same file size but with different file hashes, which suggests they may be two builds of the same tool. The pattern of using so many different tools is consistent with attackers trying one tool after another until they find something that works.

The attackers’ heavy reliance on BYOVD serves to highlight how the technique has become a standard part of the ransomware playbook, a trend we discussed in-depth in our June 2026 whitepaper: Lights Out: Defense Evasion in the Age of BYOVD.

BYOVD is commonly used to gain kernel-level access because it is effective and relies on using legitimate, signed files, the presence of which are unlikely to raise red flags. Once operating in the kernel, attackers can use them to help stop security software and prevent their activities from being detected. There are hundreds of known vulnerable drivers already in circulation and newly discovered ones are shared openly on a regular basis. Ready-made BYOVD tooling is now routinely bundled into RaaS offerings alongside the payloads themselves, making it a standard way to disable security software during ransomware attacks.

Remote access and Safe Mode

The attackers also installed the legitimate remote access tool AnyDesk, created a new local user account and added it to a local group. AnyDesk is frequently used by ransomware attackers for remote access. However, in this attack, the threat actors also ran a tool, safemode.exe, that configures AnyDesk to keep working when Windows boots into Safe Mode. They ran a registry command that registered AnyDesk as a service permitted to run in Safe Mode with Networking.

"CSIDL_SYSTEM\reg.exe" add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SafeBoot\Network\AnyDesk /ve /t REG_SZ /d Service /f

Security software generally does not fully operate in Safe Mode, which gives attackers a window to use the vulnerable drivers and switch off protections. This isn’t a new technique but it is not commonly seen.

Ransomware payload

The Anubis encryption payload was named iservice.exe. If successful, it appends the extension .anubis to encrypted files and drops ransom notes named restore files.txt and restore files.html. The note tells the victim that data was downloaded from the network and that it will be published if negotiations fail. The ransomware also has an optional wiper mode that wipes file contents, leaving files completely empty. In this attack, the payload was blocked, preventing the attackers from executing the encryption phase across the victim network.

Significance

Attackers using the Anubis ransomware appear to focus their attacks on the U.S., and this intrusion fits with established patterns of behavior by the group. This targeting isn’t surprising given that ransomware attackers generally “follow the money” and a majority of large enterprises have a presence in the U.S.

While the overall modus operandi of the attackers is familiar, the presence of a custom backdoor and usage of large numbers of security-disabling tools makes this attack stand out from typical ransomware intrusions. Few ransomware operators build their own backdoors, and the volume of security-disabling tools used within a single hour of activity is unusual.

This suggests that the attackers were prepared for the prospect of security software getting in their way, so they arrived with a large toolbox and a second remote access route configured for Safe Mode operation to help them gain an advantage. Despite all this preparation, the attack appears to have largely failed at the last hurdle because the encryption modules were successfully blocked from execution.

Protection

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.
