Title: The Keys Are in the Browser: Secret Exposure Across AI-Built Websites
Context: Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit
Full Text:
Cyble scanned 1.3M+ newly registered domains and found AI-built sites leaking live secrets to the browser: OpenAI keys, Stripe keys, and database tokens.

Spinning up a website no longer takes a developer. A prompt to an AI app-builder returns a working, styled, deployable site in minutes, and when one template works, the same operator clones it across a dozen domains before launch. That is also how secrets end up in plain sight.

Over a month, Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) scanned more than 1.3 million newly registered domains, identified the ones built by AI app-builders, and read their public front-end code for exposed credentials. We built our own classifiers to spot AI-generated websites as they are registered, paired with a scanner that pulls exposed keys and credentials straight from their public code. On 35 of the 22,306 AI-built sites we identified, a genuinely private secret was sitting in the browser: live OpenAI keys, Stripe secret keys, backend database tokens, and, in several cases, a single credential cloned across a whole fleet of domains.

Thirty-five is a small number, since counting every key-shaped string on an AI-built site is easy and misleading, as most are meant to be in the browser; a single reCAPTCHA key appeared on thousands of sites. We kept only the credentials that are never supposed to leave a server. Those are the findings below.

This report walks through the two leak patterns we observed, what appears exposed, what an attacker can do with these keys, and how to shut down the exposure.

AI-built Websites are leaking the keys that power them

An AI-built site generates its content with a Large Language Model (LLM), and the key to that model often ships in the page the visitor downloads. That is the plainest pattern we found, and the most on-the-nose.

Five AI-built sites carried live OpenAI API keys in their client-side code, sixteen distinct keys across them, and four of the five are confirmed AI-generated. One AI-writing site stands out on its own: it shipped twelve different OpenAI keys, one per content category, as plain values in its bundle. Figure 1 shows a single entry, with the key masked.

Figure 1 – Live OpenAI keys embedded as plain values in an AI-writing site’s JavaScript (key masked by CRIL).

A handful of sites, but each key is sensitive to exposure. An OpenAI secret key is a billing credential: anyone who reads the page can spend the owner’s balance, exhaust the rate limit, or run the bill up until someone notices and revokes it. Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit.

Clone-and-leak: one secret across a whole fleet

An AI builder makes the hundredth site as cheap as the first, so an operator clones a working template across many domains, and whatever secret sat in the template now sits on every copy. We saw this in two shapes.

A Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet. Thirteen near-identical domains, each a short word (ask, call, chat, get, hello, hey, hi, its, join, let, meet, my, see), glued to one brand, all served the same client bundle, and all embedded the same live Slack incoming-webhook URL. Figure 2 shows the URL in the shipped bundle, masked.

Figure 2 – One Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet, in each site’s shipped bundle (secret and workspace IDs masked).

Anyone who can read the page can post messages to the operator’s Slack workspace via that webhook. That works for spam, for phishing aimed at the operator’s own staff, or for flooding a channel.

One Stripe secret key across four domains and two brands. A single Stripe secret key appeared on four domains under two separate brand names. The same sk_live_ value across all four points to one operator, or one shared Stripe account, behind every site. Figure 3 shows the assignment.

Figure 3 – The same live Stripe secret key reused across four domains under two brands.

A Stripe secret key provides full API access to the account, including the ability to create charges, issue refunds, and read customer and payout records. That one key exposes the operator’s whole payment account on every domain in the fleet.

The 13-domain Slack fleet runs on Bubble, a no-code and AI app builder, as confirmed by Bubble’s x-bubble-perf response header and client markers. Bubble serves each app from a dynamic.js bundle, and any value a developer places in a client-accessible field ships inside that bundle in plain text. The Stripe cluster runs on a Next.js build instead, which shows that the pattern spans builders rather than tracing to a single platform.

What else is exposed

Four AI-built sites exposed a Supabase service role JSON Web Token (JWT) on their front ends. A service-role token bypasses row-level security and grants full read and write to the project database. In terms of impact, it sits at the top of the set because it opens the entire backend rather than a single service.

Most of the remaining secret-looking strings on AI-built sites carry no/minimal exposure.

3,824 sites shipped browser-safe values: reCAPTCHA site keys, Stripe publishable keys, Supabase anon keys, builder telemetry tokens.

2,172 sites carried Google API keys, which matter only if they are unrestricted.

1,461 sites exposed a Supabase or Firebase backend address, which is a real exposure only when that backend’s rules are open.

Filtering those out is why the confirmed count is 35, not several thousand. Table 1 breaks the 35 down by type. The values stay withheld, and a few sites appear under more than one row.

What an attacker can do with these

Every credential in Table 1 is a working key to a live account. An attacker reads a public web page, copies a value, and calls an API. Here is what that buys them, key by key.

OpenAI and other LLM keys: Run inference on the victim’s account until the bill or rate limit stops them. On a metered account, that is direct financial loss; on a funded one, it is a free, anonymous model endpoint that the attacker can point at anything, billed to the victim and running under their quota and identity.

Stripe secret key; Drive the victim’s payment account through Stripe’s own API: create and refund charges, push the account toward fraud, and pull the customer list, email addresses, and payout history. One key is a money problem and a data-breach problem at once.

Supabase service-role token: Read and write the entire production database, past whatever row-level security the app configured. That means stealing every user record, altering or deleting data, and planting content the app will serve back to its own visitors.

Slack incoming webhook: Post into the operator’s own Slack as if from inside. Flooding a channel is a nuisance case; the real risk is internal phishing.

AWS access key: With the paired secret and enough permission, reach into the owner’s cloud: spin up resources (crypto-mining is the usual first move), read storage buckets, or pivot further in.

GitHub token or OAuth secret: Read or push to the owner’s source repositories or misuse their identity integration.

One exposure counts many times over. When the key sits on a cloned fleet, it is live on every domain in that fleet, so an attacker who finds it on one site has compromised all of them.

Conclusion

AI app-builders made it almost free to publish a website, and just as free to clone one, and most of what they produce is worth nothing to steal.

The exceptions are what we went looking for. A small, steady set of these sites hand over the key that runs them, and when an operator copies one site across a fleet, the leak rides along to every domain.

Against the millions of domains registered each month, the number is tiny, but every hit is a live account an attacker can reach and exploit just by opening the page.

If you build on these tools, read your own shipped code before you publish it. If you defend an organization, assume your keys may surface on sites you never built and look for them.

Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web, deep web, and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats.

Our Recommendations

For developers and AI-builder users:

Keep every secret key (OpenAI sk-, Stripe sk_live_, a Supabase service-role token) in a server-side function or backend workflow, never in a client-accessible field.

Use only the browser-safe variants on the front end, publishable and anon keys, and enforce access with Supabase row-level security, Firebase rules, and API key restrictions.

Rotate any key that has ever sat on the client side, and treat it as already compromised.

Read your own page source before you ship, and search it for sk-, sk_live_, service_role, and hooks.slack.com. If you find them, so can anyone.

For SOCs and defenders:

Monitor public code and newly registered domains for your own keys and webhooks; don’t just paste sites.

Treat a secret found on one domain of a template fleet as exposed on all of them, and scope the response to the fleet, not the domain.

Context: For instance, the Exploit Prevention component available in Kaspersky products prevents exploits from running if the patch is not applied, or if it is a zero-day vulnerability...
Full Text:
Introduction

Back in October 2022, Kaspersky GReAT was looking into a peculiar advertisement on a hacking forum. A cybercriminal had been advertising a UEFI bootkit, dubbed BlackLotus, that could bypass Secure Boot, for $5,000. Given the low price for such powerful capabilities, the cybersecurity community initially took this advertisement with a grain of salt. As no BlackLotus samples were found in the wild, no one could at the time verify the claims made in the forum post.

BlackLotus advertisement

However, about half a year later, in March 2023, ESET confirmed that the BlackLotus advertisement was genuine. The researchers tracked down samples of this bootkit and confirmed that it can indeed bypass Secure Boot through a vulnerability called Baton Drop (CVE-2022-21894). As this vulnerability was still exploitable in 2023, Microsoft had to release multiple security updates to address it.

Since the release of these updates, the BlackLotus bootkit has gone quiet — no publicly known attacks have used it. Yet in early 2026, we discovered a malware sample similar to BlackLotus that was used in an APT campaign in Central Asia. In this report, we share our findings, including new payloads and possible attribution of this campaign.

The return of the infamous bootkit

In early 2026 we identified a complex APT attack targeting diplomatic agencies in Central Asian countries — namely Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. This attack involved a UEFI bootkit that we dubbed BlackX. Having examined it, we found it to be similar to BlackLotus.

Attackers have been deploying BlackX after compromising the victim machine networks and obtaining administrator privileges. To install the bootkit, we observed them dropping the following files:

inst.exe, an installer executable

PVMDIJGKAX2, an RC4-encrypted extensionless file containing files and strings required for the installation

The installer was launched with the command line C:\ProgramData\Intel\inst.exe PVMDIJGKAX2 Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1. The last argument here is the RC4 key used for decryption.

Curiously, the file inst.exe does not contain any malicious strings or embedded blobs. All the files needed to install the malicious payload are inside PVMDIJGKAX2, which makes it harder for incident responders to retrieve the bootkit components.

The installer package drops a set of files to both system and UEFI partitions, designed to exploit the Baton Drop vulnerability. We noted that the implementation of the exploit is remarkably similar to the one used in the BlackLotus malware. As with BlackLotus, the goal of the exploit is to install custom Machine Owner Keys (MOK), which allows loading arbitrary EFI files on the target machines to manipulate Secure Boot.

While the vulnerability exploitation chain was implemented very similarly to BlackLotus, we spotted differences between the exploits in BlackLotus and BlackX. That said, the source code of the BlackLotus bootkit has never been published online. This could mean that the attackers behind BlackX either reverse-engineered the BlackLotus bootkit or purchased its source code from cybercriminals. Either way, this is an interesting observation, as we rarely see APT actors borrow ideas or code from cybercrime actors.

Payload launched by the bootkit

The UEFI payload delivered during the Baton Drop exploitation has a classic bootkit goal — to inject a malicious driver into the Windows kernel. This driver differs from the one deployed by BlackLotus and is signed with a certificate belonging to an organization named 温江区明宇网络技术服务工作室 (English: Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio). At the time of writing, this certificate (serial number: 0bcdf5e0da32d68900b8b7638459d072) has been revoked by its issuer.

The driver aims to tamper with security solutions installed on the machine. For example, it disables process, thread, and registry callbacks related to security solutions. It also tampers with ETW providers so that security solutions cannot access their output. Curiously, some of the tampering procedures are designed to run only if Kaspersky or Avast solutions are installed on the infected machine. However, during dynamic analysis of this driver, we found that these procedures are useless — they fail to interfere with Kaspersky products in any way.

The driver also protects the bootkit’s files from tampering. It intercepts kernel requests to open these files and returns a handle to calc.exe instead of a malicious file handle.

User-mode second-stage payloads

Apart from tampering with security solutions, the driver also deploys a user-mode payload. We observed two such payloads, used for cyberespionage, in the wild. One of them is a RAT that can load further-stage .NET payloads. This RAT uses cloud storage for C2 server communications — we observed its versions using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk. Having connected to a cloud storage service, this RAT iterates over files available there and interprets them depending on the file suffix. Below is a list of supported suffixes:

File suffix

Description

Type

0X01

A .NET file. The task is to parse it and run the method TEST.Class1.RunCMD(argument_array) from the module

Input

0X02

Result of the call TEST.Class1.RunCMD(argument_array)

Output

0X03

Task to upload a file to the drive

Input

0X04

Uploaded file

Output

0X05

Task to download a file to an infected machine

Input

0X06

File download status

Output

SSSR

Contains initial system info

Output

We also observed another payload delivered through the bootkit, which we dubbed OxiDLLRunner. It is a malicious DLL obfuscated with OLLVM. It is loaded by the legitimate file googleupdate.exe (original filename: jcef_helper.exe, MD5: AF8A983B9ADA07EAE1259BF2953ABD40), which is also delivered by the bootkit. The DLL decrypts the contents of the file v8_context_snapshot.bin, which resides in the same folder, and then jumps to the beginning of the decrypted content. The decrypted data starts with shellcode followed by a PE file, which is a Rust payload designed to communicate with the www[.]archivetj[.]com C2 server. During communication, this payload is supposed to receive DLL files exporting a function named create_plugin, which are then executed in separate threads.

Attribution

Based on the following facts, we have attributed this attack to the APT41 threat actor with medium confidence:

In June 2026, ESET published a blog post on attacks by the FishMonger threat actor, which the community assumes to be related to APT41. This post describes a kernel implant with a PDB path starting with C:\Users\xdd\Desktop. While describing the campaign, the post also suggests the possible use of an unspecified UEFI bootkit component, which might exploit CVE‑2023‑24932. We observed the identifier “xdd” used multiple times in the BlackX bootkit payloads, so we assess that BlackX is the UEFI bootkit referenced in the ESET blog post;

The payloads deployed by BlackX are loaded using a legitimate executable abused via DLL sideloading, and an encrypted file — this pattern is common among Chinese-speaking threat actors;

The OxiDLLRunner file has been obfuscated with OLLVM, an obfuscator commonly used by Chinese-speaking actors.

Why did the target organizations get infected?

During our initial analysis of BlackX, we thought that attackers succeeded in deploying it due to the negligence of the target organizations. Baton Drop, the vulnerability used to deploy BlackX, was disclosed back in 2023 and was patched, so we first thought that the infected machines lacked the relevant updates. However, our investigation proved this wrong — the targeted machines were fully patched.

Instead, we found out that the problem was with the patch itself. As it turned out, the patch for the Baton Drop vulnerability is designed to revoke the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate used to sign vulnerable UEFI components. However, this revocation does not happen automatically upon patch installation — the user has to trigger it manually. This is done with the following steps:

A registry flag is set inside HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Secureboot;

A scheduled task named Secure-Boot-Update is created.

This patch is designed to be applied manually — for instance, applying it automatically could break dual-boot systems relying on the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate to load. At the same time, this patch deployment practice creates a problem — as it is extremely unusual for a system administrator to take extra steps after installing an update. Usually, when applying patches, system administrators take no further action unless an installation failure occurs. These instructions for activating the patch are buried deep on the Microsoft website, and we assess that they are quite hard for an average IT administrator to notice.

Curiously, Microsoft’s plan for deploying the Baton Drop patches mentions an “Enforcement Phase” that involves revoking the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate automatically, without user interaction. At the time of publishing this post, this stage has not been implemented. On October 19, 2026, this certificate expired, but this does not prevent the vulnerable binaries from loading unless the certificate is blocklisted.

It is likely that the threat actor behind this campaign took into account that few organizations realized the importance of manually activating the Baton Drop patch. As such, we believe they decided to invest time in understanding how BlackLotus works and creating a copycat of this bootkit.

Conclusion

Patch management is important for every organization, as updates from vendors help protect software and hardware against known vulnerabilities. However, sometimes installed patches fail to protect against the flaws they address. The BlackLotus story we described is not the only such example — for instance, in 2025 Microsoft released an update against the ToolShell vulnerability that also had to be applied manually.

However, modern security solutions are designed to account for such cases when installed patches fail to protect against security flaws for one reason or another. For instance, the Exploit Prevention component available in Kaspersky products prevents exploits from running if the patch is not applied, or if it is a zero-day vulnerability with no available patch. It is thus crucial to equip all machines in an organization with security solutions and constantly monitor the alerts they raise.

Title: Behind Japan’s Warnings of a Cyber Crisis

Full Text:
At least two features set the Q3 Japan breaches apart from other such breaches. The first is the breadth of the attacks: victim organizations spanned the retail, rail, logistics, media, education, and software industries, and the intrusions involved ransomware, stolen cloud credentials, and exploited web-facing systems. The second is the scale of the attacks: single incidents now routinely affect millions of user records or organizations downstream that rely on the targeted services, such as roughly 33 million records leaked from the EPARK PeakManager reservation platform in July and 6.6 million accounts from Times Car in September.

This trend has continued into Q4. On October 7, a ransomware incident affected IDCFrontier, a Japanese cloud provider, disrupting 495 companies and local governments. Almost a week later, on October 13, 2026, a data breach affected the Japanese software company Sourcenext. In this incident, an unidentified third party misused the company’s member information retrieval API to compromise 22,519,960 customer records containing personally identifiable information, including email addresses, passwords, names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, employment information, and more.

Our observations complement October 2026 warnings issued by several Japanese agencies, including the Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center (JPCERT/CC), the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC), and the Innovation Platform Agency (IPA), regarding a series of cyberattacks targeting Japan-based organizations. JPCERT/CC’s notice warned of at least four consistent tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) linked to recent incidents:

Exploitation of known vulnerabilities in unpatched systems or misconfigurations;

Attacking internal and external APIs, sometimes using stolen API credentials;

Exploitation of CVE-2026-72898 (CVSS score 10), a SQL injection vulnerability, in the Metabase application;

The deployment of web shells contained within .war and .jsp files on internet-accessible web servers.

Later reports attributed the cyberattacks targeting Japanese company websites to artificial intelligence (AI) agents linked to activity ranging from basic website scanning to extended attack sequences that involved multiple tools and techniques.

Japan-based Macnica Security also reported a surge in cyberattacks since July 2026 involving personal information leaks from web systems. The company noted that this increase is unique to Japan compared with other countries. According to Macnica, of the 119 cases disclosed in 2026, approximately 68% were announced since July. This accounts for about 31% of the total 265 cases over a 34-month period. The company similarly observed unauthorized access through weak authentication, stolen credentials, or exploited software vulnerabilities and site-specific flaws in application design, APIs, or access controls. Macnica could not confirm the use of AI in these attacks.

Explaining the Increase in Incidents

Multiple factors are likely responsible for the recent increase in attacks affecting Japanese organizations.

High Demand in the Criminal Ecosystem for Japanese User Data: Criminals on the dark web place a premium on data from Japanese organizations due to Japan’s financial and identification requirements and its status as a wealthy, developed economy.

Widespread Use of Legacy Systems and Software: According to an April 2026 article by Money Forward, more than 60% of Japanese firms still use legacy systems, end-of-life software, and older operating systems. Such systems no longer receive security updates and official patches from vendors, leaving known flaws exposed to increasingly automated attempts to exploit them.

Operationalization of AI Tooling: While the specific models abused are not yet confirmed, commercial AI products are widely believed to have been leveraged in the recent spate of attacks against Japanese organizations, both for automating the attack sequence (such as automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation), and for reducing the barrier-to-entry historically attributed to the complexity of the Japanese language (such as through the easier drafting of convincing phishing emails in proper business Japanese). Notably, financial institutions in neighboring South Korea were recently the target of an intrusion campaign leveraging ARTEX, a Chinese open-source AI penetration-testing tool attributed to a group Recorded Future refers to as TAG-217. On October 19, the Japanese cybersecurity company GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae reportedly concluded that ARTEX was used in attacks against roughly 80 Japanese companies, with 8 of those attacks occurring in the 30 days prior to its report.

New Incident Reporting Requirements: Effective October 1, 2026, Japan’s new Active Cyber Defense (ACD) Law imposes mandatory reporting requirements on designated critical infrastructure operators. This is unlikely to account for the surge in reported incidents due to the law’s implementation date in Q4 2026, but it does imply that we will very likely continue to observe a higher volume of incident disclosures from Japanese organizations going forward, and the impending implementation of the law may have induced some organizations to disclose incidents in Q3 that would otherwise have gone unreported.

Recommendations

Insikt Group recommends that Japanese organizations consider the following:

Migrate away from and/or update legacy systems. Outdated and unpatched devices or software (including operating systems) provide an attractive, easy vector for threat actors to compromise organizations via previously disclosed vulnerabilities and exploits. AI-enabled scanning and automated exploitation have further increased the risk to these systems. Where possible, replace end-of-life hardware and software.

Harden internet-facing systems. Secure internet-exposed hardware and services such as virtual private network (VPN) servers, web application firewalls, load balancers, small office/home office routers, IP cameras, and DVRs by patching known vulnerabilities, restricting administrative access, enabling additional logging, and disabling unnecessary services. These devices have been increasingly exploited by cybercriminals and state-sponsored actors alike over the last several years for initial access.

Strengthen API controls. Verify authorization for every API request, test whether users can access other customers’ records, restrict API key privileges, and limit bulk data retrieval.

Protect accounts against phishing. Require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) and train staff to be vigilant against increasingly well-crafted Japanese-language phishing messages.

Limit data exposure and prepare for disruption. Delete unnecessary personal information, restrict data export permissions, test restoration from protected backups, and establish manual alternatives for critical services such as reservations and dispatch.

Adopt privileged access management (PAM). Limit administrative and super-user accounts, providing elevated rights only on a temporary, just-in-time basis.

Use Recorded Future Threat Intelligence. Customers can proactively monitor for threat actor mentions of their organization and leaked data on dark web forums, chat rooms, and ransomware leak sites by configuring alerts on the Recorded Future Intelligence Platform, regularly ingesting Insikt Group research, and blocklisting known malicious indicators of compromise (IoCs).

Full Text: IntroductionIn October 2026, Zscaler ThreatLabz investigated AI-assisted cyberattacks that combined the ARTEX penetration testing framework with AI coding assistants and custom automation scripts. Initial reporting of the incident identified the targeting of South Korean financial institutions. However, ThreatLabz discovered additional information about the attack, which went far beyond South Korea. The AI-assisted attacks were widespread and targeted organizations around the globe and in multiple industry sectors.In this blog post, ThreatLabz examines the operator’s working environment, explains the roles assigned to AI models and tools, and analyzes the targeting and objectives reflected in the operator’s prompts. Key TakeawaysIn October 2026, ThreatLabz discovered information about an AI-assisted attack combining a customized ARTEX deployment with Claude Code, Codex, and Grok workspaces. Custom scripts shared instructions and supported handoffs between AI sessions.ARTEX was configured to use a DeepSeek model through an OpenAI-compatible gateway, but other configurations also specified DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok.Prompts directed AI models to divide investigation tasks and review one another’s findings, including instructions for GLM to review work performed by DeepSeek and its subagents.Saved project records and synchronization scripts were designed to preserve investigation context and progress across accounts, servers, and AI sessions. Prompt histories revealed targeting across multiple industries and geographic regions. Requests for bulk personal and transaction data, alongside questions about selling stolen data, suggest the attacks were financially motivated. BackgroundThreatLabz identified an ARTEX deployment that included AI assistant configurations, synchronization scripts, network routing tools, and a Claude Code prompt history. The recorded prompts spanned August 4 through October 4, 2026 (UTC). CrowdStrike separately reported on related ARTEX infrastructure and the targeting of South Korean financial organizations on October 7, 2026. This blog examines the broader working environment of the attacks and targets. The jump server, 38.244.50.120, served as the default route for connections to targets.The jump server also ran additional AI sessions. The operator delegated research tasks to Grok on that server and instructed a separate AI session to review Grok’s findings. This setup divided work between the two servers, with the operator providing oversight and direction. Three custom scripts synchronized shared AI instructions and supporting files across accounts, which are described in the table below.Script namePurposetools/sync-all.shUses SSH and rsync to copy AI instructions, reusable task guides, saved notes, and tools to the jump server's root, claude, grok, and gemini accounts.sync-memory.shCopies saved AI notes, known as memory files, to locations on the jump server.tools/sync-cc-users.shCopies shared Claude Code instructions and supporting files to the gemini and glm accounts on the work server.Table 1: Custom synchronization scripts and their purposes for AI-assisted attacks.Each account maintained its own AI service settings. Full Text:
Executive Summary

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 to fix two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2. The two flaws are known together as PHP2Shell. They were disclosed by the security firms Calif and Wiz and by OpenAI, working with the PHP security team, after AI-assisted auditing turned an out-of-memory weakness that a 2024 audit had flagged but could not prove exploitable into working remote code execution.

Both vulnerabilities sit in PHP's memory management and error handling, code that nearly every request touches, and the earliest affected path dates to PHP 5.4.0. An unauthenticated attacker can execute code on the web server or read its process memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys belonging to other requests. On Apache with mod_php, the attack runs before any application code executes, which means an application with no bugs of its own is still exposed. As of October 21, 2026, no verified proof-of-concept code is available publicly. Attack attempts have been observed by Cloudflare after the leak, but no confirmed in-the-wild compromise has yet been reported.

While upgrading every PHP runtime remains the primary control, SentinelOne agent detects attackers’ post-exploitation activities. Once an attacker has code execution on the web server process, the behavior that follows web server flaws: execute shell commands, drop and invoke webshells, download and execute custom payloads and outbound connections. On managed hosts, the Singularity™ agent and Singularity AI SIEM detection content look for such behaviors, and Purple AI® can be used to hunt for it during the patching window. The separate memory-disclosure path runs no code on the host, so it leaves no process behavior to detect; that path is instead surfaced through web server, WAF, and CDN telemetry forwarded into AI SIEM.

This report details PHP2Shell's mechanism, affected versions, and confirmed activity, and outlines how SentinelOne customers can strengthen their defenses.

Key Highlights

The flaw is in PHP itself, not in any application. WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, Laravel, and other web applications are all exposed on an affected PHP version, because the vulnerable code is in the runtime beneath them.

The patch is the only complete fix. PHP states plainly that no configuration change fully closes the vulnerability. Every interim mitigation reduces one attack path and leaves others open.

The unauthenticated path runs before your code does. On Apache with mod_php, a single crafted HTTP request triggers the flaw during request startup, so application-level controls never see it. PHP assesses the risk as highest for mod_php.

Memory disclosure leaks secrets without a shell. One path reads live worker memory and returns passwords, tokens, API keys, and certificates with no code execution, which makes it quieter than a shell and harder to catch with execution-focused tooling.

End of Life PHP will not get a patch. Organizations running PHP 8.1 and prior will not receive an official release. Source-only backports exist for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, and distribution or LTS vendors may offer fixed packages.

Leverage SentinelOne platform post-exploitation coverage. The detection by the agent is agnostic to the vulnerability and exploit chain and focuses on attackers activity following the exploit, including but not limited to, installation and usage of webshells, command executions and outbound connection behavior that follows the code execution.

Organizations should take the following steps immediately:

Update every PHP runtime to a fixed version and restart Apache, PHP-FPM, and any long-running workers.

Inventory internet-facing PHP, including the copies bundled inside appliances, control panels, and vendor software.

Isolate end-of-life PHP (8.1 and older) from the internet until it can be upgraded.

Rotate credentials, tokens, and keys that a PHP worker could hold in memory on any exposed, unpatched system.

Monitor the official PHP changelog for relevant updates

What is PHP2SHELL

PHP2Shell is a family of memory-safety vulnerabilities in core PHP, grouped under two CVEs that share one root cause. When PHP hits a fatal condition such as exhausting its configured memory limit, it does not unwind cleanly. It abandons the current operation with a “longjmp” out of the C call stack, so no cleanup runs and nothing records that a data structure was left half-built. A later cleanup routine, or a later request, then trusts that state.

CVE-2026-109618 is the out-of-memory case. PHP marks request data as valid before allocating memory for it. If that allocation hits the memory limit and fails, the entry is left pointing to uninitialized heap memory. When the failed request runs its cleanup routine, it processes these stale bytes, leading to corruption..

CVE-2026-109619 is the stale-state case. When a fatal error occurs, PHP fails to clean up properly, leaving a global pointer pointing to memory that has already been freed. Because worker processes handle multiple requests, a subsequent request on the same worker can interact with this freed memory before initialization resets it – resulting in a use-after-free condition. Session upload progress (enabled by default) is a confirmed trigger for this behavior.

Both flaws were discovered through AI-assisted auditing under OpenAI's “Patch the Planet” program. Calif and OpenAI independently reported the root cause to the PHP security team on August 11, 2026, and Wiz reported additional attack vectors on August 24, 2026. PHP first saw signs of the underlying out-of-memory problem during a 2024 audit by OSTIF and Quarkslab, but no exploitation path was proven at the time and the fix stalled. The PHP Foundation has since described that delay as a structural failure in its security process.

On October 20, the two CVE identifiers leaked on social media. PHP released a patch on October 21, 2026.

Am I Affected?

Assume exposure for any PHP runtime below the fixed version for its branch. Check the version the web server actually loads, which can differ from the command-line version, using php --version for the CLI and the equivalent for PHP-FPM or the Apache module. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patch in advance, and a packaged build may carry the fix under an older version number, so confirm against your vendor's advisory rather than the version string alone.

PHP states that all installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, and rates the risk highest for mod_php. Do not use configuration to rule out exposure. PHP validated mod_php code execution with default input and memory limits, and states that no configuration change is a complete mitigation. OpenAI has published a PHP version checker, which should be reviewed before you run it.

Why This Matters

A flaw in PHP itself reaches far further than a flaw in any one application. PHP is widely used across the internet, and it is embedded in content management systems, control panels such as cPanel and Plesk, and a variety of vendor applications. The hard part of this response is not applying the patch. It is finding every runtime that needs it.

The patch is also the only complete fix, and a large share of PHP cannot receive it. PHP 8.1 and older are at end of life, and Talos estimates from open-source data that around half of internet-facing PHP runs on branches with no official update. Those systems need to be upgraded to a supported branch or taken off the internet, not merely reconfigured.

Exploitation is also hard to see. The memory-disclosure path returns secrets from live worker memory without running code at all, which Wiz notes makes it harder to catch with tools focused on malicious code execution. Because the flaws execute below the application layer, Wiz also reports that application logs may contain little context, and the clearest traces are in web server and PHP error logs rather than in application telemetry.

Attack Chain

Stage 1: Reaching the Flaw Over an Unauthenticated Request

The attacker sends a crafted multipart HTTP request that places PHP's memory under pressure or forces a fatal error during request startup. A chunked or lengthless request slips past the post_max_size check, and empty file controls with deeply nested field names expand a small request body into large internal allocations.

Stage 2: Corrupting Worker State

The forced out-of-memory condition or fatal error interrupts PHP in a context that does not account for the early exit. For CVE-2026-109618, Apache with mod_php runs its request shutdown unconditionally and processes the partially initialized state as if it were valid. For CVE-2026-109619, a global pointer is left referring to freed request memory, and a later request on the same worker consumes it.

Stage 3: Code Execution or Memory Disclosure

With the heap arranged to reclaim the freed or invalid memory with attacker-controlled bytes, the corrupted state becomes a memory-corruption primitive that yields code execution as the web worker. PHP confirmed complete remote code execution against mod_php with default input and memory limits. On a separate path, the attacker instead reads live worker memory and extracts passwords, tokens, API keys, and certificates belonging to other requests, returned through the PHPSESSID response cookie, with no code execution at all.

Stage 4: Post-Exploitation

Code runs with the privileges of the web server worker, commonly www-data. From there, operators drop a web shell into the web root, spawn shells and tooling such as sh, bash, python, curl, and wget, and move laterally using any credentials recovered through memory disclosure.

Hardening Recommendations

These steps apply to any PHP estate, independent of security vendor. Patching is the only complete remediation. Everything else reduces exposure during the window before every runtime is updated.

Patch Every PHP Runtime and Restart Workers

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or to the fixed package from your Linux distribution or hosting provider.

Restart Apache, PHP-FPM, and every long-running PHP worker after updating. The running process keeps the vulnerable code until it is restarted.

Remember that updating an application, CMS, or framework does not update the PHP runtime beneath it.

Assess Your Exposure

Inventory every PHP runtime: web servers first, then vendor appliances, Windows software that bundles php.exe or php-cgi.exe, control panels such as cPanel and Plesk, and any WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, or Magento install.

Isolate end-of-life PHP (8.1 and older) behind a VPN or take it off the internet until it is upgraded to a supported branch.

Apply Interim Settings Only as a Bridge

For CVE-2026-109618, set memory_limit=-1 administratively so applications cannot override it, and keep post_max_size low. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable path.

For CVE-2026-109619, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0, and on PHP 8.5 set fatal_error_backtraces=0, applied before request parsing and followed by a worker restart.

Treat all of these as partial. PHP confirms there is no complete configuration mitigation, and hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors, or the @ operator does not help.

Constrain the Request at the Edge

At the proxy or web application firewall, enforce limits on decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count per part, and nesting depth, including requests that arrive without a usable Content-Length.

Enable your WAF or reverse proxy vendor's managed rules for PHP2Shell, which several vendors published on October 21, and test first because rules can block legitimate traffic.

Treat the WAF as a layer, not a fix: Cloudflare saw attackers mutating payloads to bypass its rules.

If an application does not use multipart form data, block multipart requests to it before they reach PHP.

Limit Worker Reuse and Blast Radius

Lower PHP-FPM pm.max_requests so workers recycle more often, reducing how long the corrupted state can persist.

Use a cgroup memory.max as an availability boundary that kills only the affected worker, not the whole pool.

Apply SELinux or AppArmor policies to restrict what a web worker can execute.

Rotate Secrets Reachable in Process Memory

Assume any credential, session token, API key, or certificate held by a PHP worker on an exposed, unpatched system may have been disclosed.

Rotate them now rather than after confirmed compromise, because memory disclosure leaves little trace.

Hunt for Post-Exploitation

Review the web root for newly created files and web shells, and watch for new cron jobs, scheduled tasks, and accounts.

Alert on PHP worker processes (php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd, apache2, w3wp) spawning shells, interpreters, or download tools, including cmd.exe and powershell.exe on Windows.

In web server and PHP error logs, look for unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit fatal errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, and for unexplained PHP worker churn (Wiz).

Check response headers for unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID cookies, which Wiz identifies as a sign of the memory-disclosure path.

Enable log_errors, a working error_log, and error_reporting=E_ALL in startup configuration for an isolated audit, as PHP recommends, and treat a clean log as supporting evidence rather than proof of safety.

Treat these signals as leads, not verdicts. They come from public research rather than confirmed attack traffic, and memory-limit errors and HTTP 500s also occur on healthy systems.

How SentinelOne Protects You

PHP2Shell executes inside the web server worker process, below the application. SentinelOne’s visibility begins where that worker runs on a host with the agent installed. The agent cannot see internal application activity which doesn’t interact with the OS or other processes as the memory-disclosure path. What SentinelOne can address is the behavior of the code executed by the attacker.

The Behavior After Exploitation

Code execution through a web server worker process has the worker’s privileges. From there the sequence is familiar. The attacker runs host and user discovery, pulls a second-stage payload with a built-in download utility, writes a web shell into the document root so a fragile memory bug does not have to be triggered twice, opens an outbound connection to attacker infrastructure, and reads application configuration files for database credentials.

Detection on the Host

The Singularity agent builds a storyline of every process group activity on a host, including the web server workers PHP2Shell targets. These workers have a predictable life: they answer HTTP requests. They do not normally start /bin/sh, run reconnaissance commands, download executables into /tmp, write new .php files into the web root, or open outbound connections to arbitrary hosts. Behavioral detection looks for that deviation from the worker’s normal behavior. With the policy mode set to protect, the agent can terminate the process tree and quarantine dropped artifacts.

Detection in Singularity AI SIEM

Platform detection content looks at what happens on the host after exploitation, not at the request body.

Attacker Step

Telemetry

Visible Indicators

Code execution in the worker

Process creation

Web server and script-interpreter processes spawning system shells, enumeration utilities (id, whoami, uname, hostname), or sensitive file reads

Tooling download

Process Creation, File Creation

Downloaders (curl, wget, interpreters) fetching to world-writable paths, and executables written and then run from /tmp

Webshell drop

File creation

Web server processes writing .php, .jsp, .sh, or other script files into web-served directories, correlated with the inbound HTTP connection that preceded it

Reverse shell and C2

Process Creation, IP Connect

Shell processes with socket-redirection patterns (/dev/tcp, nc, socat) and unexpected outbound connections from web workers

Novel child process

First-seen analytics

A PHP or web server process spawning a child it has never spawned in that environment

Correlation rules tie these together. An inbound HTTP connection followed by a file drop or process spawn from the same worker is the shape of a successful PHP2Shell chain.

Visibility at the Edge

The memory-disclosure path never starts a process, so host telemetry alone will not see it. It can leave traces in web server, WAF, and CDN logs: unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or bursts of HTTP 500s, malformed or oversized PHPSESSID cookies, and unexplained worker churn. Singularity AI SIEM can ingest those sources alongside endpoint data if you forward them. Existing content covers allowed web shell uploads, successful POSTs to server-side scripts that have never received them before, and web shell command execution at the network layer.

Hunt with Purple AI While You Patch

Patching is the only complete fix, and the Hardening section covers interim settings. While that work runs, analysts can ask Purple AI questions such as:

Show me web server workers that spawned a shell in the last 72 hours.

Show me new files written to web roots by php-fpm.

Show me hosts with a spike in 500 responses followed by a child process from Apache.

Show me outbound connections from www-data to destinations we have never seen.

The 500-response question depends on web server logs being ingested.

Confirm Agent Saturation on Web-Facing Servers

Confirm the agent is deployed, healthy, and in protect mode on every server that serves PHP, including internet-facing Linux hosts.

Conclusion

The exploitation picture for PHP2Shell is moving quickly. As of October 21, 2026, no verified proof-of-concept code is available publicly. Attack attempts have been observed by Cloudflare after the leak, but no confirmed in-the-wild compromise has yet been reported. SentinelOne is monitoring PHP2Shell activity and will update this report as exploitation evidence, vendor guidance, and detection content change.

SentinelOne recommends customers follow vendor guidance and prioritize patching as the primary defensive tactic. Interim settings, WAF rules, and detection reduce risk while it is deployed. Update every PHP runtime to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, restart the workers, and confirm the fix is running on the version the web server actually loads. Move PHP 8.1 and older to a supported branch or off the internet, and rotate any secrets that a worker on an unpatched, exposed system could have held in memory.

Information contained herein is current as of October 21, 2026, and is subject to change as patch releases and threat activity evolve. Recipients should not rely solely on this report for security decisions and should consult with their security teams and SentinelOne account representatives for current guidance.

Title: Two critical RCEs in PHP core
Context: Splunk Enterprise Security customers have an Enterprise Security Content Update with detections available
Full Text:
Update 10/22: Added section detailing observations of in the wild exploitation and associated IOCs.

Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws in PHP core, dubbed “php2shell”, triggered by a plain HTTP request and exploitable before any application code runs, affecting every PHP build since 5.4. Based on the entities involved in the disclosure, artificial intelligence and associated technologies played a key role in the discovery of these vulnerabilities — yet another example of how these technologies are forcing change across the landscape, most notably on patching processes for organizations because of the wave of vulnerabilities being disclosed.

Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359, 67360, and 67375. These rules are also available in the Community Ruleset for open-source customers. Splunk Enterprise Security customers have an Enterprise Security Content Update with detections available. Please refer to the following recommendations, detection, and coverage guidance for more information.

Details

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both critical vulnerabilities with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.

CVE-2026-109618 occurs when out-of-memory handling interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 occurs when a stale internal state is reused after its backing memory has already been freed, before normal initialization resets it.

Impact

The potential blast radius is enormous and extends across the PHP ecosystem. The vulnerability sits in PHP core, so applications running affected versions — including WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and Laravel, plus PHP sites hosted through cPanel or Plesk — may be exposed. Note that many older branches will no longer receive fixes, so customers are urged to upgrade to a supported version as soon as possible.

Talos regularly investigates threat actor exploitation of vulnerabilities. State-sponsored and affiliated threat actors, as well as ransomware and other financially motivated groups, all employ tactics to exploit RCE. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched.

PHP 8.1 and older are end of life (EOL), and PHP 8.2 security support ends Dec. 31, 2026. Talos’ initial estimates based on open-source intelligence show a significant corpus of PHP systems that will not receive a patch (~50%). If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older.

Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these CVEs and has not seen them being exploited in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC/10:00 a.m. ET).

Observed Exploitation

Cisco Talos began observing exploitation attempts within hours of the vulnerabilities’ disclosure. So far, most of the activity is scanning, along with some uncoordinated attempts to deliver various payloads. This is expected: scanning or basic exploitation with public proof-of-concept (PoC) code takes far less effort than integrating a vulnerability into an actor’s own tooling. We expect exploitation volume to grow in the coming days, and campaigns to become more sophisticated and coordinated as more capable groups finish updating their tooling and begin deploying it.

Recommendations and detection guidance

Talos strongly recommends all PHP users to upgrade to the available fixed releases. There are no intermediate or temporary controls that provide comprehensive protection; however, PHP advises that the following measure may reduce exposure to specific attack paths:

CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can't override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.

Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don't require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length.

Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.

CVE-2026-109619

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.

Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors, or @ does not help.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing, and cleanup.

This is another vulnerability that owes its discovery to AI and its associated technologies. As we move through 2026, the wave of vulnerabilities and related patches is building. Talos advises organizations to work on a triaged process for prioritizing vulnerabilities with a specific focus on public-facing systems and vulnerabilities that are under active exploitation. The glaring need to prioritize vulnerabilities along with a streamlined process for rolling out patching strongly indicates that the historic trend of “baking in” patches before deployment is not going to survive the AI era.

The true impact of this vulnerability will take time to evaluate. These types of vulnerabilities that impact core technologies tend to cascade into other platforms and applications as they evaluate impact and provide associated patching, harkening back to the waves of exploitation that we saw after Log4J.

Coverage

SNORT® SIDs covering these vulnerabilities for subscribers: 67359, 67360, 67375. Free community rules are live through our Community Ruleset.

Splunk has released an Enterprise Security Content Update (ESCU) related to the ongoing PHP2Shell activity with additional detections. Splunk Enterprise Security customers are urged to download and apply.

Talos would like to highlight the efforts of Ankur Tyagi, Dalton Schaadt, Brandon Stultz, and Matt Killion for providing emergency coverage and mitigations for these threats.

In this video, Talos’ Nick Biasini explains what the vulnerabilities allow adversaries to do, how to assess your exposure, and what defenders should prioritize.

Title: New PhaaS Platform Uses AI to Craft Phishing Lures and Mask Malicious Activity
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Abnormal AI noted that the AI Studio gives threat actors another way to prepare phishing content without writing every lure from scratch or relying exclusively on ready-made materials. They can instead request content tailored to different pretexts and audiences.

AI Studio is integrated into Athena StealthRoute's broader offering, which also combines domain and link management, a marketplace for campaign materials, visitor monitoring and cloaking controls.

Athena StealthRoute still relies on external infrastructure for credential and token harvesting, but much of the preparation and delivery workflow can be managed through a single console, the researchers noted.

Five of the six offerings in the AI Studio focus on the creation of phishing lures and related materials. However, the sixth option extends to decoy content intended to conceal the phishing attempts. The White Page option produces structured, benign-looking content that could be used as a cover when Athena StealthRoute's cloaking layer directs scanners and other unwanted visitors away from malicious destinations.

How to Detect and Defend Against Athena StealthRoute

Abnormal AI said that for defenders, the platform’s combination of cloaking and customizable content reinforces the limitations of relying on individual messages or link inspections to detect phishing attempts.

“Security scanners may encounter benign content where intended victims would reach malicious destinations, while variations in lure copy can make exact wording less useful for linking-related attacks,” the researchers said in their analysis.

Shared backend infrastructure, matching operator-console code and recognizable link structures offer additional signals for identifying Athena StealthRoute-associated activity even as individual domains and lures change.

Finally, because credential and token harvesting occur through separate downstream services, investigations must also account for the particular theft mechanism involved.

Title: Symantec Uncovers AI Agent Hijacking Models for Autonomous Cyber-Attacks
Context: Researchers from the Symantec Threat Hunter Team found the malicious agent using an AI honeypot – a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order...
Full Text:
A new AI agent developed to run a full cyber-attack without human intervention has been uncovered by security researchers.

The agent was designed to use hijacked AI models to autonomously run up to 100,000 malicious actions without human approval, including scanning for targets, exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, deploying cryptocurrency miners and reinfecting compromised systems.

Researchers from the Symantec Threat Hunter Team found the malicious agent using an AI honeypot – a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order to attract and study attacks against AI infrastructure.

They captured the agent's full instruction set in the summer of 2026, revealing how it was designed to operate autonomously, although the honeypot did not execute the attacker's tools. They described it in more details in a report published on October 21.

AI Honeypot Exposes LLMjacking

The AI honeypot recorded over 127,000 external requests from tens of thousands of unique addresses between its setup and the publication of the report.

Upon analyzing this activity, Symantec researchers discovered that the agent searches for exposed endpoints linked to large language models (LLMs), including self-hosted models, AI gateways and model context protocol (MCP) servers, to use their computing power without paying for it. This technique is sometimes called ‘LLMjacking.’

“Running a model always costs someone money, either in processing time for a self-hosted model or in per-token fees for a commercial one. By routing its work through a stranger's endpoint or a stolen key, the operators shift that cost onto the victim,” Symantec researchers noted.

With this technique, the attackers also gain anonymity and avoid potential account bans the AI model provider would issue for abuse.

The captured instructions included about 74 tools for internet-wide reconnaissance, exploiting common web frameworks, stealing databases, harvesting credentials and managing botnets.

Notably, the attackers used layered instructions designed to override commercial AI models' safety controls, disguising credential theft as legitimate development work.

A separate request also contained an obfuscated script designed to install Monero-mining software, conceal its presence and erase logs.

Self-Directed AI Agent Lowers Barrier to Cybercrime

While Symantec researchers said none of the techniques used by the attackers in this campaign are novel, their combination into a single, self-directed agent lowers the skill required for other attackers to run a broad exploitation campaign.

“An operator can hand the model a goal and let it work,” they added.

They concluded that the activity “marks a shift in how attackers are using AI,” explaining that operators have embedded AI into offensive tools rather than trying to trick public chatbots into misbehaving.

They described the model as “a reasoning engine that plans and drives the attack,” while the tool’s own modules carry out scanning, exploitation and mining against separate victims.

Title: LiteLLM Compromised, Steals Credentials
Context: We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability
Full Text:
LiteLLM Compromised

At 11:39 UTC on October 21, a malicious version (1.107.0) of the LiteLLM package was uploaded to PyPI. This version was quarantined on PyPI as of 13:20 UTC. According to ClickPy data, the malicious version received approximately 49,000 downloads.

LiteLLM Docker containers on GHCR and Docker hub also included the trojanized version of LiteLLM. These included the v1.107.0 , latest, main-latest and main-stable tags. These were removed ~13:53 UTC.

The most recent safe version is v1.106.2.

When the malicious package is installed, three files are extracted directly into the site-packages root: cook.pth, cook.py and sitecustomize.py. These packages are designed to be executed whenever a python interpreter is started.

Per LiteLLM developer BerriAI:

malicious actions were taken through three engineers' GitHub accounts, appearing to be by way of stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens. The threat actor used one user's account triggered the project-releaser run, and another user's account to approve it. All tokens which were involved in this attack have been revoked.

And in a followup:

GitHub CLI OAuth token exposure After a thorough investigation, we have observed specific situations in which Claude Code will embed a user’s GitHub CLI OAuth token into a response body, and in situations where response bodies are logged, these tokens may appear in LiteLLM logs. Access to our internal LiteLLM deployment We identified an unexpected, innocuously named user account in our internal LiteLLM deployment, which was exposed to the public internet. We believe the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise our release workflow. We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability.

UPDATES

Payload

The payload has strong indications of LLM-aided development, including verbose variable names (encrypted_private_key_output), overly defensive error handling with generic try/except blocks, platform-specific code paths that fail silently on untested platforms (Windows marker path /tmp/ doesn't exist, fcntl/fork calls crash the remote loader), and a dead code module (exec_py) that was defined but never called. The structure suggests iterative prompting: functional on the happy path but brittle at the edges and untested.

Upon startup, the interpreter processes cook.pth, which includes a command to import cook, which loads cook.py. cook.py deobfuscates itself, runs a stealer routine and writes a maker to /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb (note this fails on Windows, as the /tmp/ path often does not exist). The stealer routine gathers system, browser, developer, cloud and AI tool secrets, encrypts them and exfiltrates to www.litellm.dev/healthcheck via a post request. This domain is attacker controlled, impersonating LiteLLM infrastructure.

Python interpreters will also attempt to execute sitecustomize.py - however, it will only run on Linux & MacOS machines. This script attempts to fetch domain.txt from a GitHub dead drop (letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt). If it receives a response, it will attempt to download a second stage python script from http://<domain>/codepy and run it. As of the time of analysis, the domain.txt file was never populated beyond initial test values. The repo has been taken down by GitHub as of 1:30 PM UTC.

The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild.

Credential Stealer

The embedded credential stealer, internally named privcollect, harvests sensitive data across 16 modules targeting browsers, cloud providers, and AI services. It extracts:

browser credentials and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari

AWS credentials from ~/.aws/, environment variables, and EC2/ECS instance metadata (IMDS)

GCP service account keys and application default credentials

Azure tokens from the CLI cache

In terms of AI-specific theft, it targets API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers stored in environment variables or config files. It also collects SSH private keys, GPG keys, and shell history files.

LiteLLM Proxy stores upstream API keys in a PostgreSQL database. The stealer queries this database directly (SELECT * FROM "LiteLLM_CredentialsTable" LIMIT 500) to extract all configured provider credentials.

Harvested data is encrypted with AES-256-CBC (key wrapped with RSA-4096) and exfiltrated over HTTP to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck using the hardcoded X-Token header and an Internet Explorer 7 user-agent string.

Attacker Commits

The payload originates with malicious commits made on github.com/Berri-AI/litellm. Note, this is a hyphenated variant of the legitimate BerriAI organization. This repository, not visible on GitHub, was used to inject the payload into the release pipeline.

Between 08:56 and 10:46 UTC on October 21, the attacker pushed 10 commits using the author email ckdi82fkoos@proton.me. The first nine commits were created on GitHub.com and therefore signed with GitHub's verified signature.

The first three (within 2 minutes) added the persistence files: cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py. Four more commits bumped version numbers to 1.107.0.

After a 39-minute gap, two commits refined the payload and added the critical data = "cook" directive to pyproject.toml, which instructed the build tool to bundle the malware into the wheel.

A final commit, made 58 minutes later with a different email (Berri-AI@users.noreply.github.com) and unsigned (suggesting a different environment), added COPY cook ./cook to the Dockerfiles.

Although the Berri-AI repository is unavailable, all commits remain accessible through the parent repository due to Git's fork object sharing. The full diff is available at: github.com/BerriAI/litellm/compare/a8113b0d...20535d8f

Post-Exploitation Activity

Wiz Research has observed abuse of stolen credentials, starting approximately 4.5 hours post-exfiltration. Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated AWS instance role credentials harvested from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes across multiple environments, from the following IP addresses:

168.100.8[.]57

165.227.201[.]8

Each credential was checked with sts:GetCallerIdentity, followed by bedrock:ListFoundationModels and a ListModels call, consistent with LLMjacking.

In a small number of environments, the attacker also enumerated IAM (ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys) and performed general discovery (ListAccounts, DescribeTrails, etc.).

Recommendations

Wiz customers should review our Threat Intel Center advisory: Supply Chain Attack Targeting LiteLLM .
