Title: AI Agent Security: Who Ran That Query?
Context: ” Investigators can settle attribution only from a session record, and they need the answer after the session ends
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why audit trails record a developer when an AI agent acted, how entitlement scope differs from action attribution, and the five facts a session record needs to show which agent ran a query and whose credentials it used.

An AI agent ran the query. The audit trail says a person did.

Why does an audit trail attribute AI agent activity to a person?

An AI agent connects with credentials issued to a person, so the audit trail records the person.

For example, at two in the morning, a database connection opens and a query runs against a production table. The audit trail records the username of a developer who was asleep at the time. A coding agent made the connection with the developer credentials while it worked through a task the developer had assigned before logging off.

Nothing in the log entry separates the developer from the agent. By its own standard, the log is complete. It still cannot answer the question an investigator will ask: Who ran that query?

In the Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report: The AI Enforcement Gap, Gal Diskin, Vice President of Research and Head of Delinea Labs, noted that actions taken with AI credentials “are very hard to distinguish between the AI and the human that launched them with existing tools and audit log limitations.”

Access models and audit trails were designed for human actors

Access models assume that the person who holds an account is the person who uses it. Until recently, that assumption held. A username answered two questions at once: Who held the access, and who used it. Audit trails follow the same design, so they record the username as the actor.

AI agents break that assumption. The account holder and the actor can now differ, and security teams need a way to talk about each one.

Entitlement scope is what an identity is permitted to reach. A developer with access to the production customer database has that database in scope, whether the developer or an agent opens the connection. Reviewers settle entitlement scope during an access review, before any session begins.

Action attribution identifies which actor used the entitlement and what that actor did. Attribution separates “the developer ran the query” from “a coding agent ran the query with the developer credentials.” Investigators can settle attribution only from a session record, and they need the answer after the session ends.

The agent never receives an entitlement of its own. It works with the entitlement already issued to the person who started it.

AI agents carry entitlements without the judgment behind them

A person receives an entitlement because someone decided that person could be trusted with access. An agent receives the same entitlement, but nobody made that decision about the agent. Nothing checks the agent against the original approval. The session record is the only place to find out what the agent did with the access it inherited.

How can security teams tell whether an AI agent or a person performed an action?

Security teams can tell only when the session record captures the initiator separately from the username. If the record captures only the username, the person and the agent look identical.

The Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report shows how often agents reach past their tasks. Of the IT and security leaders surveyed, 87% said an AI tool or agent at their organization accessed, or likely accessed, sensitive data beyond what its task required in the past year. Only 36% said their organization can always trace a sensitive AI access event back to a named human authorizer.

Example: overprivileged AI agent access

What happened. A developer asks a coding agent to look into a spike in failed customer logins. The developer has access to the production customer database for on-call work, so the agent has that access too. The agent pulls full customer records, including email addresses and phone numbers, and saves them to a file on the developer laptop. The task needed only login counts.

What the audit trail showed. The database log lists the queries under the developer username.

Why the evidence fell short. The log cannot show who pulled the records, which agent acted, or what instruction the agent followed. Without those facts, the reviewer cannot tell whether a person or an agent decided to export customer data, and the security team cannot decide who owns the response.

What should an AI agent audit trail record about each session?

An authorization record shows who approved an agent. A session record shows what the agent did with that approval; an AI agent audit trail needs both. At a minimum, the session record should capture five facts:

the identity that held the entitlement

whether a person or an AI agent initiated the session, and which agent

the resources the session reached and the actions taken on each resource

each path the agent used to reach a resource, including paths outside the Model Context Protocol (MCP)

a record the security team can reach and search during an investigation

AI agent activity can bypass MCP, so audit coverage cannot depend on MCP-only monitoring. MCP is a common standard for connecting AI agents to tools and data, but an agent with a database credential does not need it. The agent can open a database connection on its own, and a monitoring approach that watches only MCP traffic will never see that connection.

How does Delinea record AI agent activity?

Delinea records AI agent activity at the gateway, where the agent connects to the resource. When Delinea identifies the agent, the session record names both the person who held the entitlement and the agent that acted on behalf of that person. The record captures both names regardless of how the agent reached the resource.

Delinea built agent attribution by extending the gateway that already recorded human sessions. The developer and the coding agent appear in the same record, so investigators can review human and agent activity in one place.

AI agent attribution is the first step toward AI agent guardrails

Frank Vukovits, Chief Security Scientist at Delinea, framed the issue the way an auditor would: “Saying the AI agent did it is not a defensible answer.”

After a session ends, investigators use the session record to learn who ran the query. The gateway identifies the agent when the connection opens, so the same information can limit what the agent can do in the first place. Security teams can write entitlement rules for the agent itself. The developer keeps access to the production customer database, and the coding agent working for that developer does not.

Phil Calvin, Executive Vice President of AI Innovation at Delinea, tested an agent-specific rule which he documented in the blog "Your AI agent doesn't need to go rogue; it just needs you to be over-privileged". The gateway enabled him to write to a database and blocked the agent working for him from doing the same. His results show what a rule written for the agent can do.

In our conversations with security teams, we hear a consistent pattern. Teams want to audit which agent acted and which identity the agent used, but the larger concern is keeping agents out of critical production systems until the organization has a reason to trust them. Until that trust exists, the gateway can keep agents away from the most sensitive resources.

Security: Wants to eliminate exploitable risk immediately.

Engineering: Wants to maintain shipping velocity without breaking dependencies or spending time figuring out the right fix.

Cloud / Platform Operations: Wants to preserve uptime and infrastructure stability.

Full Text:
In 2028, the AI-cyber threat landscape facing the UK has almost certainly increased. Geopolitical tensions highly likely remain high, and nation states are almost certainly leveraging AI-powered cyber capabilities to project power and achieve strategic objectives.

State-sponsored actors, such as China and Russia, highly likely remain the greatest threat, through their developing AI capabilities. China, despite some quality lag in its chip development, has made significant strides in AI capabilities, with a focus on developing its own indigenous technologies. However, the increasing efficiency of AI models has reduced its dependence on cutting-edge western chip technology.

Meanwhile, it is highly likely that Russian cyber actors have leveraged open-source AI models, adapting and retraining them to suit their intelligence requirement needs, rather than developing in-house capabilities from scratch. This approach has allowed Russia to maintain a significant cyber capability without investing heavily in AI research and development. This has highly likely led to an increase in pre-positioning, espionage and intellectual property theft against UK interests.

The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal. Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally.

In 2028, it is likely that attackers will apply AI-cyber capability against known vulnerabilities in CNI legacy tech and the new opportunities in the attack surface provided by the deployment of AI tools within CNI. The use of AI within CNI has almost certainly presented an increased attack surface for adversaries to exploit. UK CNI has likely seen an increased volume of sophisticated attacks as the result of AI-cyber tools, some combatted by defensive AI tools, but implementation of defensive capabilities in UK CNI lags behind offensive ones.

Title: The 4 Elements of Exposure Prioritization and How to Operationalize Them
Context: Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will...
Full Text:
Your team is remediating more vulnerabilities than ever, yet your breach risk has barely changed. You’re spending too much time and effort on exposures attackers may never exploit, while higher-risk exposures sit, waiting in the queue. Gartner®’s report on exposure prioritization states that fewer than 10% of vulnerabilities are exploited, yet most are treated as urgent. The report also argues that CVSS scores alone do not predict actual exploitation or business impact.

Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will reduce breach likelihood by at least 70% compared to their peers relying primarily on CVSS-based vulnerability prioritization. Let’s break down how each element works, and how the Picus Platform puts all four into practice.

Severity-based prioritization made sense. Then it didn't.

Severity-driven prioritization was an entirely rational response for the era it was built in: a static attack surface, scarce adversary tooling, and remediation capacity that exceeded disclosure volume. Suddenly, that world is gone. Enterprises face tens of thousands of new vulnerabilities a year across cloud, SaaS, identity, and supply chain modalities, and AI has compressed time-to-exploit from weeks or months to hours.

Gartner is candid about why teams still anchor on severity, and it’s not a lack of awareness. In fact:

legacy metrics

compliance pressure, and

fragmented ownership

all reward what’s auditable over what’s legitimately impactful.

The result is widespread prioritization paralysis, with significant resources being funneled into remediation activity, but with remarkably little measurable risk reduction to show for it.

The smarter path is performing risk-based vulnerability management in its truest sense: measuring success by the exploitable exposures you’ve reduced, not the hypothetical vulnerabilities you’ve closed.

The four elements, and the question each one answers

Gartner’s framework rests on four pillars, and their value emerges only when added together. Sure, operationalizing one or two will bring you incremental gains, but integrating all four delivers significant reductions in both exposure windows and remediation fatigue.

Each element answers a distinct question about an exposure:

An exposure deserves urgent remediation only when all four answers converge.

The model aligns directly with the prioritization and validation stages of continuous threat exposure management (CTEM): remediation is mobilized only after priorities are validated in context.

Element 1: Threat Intelligence

Threat intelligence brings the adversary’s perspective into prioritization by showing which exposures attackers are actually exploiting. In real-world environments, many high-severity vulnerabilities are never exploited. Attackers frequently weaponize moderately rated vulnerabilities because they are easier to exploit, affect widely used systems, or can be exploited reliably. Past exploitation evidence helps teams focus their remediation efforts on a smaller, higher-risk subset of the backlog.

The operational challenge here is speed. Your team needs to use that intelligence to decide what to test and fix before a campaign reaches your environment. Track the time it takes to go from threat publication to testing and remediation.

Element 2: Asset Context and Business Criticality

An exploitable vulnerability becomes materially risky when it affects an asset that supports critical business functions, processes regulated data, or provides an easy pivot to higher-value systems. Without asset context, prioritization treats all assets as equal, and attention can easily drift to low-impact systems while crown-jewel exposures wait in the same queue.

This context already lives in tools most teams own: scanners, CMDBs, cloud security platforms, and identity systems. The practical work is to both unify it and keep it current, so its impact reflects the asset as it’s defended today, not as it appears in an inventory.

Element 3: Exploitability Modeling

Exploit prediction models such as EPSS estimate how likely a vulnerability is to be exploited, based on patterns like exploit complexity, component prevalence, and disclosure-to-exploitation timelines. These models complement threat intelligence by surfacing latent and lingering risks: helping identify the exposures that are statistically likely to be exploited before exploitation is widely observed, enabling you to shift teams from a reactive to an anticipatory or even proactive stance.

Statistical likelihood describes the world in general, not your organization’s unique environment. EPSS points to what’s probably exploitable somewhere; only validation proves what is exploitable here and now. Exploitability modeling works best as a filter that feeds validation, not as a final verdict.

Gartner’s full report goes deeper into how EPSS, KEV and similar models should be weighted against threat intelligence and control validation. Download the Gartner report on exposure prioritization to read the complete analysis.

Element 4: Security Control Validation

This is the element most programs are missing. Security control validation evaluates each exposure against the defenses already deployed around it: segmentation, endpoint protection, detection coverage, and identity controls.

An exposure that looks critical may be practically unreachable behind your existing defenses, while a less critical one on a poorly monitored asset may carry far more risk than its score suggests. Ignoring control context, Gartner warns, leads to systematic overestimation of risk and the wasted remediation efforts that follow it.

Testing shows whether attackers can realistically exploit an exposure in your specific environment today. Gartner notes this capability can be achieved with adversarial exposure validation techniques: proving exploitability with evidence, through live attack execution where testing is safe, and attack-chain analysis against deployed controls where assets can’t be touched.

How Picus Operationalizes All Four Elements into a Single Loop

The sum here is indeed greater than its parts, but the four elements only deliver their full value when evaluated together. This is, not surprisingly, where most organizations struggle as vulnerability management grows into exposure management. Why? Because in most organizations, threat intelligence sits with one team, asset context with another, exploitability scores are in a scanner, and control effectiveness only shows up in periodic assessments. Four inputs in four places do not lead to one decision.

Picus is named among the vendors in the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Adversarial Exposure Validation. The Picus Platform brings all four elements together in a continuous loop: Discover, Validate, Prioritize, and Mobilize.

Here’s how the platform maps to each element.

Security control validation deserves a closer look, because evidence is what turns the other three elements from assumptions into decisions. Picus Breach and Attack Simulation is one of three validation methods on the platform.

Picus Autonomous Penetration Testing runs real exploit paths against reachable production assets and proves which ones lead to your critical systems.

Picus Exposure Validation breaks each CVE into the techniques an attacker must use and tests every step against your existing controls on that asset, with no exploit fired, so even assets you can never test live get an evidence-backed verdict.

Together, these three validation methods give every exposure one explainable, organization-specific rating.

What Good Looks Like: Measuring the Shift

If prioritization is working, you should be able to see it in three places: your controls hold up better, you respond faster, and your team spends its time on the exposures that matter, rather than wasting it on the ones that don’t.

Here’s what our customers are reporting.

Within three months of deploying Picus, their security controls are blocking or detecting roughly twice as many attacks as before.

Response time to emerging threats drops by 89%.

Missed remediation deadlines on high and critical vulnerabilities fall by 92%, because the queue now holds only the exposures proven to be exploitable.

One customer cut their critical ticket backlog by 98%. And the full cycle, from a new threat or change being detected to actual validated findings landing with the right team, runs under six hours.

A CISO at our 2026 Validation Summit put it simply: While a severity score is a useful label for sorting, the smarter strategy is to shut down those attack paths that could actually hurt your business. The numbers above back this up.

Exposure Prioritization Is a Risk Decision. Make It With Evidence.

Gartner frames exposure prioritization as a risk decision, and we agree.

Each of the four elements answers one part of it: threat intelligence tells you whether the exposure matters to an attacker, asset context tells you what it would cost you, exploitability modeling tells you how likely it is to take place, and security control validation tells you whether it could actually happen here.

The Picus Platform runs all four in one continuous loop, so every exposure ends in a decision you can defend to your board and your auditors: so you can fix it, mitigate it, or accept it with proof.

Title: Gangsters, Money Trails, and Wuffy | Huntress
Context: " - Geoff White, author and investigative journalist Zhdanova reportedly tried Garantex first, a sanctioned Russian exchange, which only made the crypto hotter
Full Text:
Your kids spend a month begging for an AI toy dog they found online. At $30, marked down 70% from $100, it feels cheap enough to risk, and you finally cave. You know online orders like this can go sideways, but the worst-case scenario is a piece of junk and a few disappointed kids, right?

The dog arrives, and it's basically a battery-operated stuffed animal with no AI inside. You mutter a few curse words under your breath and write it off. What you never see is that your $30 went to one of more than 250 near-identical websites in the same cybercrime network.

Mastercard scam investigators ordered the same dog, aka Wuffy, and followed the money trail. The online store looked legit, with a 4.7-star rating and customer support that answered fast and in detail. But the payment record showed a company headquartered in Lithuania while the site listed a US address, and the store had 250 look-alikes that all carried a 4.7-star rating and a 70% discount. Mastercard's analysis tied an estimated $50 million a year in transactions to the network, and the full scale was likely larger.

Why nobody chases a $30 charge

Victims see the loss, but the trail behind it, who got paid and what that money funded next, stays hidden. A scam like Wuffy is built to keep it that way.

According to Ann Johnson, Mastercard's Executive Vice President of Security Solutions, scammers like credit cards because the loss lands on someone else. When a store turns out to be a scam, the bank covers the loss. Scammers rarely have to pay any of it back, and they know it. So they keep prices reasonable on purpose. They list a $100 "regular" price, so $30 feels like a Black Friday deal. They count on buyers to write off a $30 charge, since fighting it costs more time and money than it's worth.

Now multiply that across more than 250 websites. Each charge looks too small to chase, and only someone who connects the dots across all of them sees the full scale.

For the cybercriminal, a convincing cover story and a price nobody pushes back on add up to steady money with little risk. For you, it's a $30 annoyance that's easy to forget.

Where a $40 million ransom really goes

The criminals behind Wuffy hid in plain sight, making small sales incrementally through a legit-looking store and normal payment systems.

Ransomware has the opposite problem. You're the ransomware gang, and the victim just paid, which leaves you holding millions in traceable crypto. No mainstream exchange will take that much without asking questions, so you need someone who can clean it.

Investigative journalist Geoff White, who covers organized crime and technology, tells the story of one reported $40 million ransom paid by CNA Financial, a US financial firm. As he tells it, Britain's National Crime Agency (NCA), in an investigation called Operation Destabilise, followed the money and traced chunks of it to accounts it links to Ekaterina Zhdanova, a Russian socialite.

"CNA Financial's daily revenues are apparently $38 million. It's a massive amount of money. You can't go to Coinbase or Kraken with that huge quantity of money and expect them not to ask a lot of questions. So the hackers were looking for somewhere else to put that money." - Geoff White, author and investigative journalist

Zhdanova reportedly tried Garantex first, a sanctioned Russian exchange, which only made the crypto hotter. Then she turned to UK drug gangs. The NCA says she offered them a swap: their cash for her crypto. The gangs wanted to unload bulky, vulnerable piles of cash, and crypto could cross borders to buy more product.

"Where does the money from ransomware go? Suddenly you expand out into this massive world connecting all these different networks, not just criminal, but illicit and state-level." - Geoff White

The money trail keeps branching. When Russia invaded Ukraine, Russians with frozen money wanted funds in the UK to buy property or pay school fees. Reportedly, they paid Zhdanova in rubles, and she freed up the same amount in cash in the UK.

The NCA says another branch was tied to the Russian government's efforts to move money into the UK to fund spy rings. Police raided a guest house and found surveillance gear, including a Minion toy with a hidden camera. Six people were convicted, and the NCA says Zhdanova sat at the heart of the funding.

The bottom line is that a company that pays a ransom has no way to know where the money will end up, and neither does anyone who pays $30 for a toy dog.

We can all cut off the money trail

Criminals watch their margins closely, so every bit of friction helps, whether you're protecting your own card or your company's accounts.

If a deal or request is too good to be true, it is. Don't share your information. Take your business elsewhere, to retailers you trust.

If someone contacts you claiming to be your bank or a trusted vendor, stop and verify through a number or website you already know, like the one on the back of your card. Spoofed phone numbers are common, and a link a caller sends can be one digit off.

Talk about scams at home and work, especially with younger family members and colleagues, whose sense of what's private online may differ from yours.

Title: CrowdStrike Secures AI Agents Inside Claude Cowork
Context: Built in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand, this integration extends Falcon protection to AI agents across their lifecycle, from agent...
Full Text:
When Claude Cowork executes code locally, it runs inside an isolated virtual machine on the user's computer. On the host, that VM runs as a single opaque process: The agent's activity inside the VM, including the processes it spawns, the packages it installs, and the network connections it makes, is not visible to the host's endpoint security sensor. Because host folders can be mounted into the VM, sensitive data can sit within the agent's reach.

Today at Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike announced it is bringing CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian protection natively into Anthropic's Claude Cowork. Built in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand, this integration extends Falcon protection to AI agents across their lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution. It runs the Falcon sensor directly inside the Cowork VM on both macOS and Windows to bring runtime visibility and detection into the agent's execution environment.

The integration is now available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November.

How It Works

Consider this scenario: A user asks Cowork for a script to align their slides to a brand standard. While completing the task, the agent installs the latest version of a common Python package. Neither the user nor the agent knows that an adversary has compromised the package at its source. Once installed, that package reads host data through a mounted folder and sends it out to a known malicious endpoint. The Falcon sensor running inside the VM would detect it. This is exactly the type of malicious activity and potential data exfiltration the integration is built to detect as agents execute tasks.

CrowdStrike’s sensor integration with the Cowork VM will deliver:

Visibility and detection where agents execute: Process, package, and network activity inside the Cowork VM will no longer be a blind spot, so teams can detect and investigate threats with the same Falcon telemetry they use everywhere else.

The same visibility on macOS and Windows: The VM runs the same Linux environment on both, so customers get consistent coverage regardless of the OS.

Deployment and control through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform: Admins will turn the integration on through their existing device management, the same way they deploy the Falcon sensor today, and the Falcon Linux sensor deploys inside the Cowork VM. From there, the team controls it through the Falcon platform so Claude Cowork comes under the same security control plane as the rest of the environment.

Built with Anthropic

CrowdStrike and Anthropic worked together to bring Falcon protection directly into Claude Cowork's execution environment. Anthropic enabled Falcon deployment within Cowork, while CrowdStrike engineered and tested the integration across installation, real-time protection, and ongoing updates. Through this beta integration, enterprises can extend the security they already trust from the Falcon platform to AI agents in Claude Cowork, alongside the virtual machine, permissions, and admin controls built into Cowork.

CrowdStrike’s Architectural Difference

AI agents don't operate in one layer, and neither does Falcon Guardian. Agents reach out over the network to communicate with LLMs, but they also execute processes locally on the workstations where they’re installed. These actions may never cross network boundaries. The Falcon sensor and Falcon Guardian see both agentic workstreams and fuse them together in a single view from CrowdStrike’s endpoint network inspection and OS-level visibility. This unified view, CrowdStrike® Agent Graph, shows analysts not only what agents were asked to do, but what they did at runtime.

CrowdStrike also delivers agent-level enforcement controls via hook integrations for agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor.

The Claude Cowork integration extends Falcon Guardian coverage to a new place agents work. It takes Falcon Guardian’s runtime security foundation into the VM where Cowork runs its code, providing visibility and detection for what the agent executes, installs, and connects to across its lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution.

What's Next

Endpoint agents like Claude Cowork run their code inside a VM that host-only security can't see into. By running the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM on macOS and Windows, this integration will close that gap. It will bring Falcon visibility and detection to where agents execute, it will be deployed and controlled through Falcon, and it will extend the runtime foundation of the three layers of AI security in Falcon Guardian.

The integration is focused on visibility and detection inside the VM. Available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November 2026, it enables customers to deploy the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM through their existing device management tools. Their teams gain visibility and detection across the processes, packages, and network activity inside the VM.

Attackers were definitely testing our cybersecurity best practices during Cybersecurity Awareness Month. A cloud region was knocked offline in Japan. Grocery stores across the US and Europe were either taken offline temporarily or lost produce. An AI agent chained two vulnerabilities to breach an organization that was established to help others with vulnerability disclosure. And finally, there were well over one thousand vulnerability patches in a single day. No seriously. Vulnerability management was like walking into a burning building in October.

With that, let’s dive into this month’s security news.

Oct. 7: Ransomware takes down Japanese cloud infrastructure

A Japanese SoftBank subsidiary called IDC Frontier confirmed a ransomware attack began on October 7, impacting nearly 500 companies and local governments.

Allegedly, customers saw messages claiming 3.6PB of data was encrypted in seven minutes.

The ransomware group claims to have deleted snapshots.

This was in addition to other large-scale attacks across the country in October, including Burger King Japan, Nikkei, and Capcom.

Shared responsibility includes your own backups. Test restoring them somewhere that isn’t your provider.

Oct. 11: Hackers burn French fridges

Overnight, between October 11 and 12, hackers forced refrigerators in hundreds of grocery stores across France into continuous defrost mode.

For six hours, the refrigeration equipment was pushed to temperatures of 50°C (122°F).

The Danish manufacturer, Danfoss, said the stores were running outdated firmware or had reached end-of-life support, which left equipment exposed to the internet.

This caused fires and potentially tens of millions of dollars in spoiled food. Although the incident was due to operational equipment exposure, it’s a global wake-up call to the physical impact of supply chain attacks.

Oct. 20-21: Six Linux vulnerabilities dropped at once

Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent five Linux kernel reports to the Linux kernel security team and one report to the ConnMan mailing list, all of which went out to the broader public mailing lists.

ZDI-CAN-33367 is a local privilege escalation in skb_zerocopy() with a public proof of concept. It’s another gap in the Dirty Frag fix (CVE-2026-43284) from May.

Oct. 21: PHP2Shell

PHP shipped two emergency releases on October 21 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

An unauthenticated attacker can run code with HTTP requests alone, and researchers estimate 1.3 -1.9 million exposed hosts are potentially vulnerable.

Exploitation started before the patches existed. Amazon reported seeing an attempt on October 17. Organizations need to patch immediately, restart every PHP worker, and assume breach as they scan environments for signs of unauthorized access.

Oct. 21: Node2Shell

Node2Shell, also known as HTTP2Shell, landed on organizations’ radars after Node.js fixed an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder on October 21.

The first public GitHub repository tracking the CVE appeared only hours after the fix, and exploitation attempts were confirmed within days.

The decoder also ships in Bun, Python Brotli packages, and some Envoy configurations.

Additional Sysdig TRT findings

An AI agent chained two vulnerabilities to exploit a vulnerability disclosure program

On October 2, Sysdig TRT published an initial blog on the breach of the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) on September 21.

The attacker exploited two vulnerabilities in the Zammad open source helpdesk tool. These were identified as CVE-2026-102489, a remote code execution flaw, and CVE-2026-102490, a local privilege escalation flaw.

Originally thought to be zero-days, Zammad said it received a report on CVE-2026-102489 in August, before the breach.

Pickle bypasses

On October 27, the Sysdig TRT published an analysis on using pickles to bypass model-loading defenses in machine learning.

Six documented CVE bypasses beat PyTorch weights_only, Keras safe_mode, and picklescan. The check and the loader disagreed about what the file was in each case.

Loading a pickle file executes the code inside it. That’s a design flaw, not a patchable bug, so the fix is in the formatting. Switch to safetensors where possible and use runtime to detect what happens after the pickle is loaded.

Also in the news

Microsoft patches a record 1,411 flaws: Vulnerability discovery is quickly outpacing security teams’ capability to remediate. KrebsOnSecurity said the prior month’s record of 972 patched flaws was 10 times a “normal” Microsoft patch load, and October dwarfed it. The increase is due to the internal use of AI platforms to find vulnerabilities within Microsoft products. Security teams need to prioritize reachability and exploitation. This month included one actively exploited zero-day (CVE-2026-96951), two publicly disclosed ones, and 70 critical flaws.

US and European grocery store operations disrupted: Ahold Delhaize confirmed a cybersecurity incident on October 12 after taking systems offline on October 11 to contain it. Albert Heijn, Etos, Gall & Gall, Delhaize, and Stop & Shop were some of the stores affected.

Nation-state threat actors using agentic AI: China-affiliated threat group Storm-0940 used agents to compromise ConnectWise customers, according to Microsoft on October 21. The group used the open source ARTEX framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants. In multiple cases, the actors moved from targeting to privileged cloud access in less than three hours.

Closing thoughts

Look at the clocks from this month. PHP2Shell was exploited four days before the patch. There was a PoC in a public repo for Node2Shell within hours. Storm-0940 went from targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours. Patch what’s reasonable first, in a reasonable amount of time. But watch for what happens after an exploit is known. Attackers can’t hide behavior.

And we just wrapped Cybersecurity Awareness Month. If you want to take a breather and step away from vulnerabilities for just a moment, here’s a list of simple things you should be doing daily to avoid a breach.

To stay informed between our monthly wrap-ups, you can get the latest from the Sysdig TRT on our blog, or follow my bi-weekly security newsletter musings on LinkedIn.

Title: A TraderTraitor's guide to getting away with billions.
Context: Hackers targeted air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia over the weekend, sending false warnings of nuclear attacks and other threats. Cursor has released detection tools and indicators of compromise.
Full Text:
The FBI blames North Korea for a record-breaking crypto heist. Hackers hijack air raid alerts in Ukraine and Russia. European supermarket freezers come under attack again. Aur0ra ransomware operators put AI agents to work. Android’s SMS of Death gets a proof-of-concept exploit. Malicious Claude Code extensions infiltrate Cursor’s marketplace. Google offers a quarter-million-dollar bug bounty. ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Cynthia Kaiser, SVP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former Deputy Director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, sharing how the AI cybercrime economy is open for business and booming. The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Today is Monday November 2nd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

The FBI attributes last week’s record crypto heist to North Korea.

The FBI has attributed last week’s theft of more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group. Investigators say the attackers are converting stolen assets into Ethereum and laundering funds through decentralized finance platforms and instant swap services.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic reports that roughly 2.9 billion dollars has been frozen or seized, leaving approximately 3.3 billion beyond issuers’ reach, spread across hundreds of cryptocurrency wallets.

Binance says it will cover the losses, protecting customer funds. The company continues investigating what it calls a complex attack involving multiple perpetrators and a self-destruct mechanism designed to erase forensic evidence.

TraderTraitor has been linked to several major cryptocurrency thefts, including the previous record-breaking 1.5-billion-dollar Bybit heist.

Hackers target air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia.

Hackers targeted air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia over the weekend, sending false warnings of nuclear attacks and other threats.

Ukraine’s official Air Alert app was compromised late Saturday, pushing messages in Russian warning of incoming nuclear strikes, chemical threats, and street fighting. Sirens also sounded across the country. Authorities temporarily disabled notifications, warned residents against clicking suspicious links, and restored normal operations within hours.

Early Sunday, Russia reported a similar attack on its emergency alert app. Users received bogus warnings that nuclear warheads had been launched across Russia, along with instructions to stockpile food and shelter in basements.

The Russian incident may have been retaliation for the earlier attack on Ukraine, although responsibility remains unconfirmed. Both countries acknowledged their systems had been compromised.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted, remotely raising freezer temperatures and spoiling food.

Monday’s attacks affected more than 50 stores in Belgium, along with retailers in Sweden, Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg. Some freezers were reportedly set to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 Fahrenheit.

The incident follows a similar attack three weeks earlier that affected roughly 700 supermarkets in France. Authorities haven’t identified the perpetrators or established whether the attacks are connected.

Some affected systems rely on discontinued refrigeration controllers that no longer receive security updates. Technicians say certain equipment requires physical modifications rather than software patches.

The incidents highlight the risks posed by internet-connected industrial equipment, particularly when aging devices remain accessible remotely. For supermarkets, the consequences are immediate: spoiled inventory and costly repairs.

The Aur0ra ransomware group is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions.

Sophos researchers say the cybercriminal group behind Aur0ra ransomware is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions and evade security defenses.

The group, tracked as GOLD OGRE, reportedly used the AI coding tool Cursor to test endpoint security products and help conduct attacks. Human operators supplied credentials, network access, and objectives, then let AI agents handle reconnaissance, credential attacks, privilege escalation, and lateral movement with limited supervision.

Researchers observed agents adapting their techniques when initial attempts failed, sometimes gaining domain administrator access. Three organizations investigated were subsequently named on Aur0ra’s leak site.

The attackers also reportedly bypassed AI safety restrictions by describing their activities as authorized security testing.

Sophos warns that agentic AI could accelerate ransomware operations and lower the technical expertise required to carry them out.

The Android SMS of Death gets a proof of concept.

A security researcher has published a proof-of-concept exploit for an Android vulnerability dubbed “SMS of Death.” Tracked as CVE-2026-58882, the zero-click flaw allows attackers to crash phones or disrupt cellular service, including emergency calls, using specially crafted text messages.

Victims receive no visible warning, and repeated messages can trigger reboot loops requiring a factory reset.

Google reportedly patched the vulnerability in October for Android 14 through 17, although the fix wasn’t listed in its security bulletin. Older Android 12 and 13 devices remain vulnerable.

Malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension were distributed through Cursor’s marketplace.

Attackers distributed malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension through Cursor’s marketplace in a supply chain attack on October 29th.

Two compromised versions remained available for approximately eleven hours, potentially reaching 5,000 developer systems running Windows or macOS.

The malicious code collected system information and attempted to establish persistent remote access through reverse SSH tunnels. Cursor says those attempts generally failed because the extension lacked administrative privileges.

Anthropic confirmed its official distributions were unaffected.

Cursor removed the malicious extensions, temporarily suspended its marketplace, rotated security keys, and took steps to shut down the attacker’s infrastructure.

Affected users are urged to investigate their systems, since uninstalling the extension may leave malicious persistence mechanisms behind. Cursor has released detection tools and indicators of compromise.

Google offers a quarter million dollar bug bounty.

Google is offering security researchers up to $250,000 for vulnerabilities that could enable complete administrative takeover of Google Cloud environments.

The expanded bug bounty program rewards exploits that grant unrestricted control over cloud projects or organizations without requiring stolen credentials, existing access, or social engineering.

Remote code execution in Google’s underlying production infrastructure may also qualify.

Google has established strict testing rules to protect customer systems, including a cryptographic method for demonstrating unauthorized access without compromising real accounts.

The company says AI-assisted research is helping uncover increasingly sophisticated vulnerabilities.

ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit.

The parents of a 31-year-old Seattle software engineer are suing OpenAI, alleging that dangerous medical advice from ChatGPT contributed to their daughter’s death.

According to the lawsuit, Bowen Wan consulted the chatbot after losing her job, concerned that her epilepsy medication was affecting her English-speaking abilities during interviews.

The complaint alleges ChatGPT provided instructions for discontinuing her medication, discouraged consulting doctors, and reassured her when she began experiencing seizures.

Wan died from a seizure in February.

Her parents claim OpenAI failed to implement adequate safeguards, particularly for Chinese-language conversations.

OpenAI called the case heartbreaking, noting that Wan used an older version of ChatGPT. The company says newer models are better at recognizing medical emergencies, while emphasizing that ChatGPT cannot replace professional medical care.

Monday business briefing.

Cybersecurity investors are opening their wallets, with cloud and AI security companies leading the latest funding rounds.

San Francisco’s Upwind Security tops the list with a $400 million Series C, followed by Estonian DDoS protection provider Blackwall, which raised $100 million.

Agentic AI security startup Infisical secured $40 million, while Israeli security operations company Mave emerged from stealth with $34 million.

Mobile security provider iVerify and confidential cloud startup Modelyo each raised $17 million. Ultra Security secured $10 million, industrial cybersecurity firm Indurex raised $7.8 million, and Northstar Security landed $7 million. QuestorAI and Cygrid each raised $3 million.

On the acquisition front, healthcare technology provider Tegria purchased cybersecurity and cloud hosting firm CloudWave. Forte Technologies acquired managed security provider Business Cyber Security Solutions.

And Belgian developer security company Aikido Security launched a new workforce security business called Noon, combining its acquisitions of Poland’s Cyberly and Belgium’s Outkept.

The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Security researcher Xusheng Li discovered that a Lenovo fingerprint-protected USB drive, advertised as offering AES-256 encryption, was essentially an ordinary SD card in an expensive disguise.

The fingerprint reader controlled access to the USB connection, but the data itself wasn’t encrypted. Anyone with physical access could simply extract the card.

Further investigation uncovered similar problems across multiple manufacturers, including hardcoded encryption keys, exposed passwords, and hidden accounts with simple credentials.

Using AI-assisted reverse engineering, Li cracked several supposedly secure products in minutes.

Lenovo has issued fixes for affected devices, although some require owners to ship their drives back or arrange firmware upgrades.

The research is a reminder that security claims aren’t always what they seem, particularly when manufacturers rely on proprietary technology nobody bothers to examine. As it turns out, some of these supposedly encrypted drives were keeping secrets from everyone except the people trying to steal them.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Title: Your Artifactory is fine. Your Linux kernel hosting it might not be.
Context: In this scenario, a lost race only kills that one connection, so the attacker just tries again
Full Text:
Summary As we’ve written, AI is shrinking the time between “a fix is public” and “someone has a working exploit” to near-zero. JFrog products are not affected by Linux kernel CVE-2026-98432. Artifactory, Xray, and the rest of the JFrog Platform do not contain this flaw, as it lives in the Linux kernel itself. We are advising every self-managed JFrog customer to check their Linux hosts and update their kernels now to protect their environments, which may include hosted versions of JFrog products. Once your OS is updated, JFrog products are not at risk.

Our goal is always to protect your systems, and in some cases that may include advice on the protection of the environments your JFrog products operate in. JFrog Cloud customers are not affected by the Linux vulnerability, but if you self-manage JFrog, read on.

Your Linux kernel may be exposed, requiring you to patch it to protect your environment.

What happened

On October 15, the Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-98432. It’s a use-after-free in the code that sets up new IPv4 TCP connections, caused by a race condition. The bug dates back to Linux 4.4. Upstream fixed it on October 5 following main line patching on September 17; upstream was fixed a full ten days before the CVE went public.

The kernel team scores this vulnerability a 9.8. Red Hat, Oracle, SUSE and Amazon score it lower, between 5.9 and 8.1.

Then, Anthropic published research on October 27 saying its Claude model wrote a working exploit. A remote attacker with no credentials gets a root shell on servers with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener. In Anthropic’s test, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes. Getting command execution took only five more. In this scenario, a lost race only kills that one connection, so the attacker just tries again.

Importantly, Anthropic did not publish the exploit code. As of November 2, there have been no reports of attacks in the wild. MPTCP is less exotic than it sounds: since Go 1.24, Go programs request it by default on the sockets they listen on. The Go Security Team also says the underlying bug isn’t specific to MPTCP. (Tip: JFrog deployments include several Go services within versions later than 1.24.)

As a JFrog customer…

In a self-managed deployment, you own the operating system that JFrog operates in. We are responsible for the security of our products, and you for the platform underneath (host, kernel, patching) in a shared responsibility model. A vulnerable kernel under a healthy JFrog install still puts that host, and everything on it, at risk.

As of October 30, neither Ubuntu nor RHEL had released a fixed kernel. Ubuntu 22.04 through 26.10 are marked work in progress, and older releases are plain vulnerable. RHEL 8, 9 and 10 are listed as affected, with no date. Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE and Amazon Linux have shipped fixes for at least some kernels. Check your exact release, because coverage varies within each distro.

What we’re advising you to do as soon as possible

Find out what you’re running. Version numbers lie, because distros backport fixes without bumping them. Check the changelog instead.

On Debian or Ubuntu:

apt changelog linux-image-$(uname -r) | grep CVE-2026-98432

On RHEL and its derivatives:

rpm -q --changelog kernel-$(uname -r) | grep CVE-2026-98432

If the command prints nothing, your running kernel doesn’t have the fix.

Patch where a fix exists, then reboot. A kernel update does nothing until the machine boots into it. If you build your own kernel, the fix is in 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. The kernel team recommends moving to the latest stable release rather than cherry-picking the one commit.

Where there’s no fix yet, be proactive about it. Red Hat says no available mitigation meets its bar. Switching off MPTCP program by program is fragile, and the Go team says so directly: one forgotten listener and you’re exposed again. Narrow who can reach those hosts at the network layer, watch your vendor’s advisory for CVE-2026-98432, and patch the day the package is available. Another mitigation option could be using an L7 load balancer or reverse proxy with TCP termination to reduce direct exposure of vulnerable hosts. Reducing exposure doesn’t repair the bug, but it does reduce the number of people who can try to exploit it.

Make the next one simpler. If you proxy your Debian or RPM repos through Artifactory, the fixed kernel arrives in the repo your hosts already pull from. Stage it, promote it, roll it out in waves, with the same process you use for everything else. A kernel package is an artifact like any other, and it should have a system of record.

JFrog Xray scans your supply chain artifacts and images. It won’t tell you what kernel your host is running, because the kernel isn’t in either one; step one is a command you must run yourself.

The window is big, but shrinking

In an approaching-zero window from fix to exploit, rapid patching is required. The fix for this vulnerability was made public on October 5. A working exploit story hit on October 27. On October 30, two of the most widely run enterprise distros still had no update.

Our advice to protect your systems is simple:

Run the changelog check on every host that runs JFrog today. Update and reboot where a fixed kernel exists. Where it doesn’t, restrict access and subscribe to your distro’s advisory for CVE-2026-98432 so the fix doesn’t sit in a queue that could get forgotten.

Title: Anti-Oligarchy Activists Plan to Dox Elon Musk and Hundreds of Billionaire-Linked Homes
Context: Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people...
Full Text:
An underground activist group says it plans to start openly doxing billionaires as part of a phased campaign against what it calls the American oligarchy—beginning this month with a release that maps the homes of Elon Musk, his brother Kimbal, and Tesla’s board, alongside investors and suppliers that keep the corporation afloat.

Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people they consider their top lieutenants, using nearly every method available to a private investigator, and some that are not.

The pair say the group is international and includes grassroots activists, researchers, journalists, and artists, including some who received top honors in print, television, and digital media in their former careers. For security, many work in “silos” and do not know each other’s names. Through its connections, the group says it has raised more than $1.2 million from “a heartening number of wealthy class traitors” who share in the view that concentrations of extreme wealth and political power pose an “existential threat.”

In a press release Monday, the group says it intends to publish in coming releases more than 150 home addresses, most of them previously unreported. It also promises more than 3,500 records on people with a combined wealth of about $1.4 trillion, plus reporting on what the group alleges are “criminal exploits and security lapses.”

Members of the organization call themselves Capytistas, a play on Zapatistas, the Indigenous insurgents of southern Mexico.

The capybara, a placid rodent famous for getting along with almost any other animal, became the group’s avatar during the early days of Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, as a secret rival to the Shiba Inu—the Doge meme Musk used to brand the agency. (The meme has since been reclaimed by pro-Ukranian activists who post as cartoon dogs to mock Russian propaganda and raise money for the war.)

Americans have long used the term “oligarch” to refer almost exclusively to Russian tycoons who carved up state industries after the Soviet collapse. But it entered mainstream American politics decisively in January 2025, when President Joe Biden used his farewell address to warn that an “oligarchy is taking shape in America.” No one typifies the “extreme wealth, power, and influence” Biden described more than the trillionaire Musk, who held an unpaid job as a special government employee for much of 2025 and has thrown more than $700 million into federal elections since 2023; the equivalent of roughly 15 million typical donations online.

Doxing—the Capytistas’ chosen tactic—has meanwhile become a favored weapon of political guerrillas and self-appointed state informants: In March 2025, as protesters gathered outside Tesla dealerships, an anonymous site called DOGEQuest posted what it claims were the addresses of Tesla owners and DOGE staff. Months later, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement official testified that his unit drew more than three-quarters of its deportation referrals from Canary Mission—a site with similarly nebulous funding but radically different goals: building dossiers on pro-Palestinian students and professors.

Title: Threat Hunting: What It Is, How It Works, & Why It Matters
Context: threat intelligence Threat intelligence tells you what attackers are doing out there, threat detection catches known activity in your environment, and threat hunting looks for...
Full Text:
Most security tools catch what they already know: known signatures, known patterns, known behaviors.

The threats that do the most damage don't match anything in the rulebook. They show up with stolen credentials, built-in Windows tools, and quiet moves that look like a normal Tuesday. Yet in our 2025 cybercrime survey, 57% of IT professionals said they're very confident their defenses can catch an advanced attack that doesn't rely on malware signatures. Confidence is nice. Evidence is better.

Threat hunting closes that gap. Here's how.

What is threat hunting?

Threat hunting is the proactive search across networks and endpoints for signs of malicious activity that traditional security defenses missed. Instead of waiting for an alert, analysts assume an attacker could already be inside and go looking for proof. That's what sets cyber threat hunting apart: it starts with a question, not an alert.

Reactive detection waits for a tool to fire, and a tool only fires if someone already wrote the rule. Proactive threat hunting asks, "If an attacker were in here, what would they have touched?" and goes looking before the threat goes down. Think of it as spotting the smoke before the fire, catching early indicators of compromise (IOCs) before they become full-blown incidents.

Every hunt aims to find overlooked activity, cut attacker dwell time, sharpen detection rules, and share intel. So how does it work? A hunter builds a hypothesis, searches telemetry for evidence, and turns what they find into a detection so the next attempt gets caught automatically.

Threat hunting vs. threat detection vs. threat intelligence

Threat intelligence tells you what attackers are doing out there, threat detection catches known activity in your environment, and threat hunting looks for what both missed. They feed each other: intel gives hunters hypotheses, and hunts produce new detections.

Threat hunting

Threat detection

Threat intelligence

Main goal

Find hidden, unknown threats that bypassed automated defenses

Identify known malicious activity and generate alerts

Give context on external and emerging threats to inform defenses

Approach

Proactive, human-driven

Reactive, automated

Analytical, research-based

Input/triggers

Hypotheses, threat intel reports, or hunches based on internal context, plus low-priority alerts

Rules, signatures, and known indicators

Raw data, OSINT, dark web, vendor feeds, internal hunting findings

Output

New detection rules and new threat intelligence

Security alerts, incident creation

Actionable reports and feeds

Timing

Periodic or continuous

Real-time or near real-time

Continuous collection and analysis

Key tools

SIEM querying, EDR, network analysis tools, custom scripts

SIEM, EDR, IDS/IPS, antivirus

Threat intelligence platforms (TIPs), OSINT tools, feeds, databases

Primary trigger

Hypothesis-driven

Alert-driven

Research-driven

Typical data sources

EDR and SIEM telemetry

OSINT and threat feeds

Who typically does it

Dedicated threat hunter

SOC analyst

Threat intel analyst

Types of threat hunting

Every hunt falls into one of two types of threat hunting.

Structured threat hunting works from clear hypotheses and well-defined procedures, which keeps it consistent, repeatable, and scalable. Hunters know which tactic, technique, or procedure (TTP) they're after and roughly where to look.

Unstructured threat hunting is guided by curiosity, with no strict guidelines. It's data science applied to security, and it matters because advanced attackers often use never-before-seen techniques that slip past known TTPs. It takes senior-level knowledge to pull off.

Threat hunting methodologies

Structured and unstructured describe how a hunt runs. Threat hunting methodologies describe where it starts. Each uses different threat hunting techniques to reach a testable hypothesis, so the right threat hunting methodology depends on what you've got to work with.

Intelligence-driven hunts

A structured approach that starts with collected intel: file names, hashes, IPs, campaigns, IOCs, email addresses, domains. Hunters form hypotheses and test them internally.

Data-driven hunts

These unstructured hunts start with your own data, like low-priority alerts, detections, or aggregated analytics. None of it is a smoking gun, but it gives hunters a starting point for a hypothesis.

Knowledge-driven hunts

These rely on what hunters know about available data sets, your network, and adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). Frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK help them build hypotheses around techniques seen in the wild.

Hybrid hunts

Hybrid hunts combine two or more methodologies. If your data shows odd events on endpoints and intel suggests they match an active campaign, that's a sharper hypothesis than either source gives alone.

The threat hunting process

Good hunts aren't random searches. The cyber threat hunting process for a structured hunt follows three phases.

Planning phase

Gather intelligence. Hunters study risk areas, historical data, and outside sources like open-source intelligence to spot patterns worth chasing.

Build a hypothesis. Hunters make an educated guess about which threat actors, tactics, and techniques might be in play. That hypothesis becomes the north star for the whole hunt.

Identify data sources. With a hypothesis in hand, hunters determine where the evidence would live: system logs, network traffic, endpoint telemetry.

Execution phase

Query the data. Hunters scrutinize data by querying databases, analyzing logs, and doing forensic work.

Follow TTPs and behavioral patterns. Hunters chase breadcrumbs that line up with the hypothesis. Behavior beats indicators here: attackers can swap a file hash in seconds, but they can't easily change how they work, which is why living off the land binaries (LOLBins) show up in so many hunts.

Test and refine. The aim is to prove or disprove the hypothesis, refining the hunt and forming new hypotheses as new information comes in.

Reporting phase

This is where the threat hunting life cycle pays off, because every hunt feeds the next one.

Distill findings. Hunters document what they found, even when the hypothesis didn't pan out.

Create detections. Patterns inform detection rules that catch the activity automatically. If the hunt turned up an active attacker, your incident response plan takes over.

Improve the process. Hunting is iterative, so feed what you learned into the next hunt.

Threat hunting best practices

These seven threat hunting best practices keep your hunts sharp.

Know your environment. You can't spot abnormal if you don't know normal, and good cyber hygiene makes that baseline cleaner.

Use threat intelligence. Feed current intel into your hypotheses so you're hunting what attackers do now.

Keep learning. Threats evolve, so continuous training isn't optional.

Build an adversarial mindset. Be curious and skeptical, and assume breach.

Develop diverse skills. Hunting takes analytical, forensic, and scripting chops (more in the FAQs).

Set aside dedicated time. Hunting should be scheduled, not something analysts only do when they're free.

Automate successful hunts. This one's our favorite: Hunt once, detect forever. When a query finds a real threat, turn it into an automated detection rule in your SIEM (security information event management) or EDR (endpoint detection and response) solution right away. Next time that behavior shows up, your tools catch it automatically, and your hunter gets to chase the next unknown.

Threat hunting tools

You can't hunt what you can't see. A threat hunting platform pulls telemetry, search, and context into one place so hunters can test hypotheses fast. Most hunts use three kinds of tools.

SIEM. A SIEM centralizes logs and alerts from across your environment. In a hunt, that gives hunters one place to query across endpoints, identity, and network traffic, and it's where successful hunts become detection rules. That's why threat hunting SIEM workflows anchor most mature programs.

EDR. EDR threat hunting starts with endpoint telemetry like process launches, file changes, and network connections, so hunters can spot a trusted admin tool launching from a strange folder. With Managed EDR, expert analysts do the watching for you, and pairing it with identity coverage through unified EDR and ITDR keeps attackers from slipping between the endpoint and the account.

Threat intelligence platforms (TIPs). TIPs aggregate threat data from multiple sources. For hunters, that's a steady supply of fresh hypotheses without reading a hundred feeds, and it keeps intel tied to the hunt instead of buried in a PDF.

Why threat hunting matters

Automated tools can't out-think a human adversary. Machine learning is great at speed and known patterns, but a person still has to decide what's suspicious. Modern attackers know that, and they actively probe for blind spots in automated detection.

With human-powered threat hunting, a trained eye picks up on odd behavior no rule was written for, and every hunt makes your automated tools more accurate. The payoff is finding unknown threats early: before ransomware gets deployed, before malware spreads, before anyone's weekend goes up in smoke.

Full Text: If you're a customer of cloud-hosted AI workflow platform Trigger.dev, take heed, because your environment variables may have been exposed in a security incident disclosed on Sunday. Trigger offered little explanation in its Sunday security incident report, noting that its investigation had identified “exposure across a subset of organizations” and that an attacker had gained unauthorized access to environment variables belonging to those organizations. Whatever exploit was used to gain access has been blocked, the company added, and affected customers have been notified of steps they need to take to prevent further security problems. We likely don't have to tell The Reg readers how important environment variables are in SaaS and cloud services like Trigger. If compromised environment variables contain sensitive credentials, an attacker could basically end up with the keys to the kingdom, potentially gaining access to connected services and digital infrastructure. For those unfamiliar with Trigger.dev, it’s a platform for building AI agents and workflows in TypeScript, but here’s the kicker: Trigger advertises itself as a durable execution platform that handles pesky things like retries, scaling, and keeping long-running tasks going through crashes and redeployments, while providing tools to monitor what those tasks are doing. Trigger, the company’s site notes, can be used to “build durable AI agents that survive refreshes, redeploys, and crashes,” and is ideal for “long-running tasks with retries, queues, AI observability and elastic scaling.” In short, companies running their AI on Trigger probably want it to keep running, which makes stolen environment variables all the more dangerous. Elastic scaling, automated retries, and, as Trigger notes, the ability to run lots of concurrent operations without timeouts could compound the consequences of compromised API keys, depending on what those credentials allow an attacker to access. An attacker with stolen credentials could potentially interfere with a customer's connected services or workflows. Additionally, Trigger recently added webhooks to its offering, supporting services like Stripe, Supabase, and Slack, potentially expanding the range of integrations that could be affected if their credentials were exposed. This could be pretty bad for anyone affected. Trigger has some fairly high-profile customers, with companies like fashion brand Emporio Armani, Pentagon-supporting AI acquisitions platform GovSignals, SaaS calendar platform Cal.com, and others all listed on the company’s site. Trigger has not publicly identified which organizations were affected by the intrusion. We reached out to Trigger, which declined to provide any additional information on the incident. A company spokesperson instead told us to wait for a full incident report to learn more. Luckily for Trigger customers and those concerned about SaaS security now that AI is regularly coming up with new vulnerabilities in commonly used platforms, Trigger is open source and can be self-hosted, which might be a better alternative in this day and age than relying on a hosted service. ®

Title: Mutipath TCP: Use and Detection, (Mon, Nov 2nd)
Context: The only widely used implementation I have observed is iOS/iPadOS
Full Text:
Last week, an often-ignored TCP option, introduced in 2020, made the news due to a new vulnerability in Linux's implementation (RFC 8684, CVE-2026-98432)

Instead of looking at the vulnerability, I am using this diary to talk a bit about multipath TCP (MPTCP) and how you may see it used in your network.

What is MPTCP?

Traditionally, TCP is a connection-oriented protocol. Connections are established between a client and server, and host IP addresses are not expected to change for a specific connection. This restriction to a specific path does not always match modern system architecture. For example, mobile devices may switch from a local WIFI network to a cellular network at any time. Having to re-establish TCP connections may break applications. At the same time, servers often have a hard time "filling" high-bandwidth links using a single TCP connection due to limits on Window Size and the sequence number range [RFC 6182]. MPTCP is supposed to solve these problems by allowing connections to be split and handed over between different IP addresses.

The only widely used implementation I have observed is iOS/iPadOS. In this case, IPv4 connections to Apple (17.0.0.0/8) often utilize MPTCP [Apple]. MPTCP was initially used for Siri, and later for other services like Apple Music.

Two versions of MPTCP are currently defined and used: v0 and v1. At first,

MPTCP Options

The MPTCP Option (0x1e, 30) is followed by a byte containing 4 bits indicating the subtype and 4 bits indicating the version (0 or 1).

+----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+ | TCP Option | Option Length|Subtype| Version| Flags | +----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+ | 30 | variable | | 0 or 1 | | +----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+

MP_CAPABLE (subtype 0): Indicates MPTCP support. Both sides must include it in the TCP handshake for MPTCP support to be enabled. Each MP_CAPABLE option also carries an 8-byte key that will later be used to identify and authenticate the different sub-sessions.

MP_JOIN (subtype 1): A second TCP connection may join an initial connection using the MP_JOIN option. This connection will typically be initiated by the client, but may originate from a different IP address. The RFC does specifically allow the server to initiate the second (or additional) connection. The RFC states: "It is permissible for either host in a connection to initiate the creation of a new subflow, but it is expected that this will normally be the original connection initiator." Ports should be the same, but do not have to be. Of course, this also accounts for common firewall rules. The web server will likely listen only on port 443, and the client's firewall will reject inbound SYN packets.

DSS (Data Sequence Signal, subtype 2): Each TCP connection which is part of MPTCP maintains its own sequence numbers, and acts just like any other "normal" TCP connection. To stitch the content of multiple connections together, the DSS option is used. It maps the respective's TCP sequence numbers to the sequence numbers of the combined connection.

ADD_ADDR/REMOVE_ADDR (subtypes 3, 4): these options are somewhat similar to MP_JOIN, but instead of actually setting up an additional connection, they advertise (or remove) additional addresses or ports that can be used.

MPTCP Detection

The best way to detect MPTCP is to look for TCP Option 30. Here are a few ways to do so:

Wireshark/tshark: Wireshark has a "mptcp" display filter keyword. As so often, Wireshark does make it easy.

tcpdump: There is no great way to match TCP options in tcpdump. But MPTCP packets, particularly SYN packets, tend to have large TCP headers, so a quick match on TCP header length can help. For example: 'tcp[12]>0xd0'

Suricata: Use the "tcp.hdr" keyword to inspect TCP options. The tricky part is that the option length isn't always the same. But there should be at least one MP_CAPABLE message that includes both the sender and receiver key, making this option 20 bytes long. The first three bytes are |1e 14 00| for version 0 or |1e 14 01| for version 1.

Snort: Snort does not have a keyword to inspect TCP options, and as far as I know, no way to filter for multipath TCP. The snort_decoder "experimental TCP option" alert only triggers on specific option types reserved for experimental use.

Zeek: By default, zeek does not log options, but it does offer the tcp_option and tcp_options events that can easily be used to log MPTCP. For example:

event tcp_option(c: connection, is_orig: bool, opt: count, optlen: count) { if ( opt == 30 ) { print(fmt("MPTCP between %s and %s", c$id$orig_h, c$id$resp_h)); } }

[Apple] https://support.apple.com/en-us/101905 [RFC8694] https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8684 [CVE-2026-98432] https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/10/30/1
