Title: The Dishwasher Doesn’t Need a Soul, The Film Does.
Context: Nobody watches it hoping to learn the mechanics of a credential harvesting attack
Full Text:
People say they can spot AI writing a mile off. The em dashes. The word “delve.” The LinkedIn posts that begin with “I’ve been thinking a lot about leadership” and end without a single thought. I understand the reaction. I’ve read enough of them to develop a thousand-yard stare every time someone says they’re “unlocking” something.

But I also don’t believe that all AI uses need to be thrown into the waste bin. Many times it makes work quicker and easier.

Recently my dishwasher kept on turning off a couple of minutes after starting with a weird error code flashing on the screen. I diligently looked up the model number and error code to find a YouTube video featuring a very nice middle aged man with a thick Yorkshire accent in his garage. The lighting was terrible, the audio was choppy, and while he was explaining a “tricky part” all the camera could see was his elbow. But I didn’t care about those flaws, I wanted information and he delivered it.

In these scenarios AI can really help. If it can help you fix your broken dishwasher, and as long as it actually reads the instructions, it’s good to go. I don’t need to form any sort of connection with the man in the garage to find the information useful. Sure I left him a like on the video because it helped me, but I’m not subscribing to his channel anytime soon.

Compare that to a great story-driven youtuber you follow. Or a movie director. You don’t watch one of those to learn the plot as efficiently as possible. Someone chose the framing, music, colour palette, dialogue, and so much more. That’s not something you want AI to take over, you want the human touch, the artistry, the emotion, the feeling that makes you connect.

There’s information, and then there’s the art. One is for your mind, the other for your heart.

Our studios team at KnowBe4 understands that distinction and we create content for both sides. At the top end that means series like "The Inside Man," which plays more like a Netflix drama than a training module. Nobody watches it hoping to learn the mechanics of a credential harvesting attack. They watch because they care what happens to the people on screen, and the consequences of a bad decision land on them.

We also produce the practical knowledge modules which can teach people how to spot the red flags in a phishing email or how to securely transfer data, or classify it.

Giving someone information and changing their behaviour are different jobs. The garage video does the first, while cinema and drama do the second.

AI is great at helping people be more efficient. I’m happy for it to shorten meeting notes, or do a review of my blog post before my long-suffering copy editor has to set aside half their day to go through it.

I like to write, and often picture myself not writing a blog post or article, but rather ask myself how I would explain this to my best friend. The words may not be perfect, the grammar may take liberties, but those are the words I chose, and I know my friend will understand and appreciate it. That’s why we’re friends, because of our quirks, not because we speak perfectly smooth sentences with no grammatical errors.

I’m not saying that training content must be made without digital tools. People have always used tools. But those tools should support the human making the decisions, not make the decisions themselves. In this world, we can make room for AI without assuming every use of it is the same.

Use it to make information easier to find and understand. Just don’t ask it to provide the human bit.

The dishwasher doesn’t need a soul. The film does. And if you can’t tell which one you’re making, that’s not a technology problem.

Javvad Malik is Lead CISO Advisor at KnowBe4. He has asked AI to make his writing more concise. It keeps removing the good bits.

Title: Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts
Context: What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about
Full Text:
Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts

This story is interesting:

One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about.

Among the pre-installed bloatware—­or spyware, if you’re being less charitable­—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go.

It’s interesting because it exposes all the insecurities in this piece of IoT software. But I think the real story is that a random person was able to do this reverse-engineering with the help of AI. Expect a lot more stories like this in the future.

Title: Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks
Context: In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million...
Full Text:
When managed security service provider Eye Security spotted an odd update process in a client's telemetry that appeared to be reaching out to outdated — and in some cases, malicious — domains, the company decided to take a deeper look.

The updater belonged to a modified version of Time4Popcorn, a 2014-era BitTorrent client that allows movies to be downloaded from the Internet, and even after a decade, the persistent updater continued to run on more than 2.5 million Windows machines and an estimated 300,000 Macs, checking for new software, according to the MSSP's advisory. The problem: Many of the domains checked by the updater were open to registration, which could allow any would-be cyberattacker to register the domain and have an easy way to place software on millions of machines.

The situation highlights the issue of old infrastructure and the threat it poses to users and businesses, especially if the business's employees work from home, Niels Teusink, principal security researcher for Eye Security, wrote in the analysis.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

"[W]hile these users chose to install Popcorn Time, none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years, ready to run any code with full privileges for whoever controlled one of its domains," the company stated in its advisory. "With millions of systems affected and the software long abandoned, there was no vendor to fix this and no patch on the way: if we didn't act, nobody would."

The risk of domains that are dropped by a legitimate service and then picked up again, or bought by a gray-market or criminal operator — sometimes called "dropcatch domains" — have become an increasing issue as developers have stopped updating, or sold off, legacy software infrastructure. In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million HTTP requests from government and companies came in for resources that had been hosted at those addresses.

And with AI enabling a more sophisticated analysis of software projects, attackers may be able to more quickly do the necessary research to find domains that could be a backdoor into users' systems, says Benjamin Harris, founder and CEO of watchTowr.

"AI is definitely driving the barrier-to-entry down for this kind of research very quickly," he says. "We're seeing AI used to reproduce vulnerabilities, find zero days, but applied to this, AI can be used to install a bunch of software, install network taps, see what all the software reaches out to, see what's not registered, or see what's been abandoned and what we can hijack."

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

Dropcatch Domains: A Hidden Risk

Typically, there are two types of vulnerable domains that questionable operators might take an interest in. The first are homograph domains that look like their legitimate cousins and include both typosquatting domains, such as "gmai[.]com," that try to catch browsers whose users mistyped a URL, and lookalike domains that are used in phishing to visually fool users. The value of these types of domains to the owner varies, depending on the amount of traffic they attract, says Renée Burton, vice president of threat intelligence at cybersecurity vendor Infoblox.

However, dropcatch domains that are integrated into the supply chain for a piece of software are a completely different — and more serious — risk, she says. Infoblox has registered hundreds of domains that had been part of supply chains to prevent attackers from using them.

"Supply chain attacks can happen at a moment's notice, and depending on how dropped domains are integrated into existing software, a threat actor can quickly abuse a supply chain dropped domain to conduct sophisticated attacks that lead to data loss and ransomware," Burton says.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

In 2024, Chinese company Funnull bought the polyfill[.]io domain from the creator of the Polyfill service and began redirecting users to tens of thousands of websites.

The Popcorn Time issue highlights the problem. Anyone with access to the domains, and with some reverse engineering, could figure out how to tinker with the legacy updaters. In fact, that's what Eye Security did, updating the code to stop the automated process of reaching out to the old domains.

"All we needed to do was supply a link to an executable and the program would download it and then execute it with high privileges (NT AUTHORITYSYSTEM)," Teusink wrote. "There was no code signing and this process was all happening over HTTP."

Eye Security stressed that another project, confusingly also named Popcorn Time, is a 2025 effort to create a legitimate streaming service and is not impacted by the legacy update issues.

Know Your Internet Services

Companies should know the domains that their employees are reaching out to and the reputation of those domains, and should extend that monitoring and protection to remote users, says watchTowr's Harris.

"The big challenge with things like BYOD and working from home is that now the network perimeter extends from not just your corporate network ... but the user's home network as well," he says.

The community needs to come together as well, says Infoblox's Burton. While taking active defense to the same extent as Eye Security continues to be legally problematic, finding legacy and unused infrastructure is something that security communities on the Internet can continue to work on, she says.

"Threat actors understand the value of controlling a domain which is integrated into an existing supply chain and being queried by real people on a regular basis," Burton says. "We need more defenders looking for proactive ways to disrupt domain drop schemes by purchasing high-value pending drop domains before threat actors, and by looking for ways to reduce threat actors cash out opportunities from these attacks."

Title: Key Takeaways: AI Threat Readiness Survey Report 2026
Context: Closing the Gap: The AI Threat Readiness Model Defending a machine-speed attack surface requires transitioning from static reviews to an active, code-to-cloud security model
Full Text:
Today, organizations are deploying multi-cloud architectures where non-deterministic software executes multi-step operations directly on enterprise data and runtime systems. To understand how technical organizations are managing this architectural shift, we surveyed 100 senior IT and security decision-makers spanning CxOs, VPs, and directors.

The findings point to an operational gap: while autonomous execution is expanding rapidly, governance and defensive architectures remain tethered to manual review models. To unpack where enterprise defenses stand and how teams can bridge this divide, here are the key takeaways from the AI Threat Readiness Survey Report 2026.

1.Universal Adoption and Multi-System Scale

Across enterprise environments, AI adoption is nearly ubiquitous: only 5% of organizations report zero active AI usage, while 55% now actively deploy autonomous agentic systems, making agents the single most common AI deployment architecture in modern environments. Furthermore, nearly a third of enterprises (31%) are running more than 25 distinct AI systems in active production.

Production adoption extends far beyond prompt-based tools, spanning managed cloud services, proprietary in-house models, and emerging orchestration layers like Model Context Protocol (MCP) and RAG.

2. The Asset Visibility Gap and Shadow AI

While deployment surges, security tracking has lagged behind. Only 17% of organizations maintain a comprehensive, up-to-date AI asset inventory. The remaining 83% operate with partial visibility, fragmented team-level records, or zero centralized mechanisms to catalog their running models, agents, and pipelines.

This visibility vacuum has turned shadow AI into an active operational reality: 52% of organizations discovered unauthorized AI applications running inside their perimeters over the past year.

This sprawl is fueled by decentralized governance. More than a third of organizations (35%) formally permit teams to deploy AI tools without centralized approval, while nearly one in ten security leaders (9%) admits they possess zero mechanisms to detect unauthorized AI workloads at all.

3. The Autonomous Threat Landscape: Expanding Data Security

Enterprise AI has progressed beyond static prompts to active autonomous execution. Organizations are deploying agents across critical operational lanes, led by internal enterprise workflows, developer productivity tools, IT and security automation, and customer-facing production applications.

When asked about agentic security concerns, technical leaders overwhelmingly focus on business impact: unauthorized access to sensitive data (70%) and unmonitored autonomous decision-making (54%) top their concerns, followed closely by overprivileged identities (53%). However, securing data in the AI era requires looking beyond static repositories to the execution pathways enabling them.

While not as top of mind, risks like unmonitored agent actions (45%), lateral movement between systems (24%), and unvalidated tool APIs (23%) represent the operational pathways through which overprivileged machine identities interact with corporate data. Protecting enterprise data now demands end-to-end context across data posture, agent identities, and runtime execution lanes.

4. Operational Roadblocks and Fragmented Investments

When asked to isolate the single AI security headache they wish could disappear today, senior leaders did not point to technical model flaws. Instead, 26% cited governance and cross-functional ownership complexity as their primary bottleneck, narrowly outpacing concerns over agent autonomy and service account token access.

Despite governance being the primary friction point, defensive strategies remain deeply fragmented. While 43% of teams stretch legacy cloud tools to cover AI, only 38% fund dedicated AI security budgets, and over a third (37%) rely on homegrown scripts. Fragmenting capital across disconnected point tools and custom scripts creates isolated telemetry silos, leaving security teams blind to toxic attack paths connecting code, credentials, and cloud runtime.

Closing the Gap: The AI Threat Readiness Model

Defending a machine-speed attack surface requires transitioning from static reviews to an active, code-to-cloud security model. Threat readiness depends on two core variables: speed of action and breadth of visibility across the full lifecycle.

Enterprise leaders should establish a modern defensive posture across five key priorities aligned with the Wiz AI Threat Readiness Framework:

1. Treat AI Stacks as Core Production Infrastructure: Apply standard enterprise configuration, patching, logging, and admission controls to all model endpoints, registries, and pipelines.

2. Transition from Flat Inventories to Graph Context: Use integrated posture capabilities like Wiz AI Security to continuously map AI assets to owners and prioritize toxic exposure paths.

3. Enforce Behavioral Least Privilege and Human Oversight: Restrict agent credential scopes to prevent lateral movement, and mandate human verification gates for high-impact production actions.

4. Eliminate Critical Exposures and Scan with AI (Pillar 1): Deploy external AI penetration testing engines (like Wiz Red Agent) to continuously test live perimeters and validate reachable attack paths before attackers scan for them.

5. Accelerate Response with Deep Code Analysis and Agentic Defense (Pillars 2, 3, and 4): Build a closed-loop defensive architecture:

Deep AI Code Analysis: Inspect code and interactive notebooks (.ipynb) natively with advanced models to uncover complex logic flaws before production.

Accelerate Patching: Deploy agentic remediation engines (like Wiz Green Agent) to trace root causes and generate verified code fixes directly into pull requests.

Detect and Contain in Real Time: Use non-intrusive runtime sensors (Wiz Defend and Wiz Sensor) alongside automated triage engines (like Wiz Blue Agent) to isolate compromised workloads instantly.

Title: British intelligence agency misplaced 'thousands' of storage devices, years later still can't say how many
Context: " The report notes that most partners were properly restricted from accessing such material, although an internal probe found that there were inadequate arrangements in respect...
Full Text: Thousands of GCHQ storage drives containing sensitive data have been lost for years, and the British signals intelligence agency still cannot explain where they are. According to the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office’s (IPCO) annual report, the missing storage drives have been known to officials for years, and may contain data related to the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA). "I remain concerned that GCHQ has not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location, and recoverability of lost removable media that may contain IPA-related data, notwithstanding that the underlying issues were first drawn to my attention several years ago," wrote investigatory powers commissioner Lord Brian Leveson. "While I recognize the technical and practical challenges involved, the passage of time without a comprehensive account heightens the importance of sustained senior focus and assured remediation. Given the potential sensitivity of the material involved, I will continue to monitor progress closely.” Described as "a very significant number," the report notes that GCHQ has scoped the maximum number of potentially lost drives, but is unaware of the exact scale of the issue. The agency has embarked on "a program of further work" to locate as many of the lost devices as possible, which includes implementing an automated asset-tracking system by the end of the year. After this is up and running, it said it will be able to provide a more precise number of lost drives. A GCHQ spokesperson told The Register: "As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations. "We recognize the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively, and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken." Losing important devices is not an achievement that's exclusive to GCHQ. Myriad stories like this have emerged from all corners of the public sector over the years, such as the British Minidstry of Defence misplacing USB drives containing secret information in the mid-noughties, civil servants routinely losing their BlackBerry handsets, and UK police losing thousands of devices, too. The missing storage drives comprise just one of the agency's various transgressions highlighted by IPCO in its report. There are also "significant concerns" over the lax safeguards used to restrict the UK's overseas partners when accessing bulk-intercepted data collected by GCHQ. IPCO was satisfied at how GCHQ ensured its own analysts remained compliant with safeguards around accessing confidential material related to journalism, journalistic sources, and privileged legal information. However, there were concerns around how these same safeguards were applied to its international partners, which have access to its so-called bulk data interception "product." The report notes that most partners were properly restricted from accessing such material, although an internal probe found that there were inadequate arrangements in respect to one partner and their access to journalistic material. Both GCHQ and the overseas agency committed to rectifying the situation. GCHQ was also questioned after a software bug in a web app "used by a relatively small section of the public" misidentified individuals thought to be participating in terrorist activities. The agency identified and reported the flaw in the software, which it used for "target discovery work," and although it only affected a small number of individuals, the errors led to five port stops made under the Terrorism Act and caused "serious prejudice" to the victims. A port stop, for the uninitiated, involves law enforcement detaining a suspect at a UK port, airport, train station, or within one mile of the Northern Ireland border, and can be carried out without suspicion. Once detained, individuals have a legal responsibility to provide passwords to their electronic devices, which can be seized for up to seven days, and in some cases have their biometric markers taken. Failure to comply can lead to a three-month prison term. IPCO ruled, however, that there was ultimately no error made as defined by the IPA. “This is because the activity was lawfully authorised under an interception warrant and the adoption of an unintentionally and unforeseeably imperfect target discovery methodology did not constitute such an error,” the report stated. Despite the agency’s vast technical expertise, IPCO said that the issue affecting the software was not foreseeable. GCHQ was not the only offender among the UK intelligence community (UKIC), with MI5's mishandling of the infamous Agent X case taking center stage in the report. Agent X was an anonymous MI5 informant whose real identity has never been publicly released. A secret inquiry by IPCO as well as the report revealed that MI5 managed Agent X despite knowing he was a violent misogynist obsessed with extreme violence. Lord Leveson said "the case of Agent X is as serious as anything I have dealt with as Commissioner," after MI5 gave false evidence to the High Court and Investigatory Powers Tribunal to protect a foreign neo-Nazi informant who was under police investigation for abusing his partner, referred to publicly as "Beth." ®

Title: In the year AI re-wrote the infosec rulebook, it’s comforting to know crypto exchanges still have bad security
Context: 5B+ valuation for entire firm, though portion sold not specified Malware Month Ten years since the first corp ransomware, Mikko Hyppönen sees no end in sight On the plus side,...
Full Text: Crypto exchange Binance has paused trading after discovering unknown parties cracked one of its workers’ laptops and used it to make massive trades. Late on Thursday, US time, the company used its social media feeds to report “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.” The exchange insisted “User funds are completely safe” and warned its customers “should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.” The company soon froze $2.5 billion worth of assets and warned that the figure could go higher “as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.” To prevent the matter worsening, Binance halted all trading, deposits, and withdrawals. It also promised to cover any losses. About an hour ago at the time of writing, Binance posted an update on the incident that explains what it thinks went wrong. “Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” the post states. The company also hiked the amount it thinks is at risk to $6.3 billion and repeated its promise to cover any customer losses. The update also says Binance found no evidence of any wallet private key leak, suggesting that customers’ holdings remain secure. When they can use them again, as Binance is yet to resume trading. Binance hasn’t explained how attackers gained access to the engineer’s laptop. The scant details provided make it hard to rule out a successful phishing attack, or perhaps a supply chain attack on a package the developer used. Binance says it will spill once it knows exactly what happened. Cryptocurrency outfits have a long and inglorious history of falling victim to cyberattacks, perhaps starting with the 2011 raid on Mt Gox, to incidents allegedly perpetrated by nation-states, and, just last week, another situation possibly involving an AI-powered attacker. ®

Title: Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era
Context: Threat actors are taking advantage of AI tools and platforms to accelerate, enhance, and scale their attacks, whether it's social engineering schemes or wide-ranging supply...
Full Text:
AI is changing the concept of cybersecurity awareness in more ways than one.

In the latest installment of our monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea, and Dark Reading's Rob Wright discuss some of the trends they've observed during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, which has shifted during the AI era with the emergence of news threats as well as revamped defense strategies.

As we’ve seen in years past, cybersecurity awareness training often becomes a compliance checkbox exercise rather than a vehicle to educate employees and users on the latest threats. And unfortunately, the threat landscape today is changing at a frenetic pace. Threat actors are taking advantage of AI tools and platforms to accelerate, enhance, and scale their attacks, whether it's social engineering schemes or wide-ranging supply chain compromises.

Thankfully, as the editors explain, some organizations are updating their programs to take more specific, line-of-business approaches for training while also accounting for the evolving threats related to AI; some programs are even using AI to create more convincing phishing simulations. Meanwhile, several US colleges and universities have increased their education offerings for AI security.

Related:Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

The editors discuss these topics and more in this Reporters' Notebook episode.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

Eric Geller, Sharon Shea & Rob Wright: Full Video Transcript

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright, senior news director at Dark Reading, and welcome to another edition of the Reporter's Notebook. I am here with Sharon and Eric. Would you guys like to introduce yourselves and then we'll get into the topics for today?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea: Hey, I am Sharon Shea. I'm the lead editor on Tech Target Cybersecurity.

Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller: And I'm Eric Geller. I'm a senior reporter at Cybersecurity Dive.

DR's Rob Wright: And this month is Cybersecurity Awareness Month. Yay! I know it's our favorite time of the year, right? We've written a fair amount of content on this topic over the last few weeks. We're still in it. We've still got about a week to go. It's not been a great run recently. There's been a lot going on, a lot of attacks, a lot of threats, a lot of urgent stuff going on in cybersecurity. But we wanted to get into some of those things here in this video discussion. Sharon, do you want to kick us off?

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah, so I will kind of take it back to the human side of Cybersecurity Awareness Month and then we can jump into some of the attack stuff later. But you know, one of the big things in Cybersecurity Awareness Month is making sure that your training programs are up to par. And granted, it's not just this month, just like Earth Day is not just one day for the Earth. We want it to be year-round.

But it does kind of give a springboard, as we called it in one of our articles, to further focus on cybersecurity throughout the year and bring a renewed focus for this month. And one report I was reading, a SANS report, said that 19% of organizations have cybersecurity awareness training programs designed primarily to meet a specific compliance or audit requirement. And that's kind of a bad way to look at things, just doing this for compliance.

Obviously, you want to do it to be secure all the time. And, you know, we all probably groan when those awareness trainings come into our inboxes every couple months or a couple times a year. They can be boring and you just click through them just to get through them and do the checkbox. But sometimes those aren't quite as effective as they should be, as we've seen. Really, you don't want to treat it as a check space, compliance checkbox exercise.

Related:Security Threats Don't Stop at the Office: Why Executives' Families Need Training, Too

And one major thing that we learned from our reporting, or I think we've known for years, but it's not one size fits all, right? You really want to identify the behaviors within your organization that create risk. You want to map those threats to business consequences, establish baselines, and monitor for deviations from those.

Threat s like deepfakes trying to get into your help desk and reset MFA or, you know, the common Arup example of the CFO who was on a call with an employee and wanted them to wire a ton of money to them. And you know, you really have to focus those down on what departments really need specific trainings. I guess within the organization, you have so many different types of people to cover. You have your general employees, you have C-level, privileged admins, HR recruiting, customer-facing employees, and you have third parties, contractors, and you want to match the awareness to those sorts of risks.

I guess another thing that we can talk about too is updating the program regularly. You do want to talk about older tech. We all know that phishing is a major thing, right? It's still a problem, but you also want to talk about the newer tech — AI. And not just AI — GenAI, agentic AI, you know, all these newest technologies from the past couple of years. People know how to securely use them as well as preventing their inherent security issues.

And another thing I thought was kind of cool that we've covered is using AI in your awareness programs. We were talking to one CISO who uses phishing — I'm sorry, uses phishing simulations created by AI to personalize them for their employees, which you know is pretty cool, too. It's not just that generic boring watching the same old video from, you know, the 1900s, probably.

DR's Rob Wright: Probably a good thing.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah. You know, so kind of to solve some of the problems too of those boring programs. One of our sources, Kevin Walker of Black Swan, told Alissa Irei that you know, you really want to do short training sprints versus real world marathons. Those hour-long trainings, no one's going to get them. You know, they're not gonna pay attention throughout this whole thing. So make them highly relevant, personalized, and you really want to have those short, easy-to-consume bits that are good for your employees.

I guess talking about specific threats towards specific employees, Rob, you had an example that you guys have been covering on Dark Reading lately.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, there's a lot going on lately with AI-themed attacks. And one of the things I've noticed — we covered this a couple, a few times actually — is that there's a lot of SEO poisoning and malvertising. I think we think of like malvertising and threats like that as kind of like low-hanging fruit, kind of the type of attacks that aren't very sophisticated and that don't go very far. Maybe you get like some malware on your system from a flash ad or like a comb-over ad or something like that.

And we're finding that these ads are getting a lot more — I hate using the word sophisticated, I hate it so much, it's so overused — they're getting more effective. There's not a lot of ad blockers that are going to get you around ads on Facebook and Meta, for example. And there was a recent report from Gen Digital — well, I think it was almost a year now — that they found that one out of every three ads on Instagram and Facebook was malicious. It either pointed to malware or some type of phishing link, or it was a scam, like an outright scam.

And what's happening these days is that attackers know that they can use sponsored links and they can use these types of ads, not just your conventional like pop-up ads and stuff like that, which a lot of people do block. But they can use those sponsored links, you can use Google ads, you can use really effective SEO poisoning techniques to put stuff out like, 'Hey, download Claude Code' or something like that, or like a new AI tool.

And there are so many people out there looking for these tools right now. There are so many people, there's so much shadow AI that it's just easy to come across one of these malicious links, whether you're actively looking for it or you're just playing around — who knows? And they're hosted on legitimate infrastructure, they're hosted on — there was a report recently that Any.Run had, there were some stats about how many attacks, AI-themed attacks, are being deployed and there was a report about just massive use of Cloudflare Pages as infrastructure so it looks legitimate and then there's also like OpenAI Custom GPTs and that like that just it just looks legitimate because it's on like a real provider like it's on OpenAI or it's on Cloudflare.

And it's very easy to get tripped up by these things and click on something and then immediately download an infostealer that gets your credentials. And if you're a developer, there's been so many attacks on developers. And it's just bad news for an organization. So I think one of the things that companies ought to focus on right now is just trying to get people within the organization — obviously it depends on like what your privilege level is and where you are in the organization — but really for any type of employee that's out there looking for an AI tool, you've got to know the risk. You have to know that a lot of the stuff that you're going to be digging up out there, if it's not through an official app store of for an official channel, it very well likely could be a scam or some type of social engineering scheme that's going to drop an infostealer or something worse on your system. So that was kind of an eye opener for us.

Scary stuff. And we're not even to Halloween, so we'll see. Eric, what have you been seeing?

CD's Eric Geller: Well, I looked at things from the perspective of the next generation workforce. We're talking a lot about educating the workforces of today and trying to mitigate the threats of today. But we're also seeing a lot of change in the AI landscape that it's been difficult for the current workforce to get their heads around. So I kind of focused on preparing the next workforce to understand not only AI, but also how to guard against threats related to AI.

So, how to be an AI security practitioner, how to focus on AI security governance and risk management. And I looked at the university level to understand what kinds of courses exist out there to prepare students for careers in this area. It's no surprise that there's a lot of AI curriculum at the higher education level. What might be more of a surprise is that universities have actually gotten pretty good over the past few years at recognizing that there needs to be a security component to that work.

So I spoke to people at a number of schools that have tried to build or begin building curricula around AI security. Spoke to folks at Carnegie Mellon. They have a certificate program in AI security that's designed for kind of mid-level corporate workers who want to specialize in this area to go in for a class. It's a few weeks, you come out with a certificate that can kind of prepare you to be a leader in this space. But of course, a lot of this is happening at the undergraduate and graduate level. And so there's a lot of courses designed to kind of grab folks at that point in their early, early pre-careers, if you will, and teach them why this is an important subject.

So I spoke to a professor at Georgia Tech who is teaching a graduate course in LLM security and said that she was actually surprised by how much interest there's been in AI security when she teaches you know, undergraduate level sort of cyber one one and she talks about large language models, there's a lot of interest in following up outside of class and trying to learn more about that specific part of cyber.

For those of us who are perhaps a little pessimistic that college students want to focus on security when all the money and the attention is in building and deploying new products, I think this story that I wrote was kind of a somewhat of a corrective to that narrative, but also just as a source of optimism that at least according to the folks who are teaching this material, there are folks interested in learning about this kind of stuff and there are folks interested in pursuing graduate school education and getting certificates specifically in the security part of AI, which again is good to see. And I think we're going to start to see a shift over the next few years as people come out of these programs and begin entering the workforce. We're going to see a more security minded attitude, I think, toward AI development, at least if some of these colleges get their way.

DR's Rob Wright: I'm actually, I suddenly have a positive outlook, which is really rare for me. I'm normally the pessimist.

CD's Eric Geller: Well, you're welcome.

DR's Rob Wright: Thank you. Yeah, no, that's great news. it sounds like a welcome development. So maybe there is something to look forward to with AI. Fingers crossed.

CD's Eric Geller: Yeah. And the one thing I'll add is that this is not just something that's siloed at specific universities. There are coalitions of schools working together to create curriculums, curricula that that they can you know use interchangeably, taking best practices that one school has found in terms of what works for teaching in the classroom, sharing that with other schools.

This is one area where the federal government is actually kind of playing a behind the scenes role because they sponsor this nationwide coalition that has sort of different schools have taken the lead on building their own little groups of schools that they work with to kind of create lesson plans, find subject matter that works in the classroom, and then share those lessons with each other. You know, academia is obviously a very collaborative sphere, and I think that works out to everyone's benefit here because the teachers that are finding things that work are are telling other teachers and other professors in other schools, you might want to try this approach. And there's a consortium that is kind of bringing all that together and trying to make this not necessarily the exact same curriculum at every school, but shared curricula across universities.

DR's Rob Wright: That's good. I'm optimistic, and I'm never optimistic. Well, thank you guys for coming together to discuss Cybersecurity Awareness Month and I'm glad we're ending it on a positive note. Thanks guys.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Thanks, Rob. Thanks, Eric.

Title: Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever
Context: Jeopardy-style events, the kind Sentinels League runs, hand out standalone puzzles across categories such as web exploitation, forensics, and cryptography, with points awarded...
Full Text:
Artificial intelligence may be gobbling up entry-level jobs and learning opportunities for security practitioners, but it can't erase the value of hands-on experience with enterprise systems and security tools.

No matter how much agentic action cybersecurity teams embed in their security operations center (SOC) and the rest of their programs, there's got to be smart people backstopping that work. And the only way that these “humans-in-the-loop” can do that capably is if they build up the kind of judgment that's best learned from the school of hard knocks.

The problem is that with SOC tier 1 analysts becoming an endangered species and bug bounty programs on the ropes from a glut of AI submissions, the chances are dwindling for newbies to rack up real-world experience.

What's the security industry to do? There's no great fix to this career pipeline problem just yet, but some of the answers might be found in one of the industry's age-old mechanisms for both camaraderie and skill-building: the trusty capture-the-flag (CTF) competition.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

"CTFs give passionate talent the opportunity to grow and learn in ways that they might not have at their day jobs," says Jason Walker, a security engineer by day at SaaS firm Five9. An avid CTF competitor, he won the Sentinels League competition, sponsored and run by SentinelOne, beating two other finalists from a field of thousands of competitors worldwide. Besides street cred, Walker picked up a $5,000 prize for his efforts and a $10,000 donation in his name to his charity of choice, Trans Lifeline.

The livestreamed event offered the spectacle and fun of an esports competition, but it may hold deeper clues about how the industry can keep refreshing its talent pool in the coming years. As Walker puts it, CTFs are the ultimate way to expose both new and experienced cyber professionals to a wider range of problems and technologies.

"CTFs have helped me be a lot more versatile. Because if your company is running well and your program is mature, you aren't going to necessarily be firefighting new things every week. You're not going to be exposed to every new technique and threat," he says. "Doing capture the flag events and other hands-on training is a really important way to make sure you can stay up to date."

State of CTF Today

CTF competitions come in many shapes and sizes, but fundamentally challenge players to find hidden pieces of data called "flags" buried inside intentionally vulnerable systems. Most fall into one of two formats. Jeopardy-style events, the kind Sentinels League runs, hand out standalone puzzles across categories such as web exploitation, forensics, and cryptography, with points awarded per solve. Attack-defense events ask each team to defend its own vulnerable network while trying to break into everyone else's.

Related:Vulnerability Management Isn't About the Score — It's About How It Applies to You

The attack-defense format took shape at DEF CON's CTF, which began in 1996 and remains the event most closely associated with it. It has sprung forth a wellspring of CTF formats that range from grassroots industry events to big vendor-sponsored competitions like the Sentinels League.

Sentinels League grew out of ThreatOps, a set of internal games SentinelOne's solutions engineers have run since 2020 to teach customers how to hunt through telemetry for hidden flags. This year's championship built on that with four games — Endpoint, Cloud, SIEM, and AI — spread across 12 weeks of qualifiers between June and October

The opening player pool of 2,236 entrants came from more than 100 countries and competed for a total prize pool of $100,000. Smaller prizes are dispensed across the qualifier and regional events, with the bigger prizes kept in reserve for the final, which was held in conjunction with SentinelOne's annual OneCon event.

Ryan O'Grady, director of SE operations at SentinelOne, says the firm invests money in the prizes and the considerable logistics of running such a big event as a way to give back to the community, build expertise and exposure to its platform, and serve as a recruiting tool.

Related:Is Your Organization Ready for 2027's AI Accountability Era?

Whether motivated for the prizes or the training, the appetite for the event just keeps growing. This year's drew enough interest that the company had to get a bigger ballroom to accommodate spectators.

Sentinels League is just one example of what a CTF looks like, across a much broader spectrum of competitions available out there. On CTFtime, the volunteer-run archive that tracks the hobbyist side of the scene, last year's calendar alone listed more than 200 individually organized events, with active teams from countries spanning every populated continent.

DEF CON CTF, often called the World Series of hacking, pulled 673 teams through its 2026 qualifiers before finals in Las Vegas this August. The National Cyber League, a nonprofit circuit O'Grady competes in himself, drew more than 7,500 students from 670 schools and universities this spring. Kaspersky continues to run its own wildly popular SAS CTF out of Bali.

Other, more academic events like New York University's CSAW and Carnegie Mellon's picoCTF run student-focused versions. Larger consulting firms, such as KPMG, use the format to scout for corporate recruits.

Won't AI Kill CTFs, Too?

In spite of the obvious demand for CTFs, as evidenced in the number of events held worldwide and the thousands of participants willing to sink their personal time into these pursuits, many security pundits worry about what AI will do to the purpose and the purity of these competitions.

CTF organizers are thinking deeply about what this means for their rulebooks and how they enforce them. RITSEC's 2026 rules ban using AI to autonomously solve challenges outright, calling it against the spirit of the competition. Meantime, NYU's CSAW has leaned into AI, this year creating an entire track built around using large language models (LLMs) to solve past CTF problems.

DEF CON CTF's 2026 qualifier split the difference. It barred fully autonomous AI teams but let human competitors use AI tools as long as a person stayed meaningfully in charge, and it required every team to label itself No AI, Low AI, or Human-Led AI on the public scoreboard.

A recent study of hundreds of Hack The Box machines released between 2017 and 2025 found solve times dropping roughly 16% a year, with the steepest declines after 2022. The hardest tier of challenges went from a 15-hour median solve down to about five, according to penetration tester Jacob Krell of Suzu Labs, who did the analysis.

He's not the only one worried. An academic study earlier this year from IBM Research and The College of William & Mary pitted 41 participants in a live, on-site CTF against four autonomous AI agents. It found that those agents placed second overall, ahead of most of the human teams competing.

Findings like these are enough to get firms like OtterSec, a blockchain security firm, to make noise about how to "save" CTFs. This summer the firm launched a $100,000 "Save CTFs Fund" to bankroll new formats that stay meaningful as AI keeps improving.

Why CTFs Matter More Than Ever

O'Grady doesn't buy the death-of-CTFs talk. In his view, AI just forces organizers to redesign CTFs so they still force a human to think laterally, AI assistance or not.

AI may not be killing creative CTFs anytime soon, but it is definitely making cybersecurity's career ladder wobble. In the process, it may actually be making CTFs even more crucial.

SANS Institute polled nearly a thousand security leaders and found that unclear career progression was one of the top hiring challenges. It was cited by 32%, more than triple the rate last year. Only a quarter of organizations say they have a clearly defined career path, and entry-level jobs that used to train the next generation of defenders are diminishing. SOC and security analyst roles lead the AI-driven cuts, down 32%. Threat intelligence analysts are next at 26%, with incident responders close behind at 22%.

Bug bounty programs are buckling under AI’s pressure. At the start of the year, maintainers of the open-source project Curl shut their program down after a massive influx of junk AI submissions. HackerOne paused its Internet Bug Bounty program in April after a wave of low-quality, AI-assisted reports flooded in. And this month, Google Bug Hunters similarly paused its open-source bounty program due to similar problems.

These are all blows for cyber career progression, as bug bounty problems were another great place for security professionals to flex their skills publicly and for newcomers to gain a foothold into the industry.

As long as CTF organizers can keep their competitions relevant, these events will remain a valuable puzzle piece in the skills-training picture for the industry, alongside other important hands-on challenges like cyber ranges.

"With LLMs basically sweeping the table on bug bounties, it's become even harder than it already was for people to get out there, show off their skills, and get their name out there," O'Grady says. "AI has only increased the importance of CTF events like this."

Thoughts from a CTF-Runner

Ryan O'Grady offers insights into how building CTF games is a distinct discipline, and how CTF designers can begin adapting to AI.

Running a CTF isn't for the faint of heart: "It's a long process of building the games, testing them, getting the games out there and in the hands of the players, making sure everything keeps running, and then making sure everyone's playing fair."

O'Grady's team sorts challenges into difficulty tiers and tests each flag internally: "Sometimes we create a challenge that I think should be doable in five minutes, and it turns out it takes 30 minutes."

The toughest flag challenges are the most fun and most difficult to design: "To come up with a flag that is extremely challenging, I have to think laterally [to] force players to go through multiple steps or to think about things in a different way.

Using LLMs should be built into CTFs: "It adds a wrinkle to competition, and people often ask, 'Is that cheating?' That's just something we have to think about and design for as creators."

Title: Drei Tage it-sa und eine Frage, die uns nicht loslässt: Wer hat Zugriff auf was?
Context: Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Detection- und Response-Workflows sind wichtig, doch in einem KI-gestützten Angriffsszenario ist es bereits zu spät, wenn man darauf wartet,...
Full Text:
„Wenn Sie uns fragen würden, wie viele Service Accounts oder KI-Agenten wir in der Organisation haben, bekämen Sie je nachdem, wen im Security-Team Sie fragen, eine andere Antwort.” Ein CISO sagte uns das auf der it-sa 2026. Und wissen Sie was? Er war nicht der Einzige. Drei Tage lang drehte sich in Nürnberg alles um KI, Regulierung und Souveränität. Doch die Gespräche, die blieben, drehten sich um etwas viel Grundlegenderes: Welche Identitäten haben in der Organisation Zugriff auf was, und wie wird dieser Zugriff abgesichert?

Diese Frage ist der rote Faden, der sich durch viele Gespräche zog, nur jedes Mal in anderer Verkleidung: mal als KI-Thema, mal als Compliance-Thema, mal als Souveränitätsfrage.

Was wir über die Trends und Herausforderungen gehört haben, die die IT-Security-Welt gerade beschäftigen, wollen wir Ihnen nicht vorenthalten.

Silverfort, it-sa Expo&Congress 2026

Drei aktuelle Trends von der it-sa 2026

1. KI-Angriffe: Wer sie nicht erkennt, hat sie trotzdem.

Jeder CISO beobachtet genau, wie Angreifer KI als Waffe einsetzen. Die Zahlen bestätigen das: Laut der Bitkom-Studie „Wirtschaftsschutz” gehen 82 % der Unternehmen davon aus, dass Angreifer verstärkt KI einsetzen. Gleichzeitig bestätigen Schlagzeilen, dass KI-Angriffe zunehmen. Tempo und Umfang, in dem sie sich entfalten, machen sie für Verteidiger derzeit so herausfordernd.

Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Detection- und Response-Workflows sind wichtig, doch in einem KI-gestützten Angriffsszenario ist es bereits zu spät, wenn man darauf wartet, dass SIEM- oder SOAR-Erkennungen etwas Verdächtiges melden. KI-Angriffe spielen sich in Minuten ab, schneller als jede Triage und schneller, als ein Mensch etwas rechtzeitig korrelieren kann. Das Einzige, worauf jeder Angriff weiterhin angewiesen ist, ob KI oder nicht: der Missbrauch von Identitäten. Auch der beste KI-Angriff braucht am Ende einen Zugang, ein Passwort, ein Token, einen Service Account. Auf der Identitätsebene wird ein Angriff sichtbar, wenn man jede Anmeldung und jede Zugriffsanfrage im Blick hat und in Echtzeit entscheidet, ob sie fortgesetzt werden darf.

2. Compliance & NIS2: Ein Dauerprojekt.

Auf die Frage, was die EU-Richtlinie NIS2 bei Security-Teams konkret verändert hat, kam am Stand am häufigsten diese Antwort: „Wir arbeiten dran.” Das Gesetz gilt in Deutschland seit Ende 2025. Laut einer TÜV-Rheinland-Umfrage haben aber nur 14,3 % die Pflichten vollständig umgesetzt. Fast jeder Dritte (30,8 %) antwortete auf die Frage nach dem Umsetzungsstand sogar mit „weiß nicht”.

Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Unternehmen müssen bald nachweisen können, dass sie die Pflichten einhalten. Ein Großteil der NIS2-Compliance beruht auf starken Identity-Security-Kontrollen, etwa: alle privilegierten Konten identifizieren, MFA einführen, nicht-menschliche Identitäten wie Service Accounts prüfen, Remote-Zugriffe wie RDP und SSH schützen, granulare Zugriffsrichtlinien für alle kritischen Systeme und Anwendungen etablieren und mehr.

Die gute Nachricht: An der Einsicht fehlt es nicht. 60,3 % der Befragten halten NIS2 für wichtig oder sehr wichtig für mehr Resilienz. TÜV-Rheinland-Experte Michael Silvan sagt: „NIS2 ist kein Bürokratieprojekt. Es ist eine Chance, Sicherheitsstrukturen so aufzubauen, dass sie im Ernstfall wirklich tragen.” Wer jetzt auf der Identitätsebene gründlich Bestandsaufnahme macht, hat bei der Umsetzung einen Vorsprung.

3. Souveränität: Wer abhängig ist, kann nicht souverän entscheiden.

„Digitale Souveränität” war auf der it-sa an jeder Ecke Thema, und fast jeder wünschte sie sich. Aber: Der Bitkom „Cloud Report 2026″ zeigt, wie weit Wunsch und Wirklichkeit auseinanderliegen: 85 % halten Deutschland für zu abhängig von US-Cloud-Anbietern. 71 % beziehen heute Cloud-Angebote aus den USA, bevorzugen würden das nur 8 %. Als größtes Hindernis für einen Wechsel nennen die Unternehmen Lock-in-Effekte. Und das ist ein Sicherheitsthema, nicht nur ein Infrastrukturthema: Laut demselben Report sagen 87 % der Unternehmen, dass es souveränen Cloud-Angeboten internationaler Anbieter an Transparenz bei Datenverarbeitung und Zugriffsrechten fehlt.

Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Ohne diese Transparenz lässt sich die Frage, um die es in diesem Beitrag im Kern geht, nicht beantworten: Wer hat Zugriff auf was? Souveränität ist im Kern eine Frage der Kontrolle: über Ihre Daten, Ihre Schlüssel und Ihre Logs und darüber, wer entscheidet, wenn es darauf ankommt. Unsere Einschätzung: Jede Abhängigkeit ist auch ein Zugriffspfad und ein potenzieller Single Point of Failure. Wer nicht weiß, wo seine Abhängigkeiten liegen und wie schwer ein Wechsel wäre, kann im Ernstfall nicht entscheiden, sondern nur reagieren.

Die gute Nachricht: Die Bereitschaft wächst. 37 % würden für eine Cloud, die Daten ausschließlich in Deutschland und geschützt vor ausländischem Zugriff verarbeitet, inzwischen Nachteile in Kauf nehmen. Bitkom-Präsident Ralf Wintergerst sagt: „In den Cloud-Markt könnte in den kommenden Jahren mehr Bewegung kommen, wenn sich Unternehmen einen Wechsel zutrauen und gezielt nach Alternativen mit klarem Souveränitäts-Profil suchen.”

Der gemeinsame Nenner: Unternehmen erkennen, dass die Basics wichtiger sind denn je

Auf den großen Bühnen ging es wie zu erwarten um KI, in den Gesprächen am Stand jedoch um Basics. Auf die Frage nach alten Konten begegnete uns Ehrlichkeit: Das bleibt eine Daueraufgabe, die Security-Teams lösen wollen, um identitätsbezogene Lücken zu schließen. Das deckt sich mit der Bitkom-Studie: Angriffe richten vor allem deshalb Schaden an, weil sie nicht erkannt werden (59 %), Systeme falsch konfiguriert sind (57 %) und das Identitäts- und Zugriffsmanagement Lücken hat (55 %). Die häufigsten Schadensursachen seien „keine besonders ausgefeilten oder exotischen Angriffe, sondern blinde Flecken im eigenen System”, so Bitkom-Präsident Ralf Wintergerst. Oder, wie es unser CISO vom Anfang sagte: „Wie viele Service Accounts wir haben? Kommt drauf an, wen man fragt.”

Aus Identity-Security-Wahrheiten werden Prioritäten für 2027

Bei allem Gerede über neue Kategorien und neue Lösungen: Die Konzentration auf die Basics bringt viel, während Security-Teams erst lernen, wie KI-Angriffe ablaufen. Die meisten Sicherheitsstrategien setzen auf klassische Detection-and-Response-Szenarien und auf Schwachstellenmanagement. Doch in einer Welt, in der Angreifer KI als Waffe nutzen, müssen Organisationen verhindern können, dass Angreifer überhaupt erst eindringen und Schaden anrichten. Und so bleibt jedes Mal dieselbe Grundfrage: Wer hat Zugriff auf was, und was kann diese Identität tun, sobald der Zugriff gewährt ist? Das sind Ihre Prioritäten für 2027:

Jede Identität sichtbar machen, auch die nicht-menschlichen (NHIs) und KI-Agenten. Erfassen Sie Service Accounts, API-Schlüssel und Tokens, die Ihre KI-Agenten nutzen, und löschen Sie, was niemand mehr braucht. Beginnen Sie mit Sichtbarkeit und erweitern Sie von dort aus um Kontrollen, die zur Laufzeit durchgesetzt werden.

Jeden Zugriff prüfen, und zwar in Echtzeit. Gemeint ist wirklich jeder Zugriff: ob Mensch oder Maschine, in der Cloud und on-prem, auch auf Altsystemen. Und Echtzeit heißt wirklich Echtzeit, denn KI-Angriffe arbeiten in Maschinengeschwindigkeit, ihr Angriffsweg schrumpft auf Minuten. Nur eine Prüfung, die mithält, hindert Angreifer, ob KI oder Mensch, daran, mit dem Zugang, den sie zu missbrauchen versuchen, etwas anzurichten.

Nachweisen können, wer worauf zugreifen darf. Dokumentieren Sie Zugriffe so, dass Sie Ihren NIS2-Stand belegen können, und kennen Sie Ihre Abhängigkeiten. Das ist Ihre Roadmap für Geschäftsleitung und Budgetrunde.

KI-Angriffe auf der Identitätsebene stoppen: So geht es nach der it-sa 2026 weiter

Wir haben uns gefreut, Sie in Nürnberg zu treffen, und wollen das Gespräch darüber fortsetzen, wie Sie Ihre Identitätsebene zur stärksten Verteidigungslinie machen. Es mag abgedroschen klingen, zu sagen „Identität ist der neue Perimeter”, aber es stimmt: Einen Perimeter gibt es eigentlich gar nicht mehr, und Angreifer haben nur dann Erfolg, wenn sie in Ihre Umgebung gelangen.

Bei Silverfort erforscht unser Team, wie KI-Angriffe ablaufen und warum KI-Angreifer Identitäten so gern ins Visier nehmen. Wir teilen unsere Erkenntnisse gern ausführlich mit Ihnen, ob wir uns auf der it-sa gesprochen haben oder diesmal nicht zusammengekommen sind.

Vereinbaren Sie ein Gespräch, um den Austausch fortzusetzen, oder stöbern Sie in unserem AI Attack Readiness Kit, um selbst loszulegen.

Title: OpenCode User Hit with Hostile Backlash After Reporting Free AI Loophole
Context: Its developer, Anomaly, also offers hosted model access, including free models with usage limits, and paid enterprise features such as centralized configuration and SSO integration
Full Text:
An OpenCode user who reported a loophole in its free AI usage limits became the target of harassment, including comments encouraging suicide, from people who blamed the disclosure for cutting off their supply of free AI. The GitHub thread has since been deleted, although an earlier version remains available through the Wayback Machine.

OpenCode is an open source AI coding agent that helps developers write, edit, and run code from a terminal, IDE, or desktop app. The MIT-licensed software can connect to commercial AI providers or locally hosted models. Its developer, Anomaly, also offers hosted model access, including free models with usage limits, and paid enterprise features such as centralized configuration and SSO integration. The reported bypass concerned the allowances on the free hosted models.

The report drew a flood of hostility in the project’s public issue tracker, with warm pillow wishes among the mildest responses. Other participants unleashed the kind of abuse that would ordinarily get someone banned from an open source project, openly encouraging suicide and pressing the reporter for identifying information.

A Call for a Fix Turned Into a Pitch for the Bypass #

The report, opened on June 28, described limits tied to an IP address. Switching to a different address through a VPN allegedly restored access while preserving the coding session. The author claimed to have automated the process and kept DeepSeek V4 Flash and MiMo V2.5 running for weeks. They proposed tying limits to accounts and detecting rapid IP changes. The account was created 13 days before the report and has no public repositories, a sparse history consistent with a throwaway account.

In an odd reversal, the author inexplicably closed the issue as completed on July 31, then reopened it on August 24 to promote the very workaround they had originally proposed fixing. They complained about the available free models and said they wanted people who could not afford subscriptions to build more with them.

Three days later, the reporter claimed to have run 130 agents across concurrent sessions, hitting usage limits six times in four to five hours and continuing by changing IP addresses. By then, the author was advertising the same behavior they had initially proposed preventing.

The same technique was being discussed elsewhere. A September 5 Hacker News commenter described OpenCode’s per-IP limits and told readers that “if you get some high-quality proxies you can get basically unlimited agent compute.” The comment did not reference the GitHub issue, but it shows the workaround had circulated beyond that thread before the late-October backlash.

On October 1, OpenCode collaborator rekram1-node responded that enforcing limits without authentication was difficult and that abuse undermined the effort to let anyone try a coding agent at no cost.

“Broadcasting this isn't very helpful, it only serves to harm,” the collaborator wrote before closing the issue. The response did not announce a fix.

Commenters Attacked the Reporter and Kept Trading Workarounds #

In late October, users traded conflicting accounts of whether changing IP addresses still restored access. Some said it had stopped working, while others offered additional workarounds. The attacks on the reporter escalated alongside those exchanges.

One GitHub commenter accused the author of gaining nothing from the disclosure, adding, “thanks for ruining it for us.” Other commenters wished suffering on the reporter, and at least two encouraged suicide.

The pile-on also included a supposed million-dollar reward. A commenter claiming to represent OpenCode offered the money if the reporter supplied their address. Replies joined in requesting identifying information, including the reporter’s “government name.” There is no evidence that the offer came from OpenCode.

Later replies quoted a participant telling others to stop harassing the reporter, only to accuse that person of being the author posting from another account. Other commenters challenged the reporter’s reversal, pointing out that they had first recommended closing the loophole, then reopened the issue and described using it extensively.

The discussion became a mix of personal attacks, arguments over the reporter’s motives, and requests for help keeping the bypass working. Some blamed the disclosure for losing access even as others continued to claim success. It’s unclear whether OpenCode changed its enforcement in response to the report.

The blame also spread to Reddit. In a post titled “The End of Long Free OpenCode Sessions”, the author complained that sessions had shrunk from hours to one or two prompts and claimed IP-switching workarounds no longer worked. “I didn't even know about this VPN bypass stuff, people like you ruined it for us,” one commenter told the Reddit poster. A reply redirected the blame with a link to the aforementioned deleted GitHub issue.

Others welcomed the prospect of tighter restrictions. “Well, if this helps my paid subscription to work much better, then it’s more than welcome,” another participant wrote.

The thread offered no settled explanation for the restrictions. Its author asserted that OpenCode now tracked hardware IDs and account metrics, without supplying evidence, while another commenter said changing a cellular IP still worked.

VPN Users Reported Access Problems #

Reports of disrupted access predated the October 27 release. In an October 22 Reddit thread, users said free models were blocked after little activity, including users who said they were not using a VPN. An October 23 post described changing IP addresses successfully for two months before the workaround recently stopped helping.

In another Reddit discussion, a user said a longstanding VPN setup now produced a daily-limit message immediately upon opening OpenCode.

“I think the IP detection may be a bit over zealous?” the user wrote. After another participant attributed the restrictions to VPN-based abuse, the original poster asked why the offering was described as a free tier when it appeared available only to people without VPNs. Another commenter said changing servers still worked.

OpenCode contributor Tarquinen addressed network-level blocking in a separate GitHub issue, explaining that the restriction applied to the connecting network address.

“Shared VPN addresses are often flagged, and we can't make exceptions for individual users,” the contributor wrote.

The experiences remained inconsistent. In an October 27 Reddit discussion, one commenter reported usable access through a dedicated-IP VPN, while another described very low limits without using a VPN.

The Fix Status Remains Unclear #

OpenCode made several infrastructure changes in October, including routing free-model requests through a newer inference service and tightening how it handles client IP information. An October 13 change addressed spoofed IP headers, but that is different from switching to a genuinely different IP address through a VPN. Whether those changes closed the reported loophole remains unclear.

The October 27 v2.2.0 release added visibility into usage and budgets but did not announce a fix for the reported bypass. Enforcement could also have changed on the hosted service independently of an application release.

The final comments preserved before the thread’s deletion still offered conflicting accounts of whether the workaround functioned. The thread remained accessible on October 28, after the release, and was subsequently deleted without a public explanation.

Socket contacted OpenCode for comment on the reported bypass and the thread’s removal but had not received a response at publication time.

Demand for AI Compute Accelerates #

The rush to code with AI has reached a fever pitch, with developers chasing more capable models, longer sessions, and enough compute to keep fleets of agents running. AI demand is squeezing memory supplies and driving prices higher. At the high end of the local hardware market, Apple’s newly available 512GB Mac Studio configuration reached an eye-watering $29,799 with 16TB of storage.

In the OpenCode thread, that hunger for compute curdled into a pile-on. The reporter went from proposing a fix to boasting about running 130 agents through the loophole. Other users blamed them for spoiling the arrangement, hurled abuse, and kept asking how to get the free models working again. The thread captures the AI coding gold rush at its most frantic, with users scrambling to keep their agents running and searching for the next route around the limits.
