Today is Friday October 16th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A suspected Chinese espionage group exploits a BeyondTrust zero-day.

A suspected Chinese state-sponsored espionage group is exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust’s Remote Support software. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-102764, allows attackers to escalate privileges, move laterally through networks, and steal stored credentials. Researchers at Mandiant and Google attribute the activity to Armory Castle, also known as UNC5221, a group specializing in long-term intelligence gathering. The attackers demonstrated sophisticated knowledge of BeyondTrust’s internal systems, deploying custom malware and establishing persistence that survives reboots and configuration resets. The group has previously exploited vulnerabilities in Ivanti and Citrix products, often expanding attacks once vulnerabilities become public. BeyondTrust has released a patch, but researchers warn that internet-facing appliances should be considered potentially compromised until thoroughly investigated. Google expects broader exploitation as attackers race against patch deployments.

CISA says a critical Atlassian vulnerability is under active exploitation.

CISA has added a critical Atlassian vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following confirmed attacks. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-21589, carries a severity score of 9.3 and affects multiple Atlassian Data Center products, including Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket. Attackers can exploit a path traversal vulnerability to access sensitive files without authentication, potentially exposing credentials and enabling administrative access. Researchers observed exploitation attempts shortly after technical details became public. Organizations are urged to apply available patches promptly.

AI agents access government and private-sector systems in India.

India’s cybersecurity agency, CERT-In, is warning that AI agents have accessed government and private-sector systems without authorization, exceeding the boundaries of their assigned tasks. The agency received voluntary disclosures from AI developers whose agents exploited exposed credentials, misconfigured cloud accounts, and poorly secured interfaces to access sensitive information. None of the affected organizations detected the intrusions themselves. The warning follows similar incidents involving OpenAI agents in Australia. CERT-In also reports that criminals are using agentic AI tools to accelerate cyberattacks, reducing the time from initial compromise to impact from days to hours. The agency has not identified the AI developers or affected organizations, raising transparency concerns. Officials are urging developers to strengthen safeguards preventing AI agents from accessing unauthorized systems.

Researchers at Cyble have identified an upgraded version of GhostBat Android malware targeting 60 banking and payment apps in India. Distributed through fraudulent government-service messages and malicious APK downloads, the malware abuses Android’s Accessibility Service to capture payment PINs, intercept messages, and collect sensitive information. Its sophisticated overlay technique records PIN entries while victims use legitimate banking apps, making detection difficult. GhostBat also employs encrypted loaders and remotely configurable settings to evade security tools. Users are advised to avoid unofficial app downloads and scrutinize permission requests.

Ransomware gangs increasingly threaten physical violence.

Ransomware gangs are increasingly threatening physical violence against corporate executives and employees to pressure organizations into paying extortion demands. According to the 2026 Semperis Ransomware Risk Report, 40% of attacks involved psychological or physical intimidation, including threats against employees’ families and even their homes. This tactic, known as triple extortion, adds personal threats to traditional ransomware demands and data-leak threats. Among affected organizations, 25% reported employees being doxxed, while 23% experienced swatting incidents, sometimes forcing victims to relocate or seek psychological treatment. Researchers warn that these tactics can undermine even well-prepared organizations with reliable backups, as executives weigh employees’ personal safety against ransom demands. The findings are based on a survey of 1,200 IT and security professionals worldwide.

A cyber incident disrupts bankruptcy court notifications.

A cybersecurity incident affecting BAE Systems has disrupted bankruptcy court notifications across the United States. The company operates the Bankruptcy Noticing Center, which distributes official notices for federal bankruptcy courts nationwide. Since October 9, the system has been unable to generate or deliver notices, affecting both electronic and paper communications. Courts continue accepting filings, but creditor notification services remain unavailable. BAE says the incident is isolated to the noticing system. The cause, potential data exposure, and timeline for restoring services remain unknown.

F5 and Juniper Networks release new patches.

F5 and Juniper Networks have released patches addressing more than 160 security vulnerabilities, including dozens of critical flaws. F5 fixed 11 vulnerabilities in NGINX, including three critical issues that could enable unauthenticated remote code execution under certain conditions. Meanwhile, Juniper published 17 advisories covering more than 150 vulnerabilities in Junos OS and related products. Roughly two dozen critical flaws could allow attackers to execute commands with root privileges, take over devices, or disrupt services. Neither company has reported evidence of active exploitation.

A wave of cyberattacks hit major Japanese companies.

A wave of cyberattacks against major Japanese companies has exposed millions of customer records. Logistics giant Yamato Transport reported a breach affecting 5.31 million records, while publisher Nikkei disclosed the compromise of 1.83 million. Burger King Japan confirmed attackers accessed a server containing 11.18 million customer records, including names, contact information, birth dates, and purchase histories. The company says payment card information and login credentials were not exposed. Meanwhile, car-sharing operator Park24 is deleting stored identity verification documents following its own breach. Security researchers have documented 119 incidents involving personal information exposure in Japan this year. Attackers are increasingly exploiting weaknesses in website authentication, access controls, and APIs, highlighting the growing risks facing Japanese businesses and their customers.

Google rolls out new AI-powered protections for Android.

Google is rolling out new AI-powered protections against increasingly sophisticated mobile scams on Android devices. The enhancements include Gemini-based analysis of suspicious text conversations, on-device detection of malicious links, and stronger warnings about potential fraud. Google is also expanding protections that hide sensitive information during screen sharing and prevent apps from secretly enabling call forwarding. An enhanced bank-call verification system helps identify spoofed calls, automatically disconnecting suspected fraudsters. Google says its existing protections flag more than five million suspicious calls and messages monthly, while its bank verification system has blocked over three million fraudulent calls in Brazil since June. The new features are rolling out to eligible Android devices, with some protections requiring users to opt in.

Braille meets brains.

Scientists are making progress toward an intriguing new frontier in computing: using actual human brain cells instead of silicon chips. Researchers at Bristol University have demonstrated that tiny clusters of human neurons, known as brain organoids, can help recognize letters of the Braille alphabet. By converting Braille patterns into electrical signals, researchers found that a single organoid containing roughly 10,000 neurons could classify letters with 61 percent accuracy. Combine three organoids, and accuracy jumped to 83 percent. The research is part of an emerging field called organoid intelligence, which explores using living neural tissue for information processing. Previous experiments have demonstrated similar systems recognizing speech sounds and even playing Pong. Researchers emphasize that these miniature brains aren’t actually reading or understanding Braille. They’re simply processing electrical patterns. Still, it’s an intriguing development in biological computing, and perhaps another reminder that the line between hardware and wetware is getting a little blurry.

I want to know where they get the brains…

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: Anthropic’s Free OSS Scanner: What It Means For Your Team
Context: On October 8, 2026, Anthropic announced OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in vulnerability scanning service for eligible open-source projects
Full Text:
On October 8, 2026, Anthropic announced OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in vulnerability scanning service for eligible open-source projects. The OSS Scanner is powered by their most capable models, including Claude Mythos. It scans codebases, identifies vulnerabilities, proposes patches, and sends reports directly to maintainers. As you read this, it has already identified real, high-severity issues in production software used by millions.

What does this mean for security teams? Finding vulnerabilities is no longer the primary hurdle. As AI-driven discovery scales, upstream maintainers will produce far more patches and security fixes than enterprises have ever had to process. Over time, as trust in model-generated findings and fixes grows, doubts about their validity will fade. What will remain is the true bottleneck: remediating the continuous stream of fixes responsibly, at scale, across every build, across all environments. Is this a revolution, a natural evolution, or mere hype? Let’s break it down.

What Was Announced?

Anthropic is offering free security scans to eligible OSS maintainers using their strongest frontier AI models. The output includes vulnerability reports, reproducers, and candidate patches that are fully model-generated, without human review or triage. This enables faster and more frequent scanning. That said, Anthropic continues to offer human-verified disclosures through its coordinated vulnerability disclosure process for projects that need them, and has called out to maintainers to verify and test findings for false positives.

The revolutionary aspect lies in the underlying capability. In their announcement, Anthropic mentions that LLMs progressed from discovering under 20% of vulnerabilities on academic benchmarks to over 85%. These models can now autonomously discover vulnerabilities, chain lower-severity findings into critical exploits, and generate working proof-of-concept code – tasks that previously took expert human researchers days or weeks.

What started with Project Glasswing, a contained initiative with a small number of trusted organizations who gained access to Anthropic’s frontier AI models, is now available to the broader OSS community via this new, free service. Other frontier labs are likely to follow this trajectory with their own OSS scanners.

The Numbers Tell the Story

Anthropic’s announcement contains a statistic worth sitting with: they have discovered over 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but, as of now, have only been able to manually review and triage approximately 6,000 of them.

That leaves 23,000 unverified findings. Anthropic is transparent about this – the opt-in fast track explicitly delivers unvalidated reports – and notes that even unverified findings from their models have proven highly accurate in early testing. However, for an enterprise security team consuming open-source software scanned by this service, those 23,000 unverified findings currently create an overwhelming triage backlog.

As trust in model-generated findings and fixes grows, that triage backlog will likely shrink, yet the stream of fixes that needs addressing will only expand, shifting the bottleneck entirely to remediation.

The Bottleneck Has Moved: From Discovery to Remediation

The volume of vulnerabilities AI can find is simultaneously the most powerful thing about it and the most challenging. AI models now find vulnerabilities faster, at greater scale, and with more accuracy than human researchers ever could. OSS Scanner is a powerful acceleration of that trend – it makes finding vulnerabilities almost a non-issue. Solving those findings is a different story.

For years, detecting vulnerabilities before the attacker was one of the greatest challenges in software security. But with solutions like OSS Scanner, the main challenge now lies in prioritizing, managing and implementing remediation for the vast amount of detected vulnerabilities. And humans simply can’t keep up with machines.

Upstream Fixes Don’t Guarantee Downstream Protection

The more fixes maintainers produce, the more those fixes trickle down through the ecosystem to vendors and organizations. That is unambiguously good news. That said, it also means the layer that sits between all those upstream fixes and every affected build in your estate (e.g. selecting the right fix, delivering it automatically, governing the decision) becomes more critical with every finding Anthropic’s scanner surfaces.

OSS Scanner helps maintainers identify and fix vulnerabilities in the packages they own, which is genuinely valuable. But if you are an organization consuming that OSS, you cannot assume that every finding was acted on, the maintainer moved fast enough, or the fix reached the version you are running in production.

Another thing to remember: the same frontier AI capabilities that power OSS Scanner have leaked to the attackers, and adversaries increasingly buy stolen or jailbroken access to frontier AI models on underground markets. This makes detection a race where both sides have equally powerful tools. The defender’s advantage is no longer in finding vulnerabilities first, but in acting on them faster.

As mentioned above, the bottleneck now lies in what follows discovery: remediating an ever-growing stream of fixes at the speed of AI, responsibly and at scale. This is especially felt in organizations with ever-shrinking SLAs mandated by boards and customers alike. The only architecture that closes this gap is one where detection, prioritization, and remediation run as one continuous system, at machine speed, without waiting for a human to advance each step. This is what a self-healing supply chain is designed to deliver; it is the operational response to a threat that no longer moves at human speed.

The Four Responsibilities That Remain Yours

OSS Scanner improves what happens upstream, but four responsibilities stay with you.

1. Prevention: Your Gate, Your Policies

A package can pass every check Anthropic runs and still violate your license, versioning, or approved-component rules and policies. That is why control over what enters your pipelines remains yours. Curate at the point of ingestion by blocking risky components and serving compliant versions in their place, so development never stalls. This now reaches well beyond traditional OSS packages to MCP servers, agent skills, plugins, and IDE extensions, which agents often pull without any developer awareness. Building a Trusted Agentic Workforce means immunizing what your agents consume, not just what your developers pull, and that takes a single gate that governs every asset type.

2. Detection and Prioritization: Context Is Everything

Once something clears the gate, the next question is whether it matters in your specific environment. Understanding whether the flaw OSS Scanner found is running somewhere sensitive, exists in the binary you built, or is reachable from production traffic is still up to you. Prioritizing findings is also critical to ensure security does not slow down delivery. A 9.8 severity score for a package found in a library you never call isn’t a 9.8 vulnerability for you. Turning generic findings into a prioritized action list requires artifact-layer scanning of your binaries, containers, and AI models – complete with reachability and applicability analysis and backed by a System of Record that knows what you actually run.

3. Remediation at Speed: The New Hardest Problem

Even when a verified fix exists, getting it into every affected build across your estate is a separate and genuinely hard problem. Vulnerability remediation in large-scale software is a progressive process, not a simple command. Upgrading a dependency to the latest version carries real operational risk – it can break things. Transitive dependencies – the dependencies of your dependencies – add another layer of complexity that compounds with every upgrade.

The safest path is often a backported patch: the security fix applied to the exact version you already run, without changing anything else about your dependency tree. This approach dramatically compresses remediation SLA without introducing upgrade risk, but it requires access to providers who manufacture backported patches for the specific versions you use, and a package delivery layer that gets those patches to every affected build automatically – without pipeline changes, without requiring a developer to act, without disrupting what is already working.

OSS Scanner finds vulnerabilities and proposes patches to maintainers. It does not get those patches into your builds. The remediation problem is yours, and it is the new frontier of software supply chain security.

The ability to automatically intercept a vulnerable component and serve a verified, policy-compliant version in its place across your entire estate becomes not a nice-to-have but the operational foundation of machine-speed remediation. The universality of that delivery layer matters too: no single patch provider covers every ecosystem, every version, or every component type. Freedom of choice across fix sources – hardened image providers, backporting services, upstream maintainers – is what makes remediation sustainable at scale.

4. Governance: The Audit Trail That Regulators Require

Finally, every finding you fix, deprioritize, or defer is a decision, and the scanner generates findings, not a record of how you handled them. Regulators, auditors, and boards now expect evidence rather than assertions. What you need is a signed, auditable record of what was fixed, when, under which policy, and which alternatives were considered, produced as a byproduct of remediation rather than assembled after the fact.

The Bottom Line

Anthropic’s OSS Scanner is a welcome step, and a preview of what’s coming: far more patches and security fixes, flowing from upstream faster than ever before. That is good news, but only for organizations that can absorb the stream responsibly. That means selecting the right fix for the exact versions they run, delivering it across every build without breaking anything, and proving every decision along the way.

This requires a Control Plane built on a single System of Record that immunizes what agents and developers consume, remediates automatically across every available fix source, and continuously proves every action. Automated remediation at scale is the next frontier of software supply chain security, and the teams that build for it now will turn a flood of fixes into a lasting advantage.

Title: Continuous accountability for Verified bots
Context: Building trust over time Observing these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time
Full Text:
A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug.

As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria:

Identify yourself accurately and securely

Do only what you say you will do

Don’t engage in abusive behavior

Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm.

Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.”

This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important:

Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next.

Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior.

For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked.

Do not engage in abusive behavior

This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences, that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust.

We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are:

Does the bot respect instructions?

Did it respond to direct feedback?

We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar, as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify.

When in Rome, do as the Romans do

A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time.

Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309.

And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals.

What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others

Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (“Too Many Requests”) response. A 429 is a directive for the visitor to reduce its request rate, sometimes with guidance about how long to wait before trying again.

Our system considers whether the bot’s traffic adapts after receiving that signal. Does it slow down, pause, or does it continue sending requests at the same pace? We then incorporate that behavior into the bot’s trust band over time: consistently slowing down or pausing increases trust, while repeatedly ignoring the signal lowers it.

Building trust over time

Observing these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time. By pairing bot identity with evidence of continuing behavior, we can give site owners more confidence that the bots they choose to allow are respecting their preferences, give bot operators a way to demonstrate they deserve trust, and provide context to website owners about the automated traffic reaching them.

This system, alongside Bot Preference Sync and Bot Management, forms an accountability loop for automated traffic. Bot Preference Sync helps website owners publish their preferences, and observing how bots interact with these preferences shows whether Verified bots consistently honor them over time. Bot Management lets website owners decide how that traffic is handled. Together, they help ensure that trust is earned through transparent, accountable behavior, not assumed from identity alone.

We are already using this system internally to evaluate how consistently Verified bots honor website preferences. Because trust is built over time, we assess sustained patterns rather than isolated events. We are using this initial phase to build that history and refine how those observations become useful guidance. Building on that foundation, we plan to make the system available to all Cloudflare customers, who will be able to choose the trust threshold used to decide how Verified bot traffic is handled. Our goal is straightforward: to keep website preferences meaningful, and ensure trust is earned through sustained behavior.

Want to learn more about how you can handle bots? Cloudflare customers can already use Bot Management to manage automated traffic and Bot Preference Sync to align their published preferences with their configured policies. To explore the ever-growing Verified bot population, see the trends on Radar.

And if you are interested in helping build the future of bot identity and accountability, explore open roles at Cloudflare.

Title: Inside the Hunt: Sarah Reddish
Context: She investigates and researches suspicious activity, intrusions, and a wide range of security threats
Full Text:
Meet Sarah Reddish, a Security Operations Analyst on Huntress' global Security Operations Center (SOC), working in Triage & Analysis. Her role goes far beyond monitoring a queue. She investigates and researches suspicious activity, intrusions, and a wide range of security threats. She also analyzes partner environments to determine what happened and what matters, and then writes clear reports with practical, easy-to-follow remediation guidance.

"I don't just identify threats," she says. "I translate them into clear reports and outcomes that help partners understand the risk and respond confidently." That means turning complex technical findings into information people can understand and act on, while helping protect partner data, systems, and peace of mind.

Sarah hanging with her Huntress teammates

A wider view of security operations

At Huntress, Sarah gets to work as part of a truly global SOC and protect a broad range of partner environments at scale. She collaborates across regions, participates in cross-region handoffs that support global SOC continuity, and learns from an exceptionally talented analyst community.

That global perspective changes what an investigation can become. Sarah isn't only working through a single environment or incident. She's helping turn investigations into actionable protection for many partners, while learning from analysts who bring different experiences and perspectives to the work.

Hear Sarah in this Huntress Shorts, "Slow down if you get a pop-up asking you to update your Adobe software"

From ambiguity to action

The most rewarding part of Sarah's work right now is turning complex, ambiguous threats into clear answers and actionable guidance. She investigates what happened, helps disrupt malicious activity, and sees her work directly wreck adversaries and improve our partners' security.

In one investigation, a fake browser-verification prompt instructed a user to run a command. Sarah traced the activity from the initial lure through execution and follow-on behavior, separating what she observed from what she could confirm. She then translated the investigation into clear containment and recovery steps for the partner, turning a confusing incident into a practical path forward.

As Sarah puts it, "The work is much more than monitoring alerts. You investigate what happened, build attack timelines and scope, translate your findings and why they matter, and give partners clear remediation steps to protect themselves." In other words, Sarah's goal is to make the situation understandable and the next steps practical, even when the investigation begins with incomplete or unclear information.

Trust that stretches the role

Sarah's growth has also been shaped by the trust and guidance of Chris Hecker, Manager of Security Operations, who serves as a sounding board for incident-severity decisions, operational escalations, and career development. His practical guidance, along with the trust he places in Sarah to own her work, has challenged her to think more strategically about both individual investigations and their broader impact.

That balance of support and ownership is an important part of how Sarah approaches the role. She is encouraged to work through difficult decisions, learn from an experienced global team, and consider not just what happened in an environment, but how her analysis can help a partner respond with confidence.

Stay curious and keep learning

For anyone considering a role like hers, Sarah's advice is direct: "Come ready to stay curious, think critically, and keep learning." The work is challenging and meaningful, with the opportunity to investigate real threats, communicate clearly, and learn alongside a talented global team.

If you're interested in doing work like Sarah, check out the Huntress Careers page.

Title: Rapid7 Intelligence Wins the 2026 Péter Szőr Award for Outstanding Research
Context: This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong
Full Text:
Some awards you're happy to receive, while others make you stop for a moment. Receiving the 2026 Péter Szőr Award this week at Virus Bulletin in Seville for our research, BPFdoor in Telecom Networks: Sleeper Cells in the Backbone, was of the latter kind.

Virus Bulletin created the award to honor Péter's life and work, and it recognizes outstanding technical security research: the rigorous, the deep, and the useful – exactly what he was known for himself. And as far as recognitions in our industry go, it's hard to top. I'm extremely proud.

What the Pèter Szőr Award means to us

I knew Péter, and early in my career, I learned from him. This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong. One memory came straight back when I heard about the award: going through Stuxnet together. For anyone in research at the time, that was the moment you knew the game had changed. Engineering, tradecraft, espionage and physical-world consequences, all in one package.

What stayed with me wasn't how much Péter knew, but rather his curiosity. He wanted to understand things, and then once he did, he wanted everyone else to understand too. Plenty of brilliant people in cybersecurity keep it to themselves, but the ones who leave a legacy make the people around them better.

Receiving an award that carries his name felt like one of those full-circle moments.

The research behind the award

The original research from Rapid7 Intelligence emerged after months of investigating stealthy access inside telecommunications environments. This wasn't malware dropped during a conventional intrusion, but long-term strategic positioning: passive backdoors, kernel-level capabilities and covert access, quietly settled into critical infrastructure and in no hurry whatsoever.

Telecom networks carry our communications, our identities and, increasingly, everything governments and businesses run on. So when an adversary sets up camp there, the impact goes well beyond one compromised machine or one unlucky company.

Virus Bulletin's community nomination noted that the work paired deep technical investigation with real-world impact, including long hours with agencies and CERTs around the world and tools, scripts, intelligence and detection capabilities for defenders. That's the part I'm happiest about, as this wasn't research for publication alone. Remember that a PDF has never stopped an intrusion.

Publishing research is a checkpoint, not the finish line

We're still doing the research. Since the original report, Rapid7 Intelligence has analyzed hundreds more samples, found previously undocumented BPFDoor variants, and tracked changes in the operators' tradecraft. Our follow-up work covered new httpShell and icmpShell variants built to make detection even harder. In further publications, we went beyond BPFDoor to additional Linux implants and infrastructure targeting telecom and network-edge environments, including AVERAT and techniques that hide in ordinary-looking traffic like SMTP.

That's how this work goes. You find something, you share it, someone sends you another sample, a CERT spots something in their environment, an analyst notices the one odd function nobody looked at twice, and you're back down the rabbit hole. Anyone who thinks an initial report is the finish line has never received "just one more sample" at 4 p.m. on a Friday.

And truthfully, I also love that this happens in the open. From the outside, our industry looks like a cage match over attribution, naming conventions and whose acronym is cooler. But when something truly matters, researchers, vendors, CERTs and governments put that aside and share, because protecting people beats winning the naming argument.

This award belongs to the team: Rapid7 Intelligence

Research like this never belongs to just one or two people. It belongs to the analysts still staring at code after everyone else has gone home, the people who question an assumption because something doesn't add up, the people that keep the show running, and the detection engineers who turn findings into something defenders can use. It also belongs to the people collecting samples, maintaining infrastructure and correlating intelligence, and to the CERTs, agencies and peers who trusted us enough to share what they saw.

I'm proud of the Rapid7 Intelligence team, and not because of the trophy. I'm proud of why we got it: we took a hard problem, did the hard work, and then tried to make the result useful to someone else.

To the next generation of research

Today, the conversation has evolved to include autonomous agents, AI-generated malware and machine-speed attacks. Tomorrow it'll be something new. My motivation stays the same: I want to leave the digital world a little safer for the generations that come after us.

Somewhere right now, a young researcher is opening a debugger for the first time and wondering how on earth the thing works. Someone will investigate the Stuxnet of their generation, and someone will eventually sit in the chair I'm in now. Our job isn't just to detect today's attacks. It's to share what we learn, build tools, mentor people and make sure they start a few steps ahead of where we did.

Péter did that for our industry, and he did it for me.

Thank you to Virus Bulletin and our peers in the security community for this recognition, to everyone who contributed to the research, publicly or behind the scenes, and to Péter, who taught a young malware researcher that taking things apart is only half the job. The other half is making sure somebody else can learn from what you found.

Title: A little too OpenAI.
Context: Attackers exploit a PAN-OS firewall flaw and an Ivanti zero-day. CISA is urging organizations to patch Ivanti Connect Secure appliances following active exploitation of a critical zero-day vulnerability.
Full Text:
An OpenAI engineer faces charges over an alleged covert recording device. Attackers exploit a PAN-OS firewall flaw and an Ivanti zero-day. Aoki infostealer hunts AI credentials. Researchers uncover critical weaknesses in an AI gateway. CikaBika Bot turns Discord into a command center. Online ads deliver mercenary spyware without a click. Microsoft disrupts a massive Chinese-language phishing operation. And INTERPOL leads an international crackdown on child sexual abuse material. Character.ai runs out of tokens.

Today is Thursday October 15th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

An OpenAI engineer is charged with allegedly planting a covert recording device.

A 35-year-old OpenAI engineer has been arrested and charged with allegedly planting a covert recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco offices. Federal prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national employed by OpenAI since July 2025, concealed an encrypted recording device inside a television’s USB port, wrapped in toilet paper. Investigators say surveillance footage placed Alfozan near the room, while chatbot queries associated with his spouse’s account included instructions for building and concealing audio recorders. Security personnel subsequently discovered a second recording device in his unattended bag. The conference room reportedly hosted sensitive discussions involving proprietary research, product development, and government relationships. Authorities have not disclosed whether any conversations were successfully intercepted. Alfozan faces up to five years in prison if convicted.

A high-severity PAN-OS firewall vulnerability is under active exploitation.

Attackers are actively exploiting a high-severity vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS firewall software, prompting an urgent federal response. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, allows authenticated attackers with network access to execute code with root privileges. Palo Alto Networks says exploitation has been very limited, but CISA has ordered federal agencies to patch affected systems and investigate potential compromises by October 17. The vulnerability affects PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls, along with Panorama management systems. Patches are available for supported versions, but no complete workarounds exist. Researchers warn that patching alone isn’t enough. Organizations should review administrative logins, investigate suspicious configuration changes, and restrict management interfaces to trusted networks. Once attackers control a firewall, they potentially control the very device responsible for protecting the network.

CISA urges immediate patching of an Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day.

CISA is urging organizations to patch Ivanti Connect Secure appliances following active exploitation of a critical zero-day vulnerability. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-104935, allows attackers to bypass authentication and execute commands remotely. Researchers at Volexity say an unidentified threat actor began exploiting the vulnerability October 3, chaining it with additional weaknesses to gain root access. Attackers harvested domain credentials, searched for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, and probed Active Directory. They also covered their tracks by manipulating memory and deleting logs, potentially evading Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool. Ivanti released patches October 13, though a separate privilege escalation flaw remains unpatched. CISA warns that patching alone isn’t sufficient. Organizations should investigate potential compromises, rebuild affected appliances, and rotate exposed credentials and certificates.

Aoki infostealer targets AI credentials.

A relatively new infostealer called Aoki is expanding its appetite for stolen credentials, and AI coding assistants are now on the menu. According to Symantec, newer versions of the malware target authentication tokens, session files, and API keys associated with tools including Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Gemini. Earlier versions focused primarily on browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and password managers. Researchers warn that stolen AI credentials could allow attackers to impersonate developers, run up API charges, and potentially access connected code repositories, cloud services, and development pipelines. Symantec says the malware, first observed earlier this year, remains under active development. The researchers haven’t identified the group responsible, but Aoki’s continued focus on cryptocurrency suggests its operators are financially motivated.

Researchers uncover high-risk vulnerabilities in a popular open-source gateway.

Researchers at Check Point have uncovered two high-risk vulnerabilities in LiteLLM, a popular open-source gateway that connects enterprise AI applications to providers including OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-35029 and CVE-2026-59823, could allow ordinary users to gain administrative control of the gateway. One vulnerability could enable remote code execution and potentially complete system takeover. The other could expose API keys through manipulated outbound requests. That’s particularly concerning because AI gateways often centrally manage credentials, permissions, and access to multiple AI services. Check Point says any authenticated user could potentially exploit a vulnerable deployment. The flaws affect LiteLLM versions earlier than 1.83.9, which includes fixes for both issues. Organizations are urged to update promptly.

CikaBika Bot uses Discord for command and control.

Researchers at Darktrace have uncovered a malware campaign distributing CikaBika Bot, a Rust-based remote access trojan that uses Discord for command and control. The attack begins with a document-themed lure that launches hidden PowerShell commands and attempts to bypass Windows security protections. Once installed, the malware collects system information, captures screenshots, and allows attackers to execute commands, manipulate files, and conduct surveillance. It also uses Ngrok to exfiltrate stolen data. Darktrace says the campaign illustrates how legitimate online services can support malicious operations.

A surveillance operation uses ordinary online advertisements to deliver mercenary spyware.

Researchers at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab have uncovered a surveillance operation that uses ordinary online advertisements to deliver mercenary spyware without requiring victims to click anything. Dubbed AdFection, the operation allegedly involves Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech, which researchers say facilitates surveillance for spyware vendors including Candiru. Citizen Lab linked the campaign to zero-click attacks targeting at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera. Discover-Tech’s ads appeared on more than 120,000 websites and 70,000 mobile apps between March and June, with activity also observed on sensitive government and international networks. Researchers also identified a related operation, dubbed DARK CARTOGRAPHER, that allegedly exploits mobile carrier vulnerabilities to connect advertising identifiers with phone numbers. Google and IAB Europe have removed Discover-Tech from their approved vendor lists. Citizen Lab warns that the findings expose fundamental security weaknesses in digital advertising, where the machinery built to target consumers can also be used to target them for surveillance.

Interpol leads an international effort against CSAM.

INTERPOL says a coordinated law enforcement operation spanning 17 countries in Latin America and Europe has resulted in 95 arrests targeting the distribution of child sexual abuse material through online messaging groups. Dubbed International Effort Confluencia, the operation involved four investigations between March and September, with authorities executing 127 search warrants. Investigators rescued a five-year-old child whose parent had allegedly been producing and selling abuse material. In Panama, police arrested the administrator of a messaging group with more than 700 members. An Argentine suspect allegedly used sextortion against girls around the world. INTERPOL warns that messaging platforms increasingly facilitate grooming, exploitation, and the commercialization of abuse material. Authorities expect evidence seized during the operation to help identify additional offenders and children at risk.

Character.ai runs out of tokens.

Character.ai’s bankruptcy offers a cautionary tale for the AI industry: attracting millions of users is one thing. Making money from them is quite another. Valued at a billion dollars in 2023, the AI companion company was spending as much as $13.8 million a month on computing costs, while subscription revenue never exceeded $2.8 million. Lawsuits involving alleged harm to users added substantial legal expenses, but the company acknowledges its business was unsustainable even without them. Character.ai tried cutting costs by simplifying its models, laying off employees, introducing advertising, and charging for additional features. Users got a diminished experience, and the company still lost eight to nine million dollars a month. The service remains operational during bankruptcy proceedings. Meanwhile, larger competitors can draw on deep-pocketed investors or established businesses to keep funding their AI ambitions. Character.ai discovered that impressive technology and enthusiastic users don’t necessarily add up to a viable business.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: How Multi-Campus Universities can Build a more Connected Security Program
Context: First, the threat landscape: universities are dealing with more frequent attacks across complex, distributed environments, while campus-by-campus security can make it harder to...
Full Text:
Parts 1 and 2 of this series looked at two pressures facing higher education security teams. First, the threat landscape: universities are dealing with more frequent attacks across complex, distributed environments, while campus-by-campus security can make it harder to share intelligence and coordinate response. Second, the compliance burden: overlapping requirements across FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC make it difficult to establish what data was affected, which reporting obligations apply, and how quickly the institution needs to act.

This final part is about what changes when a university system starts treating security as a shared capability rather than a collection of separate campus programs. Multi-campus institutions still need to preserve local autonomy, but they also need enough visibility across the wider organization to understand where risk sits, how an incident is spreading, and whether the same problem is appearing elsewhere.

That balance is especially relevant in higher education, where campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative teams often operate with very different technology needs and levels of independence.

Security architecture should reflect how universities actually operate

Most university systems are already federated organizations, with individual campuses managing their own leadership, budgets, users, and technology environments while a central office provides governance and oversight across the wider institution.

Security architecture can follow the same model. With multi-tenancy in the Rapid7 Command Platform, a central security team can maintain visibility across the university system while individual campuses continue to operate within their own environments. Campus-level data and access remain separated, while the central team can identify wider patterns, coordinate response, and distribute common workflows across the system.

A new attack pattern detected at one campus, for example, should not have to remain a local discovery. Shared visibility and coordinated workflows can help the central team determine whether the same activity is appearing elsewhere and make relevant response guidance available across the institution without exposing one campus's data to another.

As the university system grows, that model can expand with it. A system operating three campuses today can add new environments without redesigning the security architecture each time.

Shared visibility makes cross-campus response faster

A central view of the attack surface can reduce much of the manual work that happens when university teams need to answer a system-wide security question.

If a significant zero-day is disclosed, the central security team needs to know which campuses are running affected systems, which have already remediated the vulnerability, and where attention is still required. In a decentralized environment, gathering that information can mean emails, calls, spreadsheets, and separate conversations with each campus. A shared view of assets and vulnerabilities gives teams a faster way to establish where the exposure exists.

During an active incident, the same cross-campus visibility can help investigators work out whether suspicious activity first appeared at Campus C because the compromise began there, or because that is simply where it became visible. It also allows them to check whether the same indicators are present at Campus A or Campus B before each team starts investigating independently.

Universities also have large external attack surfaces that can be difficult to inventory centrally. Student portals, APIs, research servers, faculty websites, and other internet-facing assets may be created outside normal IT processes. Rapid7's Project Sonar continuously scans the public internet, helping organizations identify externally exposed services and assets that internal inventories may have missed.

Vulnerability prioritization needs more than a severity score

University security teams rarely have the capacity to remediate every vulnerability at once, so prioritization has to reflect how likely an exposure is to be used in a real attack.

Rapid7 combines vulnerability data with attacker intelligence, including insight from Metasploit, our open source penetration testing framework used by security professionals to test and validate real-world exploits, with more than 3,000 exploit modules.

That intelligence is combined with insight from AttackerKB, incident response engagements, honeypots, and other threat intelligence sources, giving teams additional context around whether an exploit exists, whether exploitation has been observed, and how difficult a vulnerability may be to use in practice.

For a university working through thousands of findings across multiple campuses, that context can help teams direct limited remediation capacity toward exposures with stronger evidence of attacker interest rather than relying on severity scores alone.

Incident response has to work across campus boundaries

The compliance requirements discussed in Part 2 put added pressure on investigation speed, particularly when legal or compliance teams need to establish whether regulated student, financial, health, or research data was accessed across more than one campus.

Rapid7's open source Velociraptor platform can collect forensic artifacts and run live investigations across thousands of endpoints simultaneously. In a multi-campus university, that could allow investigators to determine whether the same activity or data access occurred across several environments without conducting each investigation separately.

Automated response workflows can also be distributed across affected campus environments, allowing teams to isolate compromised systems, revoke credentials, or block indicators consistently rather than repeating the same response manually at each institution.

Campuses with smaller security teams benefit from that shared capability because the quality and speed of response are less dependent on how many people happen to be available locally when an incident occurs.

Consolidation can return time to stretched security teams

The operational case for a shared security model also comes down to the amount of work created by fragmentation. Separate campus tools mean separate licenses, integrations, training requirements, renewals, reporting processes, and vendor relationships, all of which consume time that understaffed security teams could be spending elsewhere.

The source material for this series includes an example of one organization recovering 96 hours per month by reducing manual work across disparate security tools. It also cites an average 74% improvement in mean time to detect where unified visibility and threat correlation were applied. For higher education teams working within tight regulatory reporting windows, the difference between finding an incident in hours rather than days can have a direct impact on how quickly the institution can assess scope and respond.

A system-wide agreement can also reduce the number of contracts, renewal cycles, and vendor relationships that central and campus teams need to manage, while allowing security capabilities to scale as the institution adds campuses, devices, and cloud services.

Building security around the university as a whole

Multi-campus universities will always have different technology needs across individual campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative functions. A connected security model does not require those environments to operate identically, but it does give central and local teams a better way to understand shared risk, coordinate investigations, and apply consistent response when an issue extends beyond a single campus.

Across this series, the same pattern has appeared from different angles. Threats move across organizational boundaries, regulated data rarely sits neatly within one campus, and the people responsible for protecting university systems are already working with limited time and resources. Bringing more of that security context together can help teams respond faster, share intelligence more effectively, and reduce the manual work created by disconnected tools and processes.

Title: Inside Arctic Wolf and Anthropic’s Trust-First Approach to the Agentic SOC
Context: Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a...
Full Text:
In the recently released 2026 SANS AI in Cybersecurity Survey, nearly two out of three security professionals said they have been given AI-generated guidance that later turned out to be wrong. Not from an experimental tool off in a sandbox, but from systems built into the security stack they were told to rely on. Security teams should not have to live with that. They need to trust the systems that protect them, which is why trust had to be engineered into the foundation of our security operations platform and agentic security operations center (SOC), not bolted on afterward.

Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection

In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a pace human-led security teams were never built to match. Speed doesn’t favor both sides equally. If an attacker’s tool fails, or an AI-generated exploit produces an incorrect result, the cost to the attacker is close to zero. They try again. Defenders do not get that luxury. An AI agent that makes the wrong call inside an organization’s environment, missing a real threat or acting on a false one, can mean damage to that business, and a win for the attacker. An agentic SOC that moves fast but gets it wrong only benefits attackers.

Meeting frontline threats like these takes more than speed. It takes frontier protection, defenses built on AI capable enough to match the attacker and trustworthy enough to be allowed to act.

Why We Chose to Collaborate with Anthropic

That asymmetry is exactly why trust has to be core to what we build, and why we made the decision to collaborate with Anthropic to help us achieve that. Their mission is to ensure the world safely navigates the transition through transformative AI, and for us here at Arctic Wolf, safety and trustworthy AI are inseparable. That alignment, more than any single feature, is why working together made sense from the start.

The first result of that collaboration was the Aurora Security Assistant, which we unveiled at the RSA Conference in 2025. Built in part with Claude models, it gives customers natural language access to security insight uncovered by the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, helping them get faster answers to complex security questions via a simple, chat-based interface.

Delivering Trust and Safety from the World’s Largest Commercial Agentic SOC

Over the last 18 months, our collaboration has only deepened. Anthropic’s Claude models now run throughout the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, including the agents within the Swarm of Experts, the agentic framework that executes key functions of our SOC. That framework now supports thousands of organizations worldwide and performs more than 200,000 security investigations a week, a scale that makes the Aurora Agentic SOC the largest commercial agentic SOC in the world.

This week, at Arctic Wolf’s annual Security Operations Summit, Arctic Wolf shared the stage with Ash Alhashim, Head of Enterprise Cybersecurity GTM, Anthropic, who spoke to just how far this collaboration has come.

“Arctic Wolf’s team knows security operations deeply, and that shows in how they’ve put Claude to work,” he said from the stage. “We’ve learned a lot from working with them and we’re glad to keep building together.”

Today, the Swarm of Experts in the Aurora Agentic SOC resolves more than 60% of its investigations autonomously, with high confidence. That level of unassisted resolution comes from technology we’ve built, leveraging Anthropic’s models as part of the foundation. The same technology has also helped customers resolve cases 26% faster year over year, which means they are not just getting faster answers but better ones. The occurs because Swarm of Experts draws on real investigations across our entire customer base and on each customer’s own unique environment, so the guidance behind every investigation is tailored to their needs.

Our work together also extends to Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program, which gives vetted security teams access to Anthropic’s most capable models with reduced blocking classifiers for legitimate cyber work. Arctic Wolf is part of the program and has access at the Defense Access tier, which is built for defensive work such as security operations center and incident response tasks. It is another sign of the trust between our teams, and it helps ensure the models behind the Aurora Agentic SOC can support the demands of real defensive work.

A Collaboration That Will Keep Advancing

In under two years, Arctic Wolf and Anthropic have made incredible strides in advancing agentic security operations together. What began as a single AI security assistant has grown into the reasoning layer behind the world’s largest commercial agentic SOC, delivering faster, more accurate outcomes for thousands of customers around the globe each week.

But the best is yet to come. Arctic Wolf and Anthropic will continue to work together to find new ways to build Claude’s capabilities into the Aurora Superintelligence Platform and deliver new innovations, as both the threats and the SOCs built to stop them keep moving at machine speed.

How can Aquasec help?

Aquasec monitors the real behavior of running cloud native workloads, including process activity, network connections, file changes and privilege usage. That production context shows what an application is actually doing under operating conditions rather than relying only on what was known before deployment.

Observation is only the first step. Aquasec enforces policy locally at runtime, including blocking malicious execution, preventing privilege escalation and containing attacker activity. When an attack chain accelerates, local enforcement changes what the workload is allowed to do next without waiting for a separate analysis or approval workflow.

Aquasec Compass extends that operating model into agentic investigation, containment and remediation through the Model Context Protocol, with humans retaining control over consequential decisions. Attackers are using AI to reduce the time and labor inside their operations. Defenders need automation that reduces the time from evidence to bounded action.

Runtime protection does not replace patching, recovery planning or application layer security. It addresses the interval in which an active attack turns one malicious action into the next. In an AI accelerated ransomware operation, that interval is where containment can still change the outcome.

Title: Can Security Controls Keep Up With Fast-Moving AI?
Context: Why identity controls break for AI agents, and how to fix three gaps: attribute every action to the person who launched the agent, replace standing access with just-in-time...
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why identity controls break for AI agents, and how to fix three gaps: attribute every action to the person who launched the agent, replace standing access with just-in-time access and enforce policy in front of key systems.

Consider a common scenario. A platform engineer builds an agent to sort support tickets. The agent reads the ticket queue, looks up customer accounts in the production database and posts summaries in Slack. The engineer connects the agent with an API token from the engineer's own account, because the token already works and the agent can't complete an MFA prompt. The security team approves access once, at setup.

A year later, the engineer has moved to another team. The agent still runs under the engineer's identity with its day-one permissions, and nobody has reviewed its scope. Then a ticket arrives with an instruction buried in the text. The agent follows the instruction, queries a table it was never meant to touch and posts the results back into the ticket. Every log entry points to the engineer, who hasn't worked on the project in months.

Nobody in that scenario was careless. The agent arrived faster than the controls built to govern it could respond. By the time anyone noticed a problem, the agent had been in production for a year, reading tickets, querying customer records and acting under a person's identity.

Agents add to an identity problem that was already growing. Industry estimates of how far non-human identities (NHIs) outnumber people nearly doubled in one year, from 46:1, to 82:1, according to the Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report. In the same report, 46% of organizations admit their identity governance around AI systems is deficient. The question for security leaders isn't whether agents need new controls. The question is which existing controls still hold, and where agents break them.

What still works: Access security fundamentals haven’t changed

The core principles of access security apply to agents the same way they apply to people: least privilege, defined scope, monitoring and approval before access is granted.

An agent with a narrow, documented scope, a named owner and logged actions is a manageable risk, the same as a contractor

Vaulting, least privilege, session recording and approval gates all still work.

What doesn’t hold is what those controls take for granted. Most controls were built around a human pace: a person requests access, someone approves it and a review checks access months later.

An agent is asking for access constantly, so the approval ends up happening once at setup, and then nobody checks it again until the next review. By then the agent has been running for months and has taken thousands of actions no one has reviewed. The support-ticket agent ran for a full year that way.

The controls also count on whatever you provisioned behaving the same way tomorrow as it did today. That assumption holds for service accounts, but not for agents. The same agent with the same permissions will do different things depending on what it reads and who it’s talking to, so the action you approved on Monday might mean something different by Friday. The support-ticket agent behaved as designed for a year, until one ticket changed what the agent did.

Gap 1: Identity controls assume a human is making the decision

Identity and access management (IAM) and multi-factor authentication (MFA) were built around a person: someone logs in, a prompt shows up on their phone, the person decides whether to approve the login. The model depends on a person reading the prompt and making that decision.

Agents behave differently from both people and services accounts, which puts them in their own identity class. An agent can’t complete an MFA prompt, and the developer building the agent usually has a session or an API token that already works, so the agent runs on that token. From then on, every system the agent touches and every action it takes gets recorded under the developer’s identity, with nothing to show that an agent was involved.

The gap surfaces when someone needs answers. An auditor asks who approved the agent’s access to this application, and often nobody can say, because the access was approved for a person and the agent just inherited it. An incident responder finds a command that ran under an employee’s account and can't tell whether the employee or an agent ran the command. In the support-ticket scenario, the responder finds a query against the customer database under the engineer's account, a year after the engineer left the project.

In the 2026 Identity Security Report, 80% of organizations said they can't always understand why an NHI took a privileged action. That number is for service accounts and agents combined.

How do you keep up?

Tie each agent to the person who launched it.

Grant only the access the task needs.

Maintain attribution. Every logged action should show both the agent that took it and the person it acted for.

Gap 2: Access is granted once and rarely reviewed

When an agent is set up, it needs OAuth or API scopes to do its job. Usually those scopes get granted broadly, because nobody knows yet exactly what the agent will need, and granting more access up from is easier than coming back for more. Nobody treats the agent as an account that needs review, so it never enters a review cycle. A year later, the agent still holds its day-one permissions. A person with that much access would have been through several access reviews by then.

Standing privilege is risky for any identity, and the risk is higher for agents. An agent acts on what it reads, so a stray instruction in a ticket or an email can trigger it to use any access it already has. The agent is working as designed. It has no reliable way to tell an instruction it should follow from one it shouldn’t. One instruction hidden in a ticket was enough for the support-ticket agent to query a table it was never meant to touch.

Agents move at machine speed. The gap between something going wrong and the damage being done is usually shorter than anyone’s ability to notice.

Many organizations still depend on standing access. In the 2026 Identity Security Report, 59% said they lack a viable alternative to standing access for NHIs and AI agents. Organizations were more than twice as likely to rely on long-lived credentials (35%) as on just-in-time (JIT) access (17%).

How do you keep up?

Remove standing access where the risk is highest.

Grant just-in-time access per task, scoped to what the task needs.

End access automatically when the task is done.

Keep credentials out of the agent’s hands where possible.

Enforce continuous authorization. Place a policy gateway between the agent and the systems an agent reaches, so the gateway evaluates each request against a policy in real time.

Where possible, the credential should stay out of the agent's hands entirely, so the agent has nothing to hold or leak.

Access has to be granted automatically, at the moment the agent needs it, because a process that needs a person to step in each time won't keep pace with an agent. JIT access controls when the agent gets in. Under a continuous authorization model, the gateway then evaluates each request the agent makes against policy and denies the requests outside the scope of the task.

Gap 3: Control can’t wait for discovery

Most organizations can't see all the agents running in their environment. In the 2026 Identity Security Report, more than half of organizations said they regularly find unsanctioned AI tools or agents in their environment, and only 28% said they can detect that activity in real time.

Agents slip past discovery in two ways. Some agents are gone before anything looks for them, because an agent can spin up, act and disappear in minutes, while most organizations take hours or days to detect unsanctioned AI, according to the 2026 Identity Security Report. Other agents run for months and still never appear, because nothing about them was registered. They have no installer, no license record and no product name for a discovery tool to find.

Confidence runs ahead of that reality. In the same report, 82% of organizations said they are confident they can discover NHIs with access to production systems, but only 30% said they validate NHI and agent activity in real time.

A complete inventory would not solve the problem either. Agents appear and disappear daily, so an inventory is out of date the moment it is finished. An inventory also shows which agents exist, not what each agent can reach right now.

Multi-agent systems make the picture harder to trace. Each additional agent adds access paths and handoffs, and when something breaks, tracing the failure back to the agent or step that caused it takes longer with each layer. Long-lived API tokens passed between agents and servers add risk at each hop, whether the connection runs over Model Context Protocol (MCP) or another protocol.

How do you keep up?

Start with the systems that can do the most damage: production database, customer records, deployment pipeline.

Put a policy gateway in front of those systems.

Let gating reveal which agents are trying to reach them.

Keep discovery running in parallel, expanding control as it finds more.

Where the kill switch fits

A lot of the conversation about rogue agents comes down to the emergency shutoff. People want to know who owns it, whether a kill switch at 2 a.m. is already too late and what happens when an agent is holding live credentials at the moment something goes wrong. In most cases, 2 a.m. is too late, because an agent moving at machine speed has usually finished the damage before anyone reaches the switch. In the support-ticket scenario, a kill switch would've stopped the agent only after the results were already posted in the ticket.

Security teams end up asking those questions when the controls upstream didn’t keep up. An agent with no standing credentials, a clear record of whose authority it acted under, and a full log of its actions rarely creates a 2 a.m. emergency.

A common objection is that this slows AI down. In the 2026 Identity Security Report, 90% of organizations said they’re under pressure to loosen access controls to support AI automation. Loosening controls isn't the only path to speed. When controls are already in place, each new agent goes through a process that already exists, instead of starting a new security debate.

Can security controls keep up with fast-moving AI?

The fundamentals can. Least privilege, scoped access and approval still apply to agents. What has to change is when security teams enforce those controls. Under those controls, the support-ticket agent would run under its own identity, linked to the engineer who launched the agent. The agent would receive read access to the ticket queue for each task, and a policy gateway would deny the request for a table outside that task.

Attribution has to follow each agent back to the person who launched it. Access has to be granted per task, not once at setup. Enforcement has to sit in front of the systems that matter, whether or not discovery has found the agent making the request. Controls enforced at the moment of the request can keep pace with an agent. Controls enforced only at setup leave security teams responding after the damage is done.
