Secret scanning works best when developers are confident in the findings. Catch too little, and real credentials can remain in a repository. Alert too often, and developers may spend time investigating strings that aren’t secrets.

Generic secrets make that balance especially difficult. The same string could be a real credential or a documentation placeholder, so detecting it requires understanding the surrounding code and text.

To address this challenge, we trained a secret classifier specifically for GitHub’s product needs: distinguishing real credentials from lookalikes while meeting the speed and efficiency requirements of scanning at scale.

In our companion post, Secret protection must scale with software, we explained why secret protection must keep pace with AI-accelerated development. Here, we go behind the scenes of the context-aware classifier powering that effort: how we designed, trained, and evaluated it to find more real secrets with less noise.

What we enabled

GitHub secret scanning operates at two key moments:

Push protection helps prevent secrets from entering a repository by scanning changes before a push is accepted, giving developers an opportunity to address the finding.

Post-push scanning works after code has been committed, continuously scanning repository content and creating alerts when potential secrets are detected so developers and security teams can investigate and remediate them.

We developed a fast classifier that reduced median post-push scan execution time by 86% compared with the previous LLM-based pipeline. That efficiency made it practical to extend generic secret detection to push protection, returning results before developers push changes, not only after code is committed.

Secret scanning blocks a commit with push protection after the model detects a secret on line 5 of the file.

Why secrets are hard to detect

Structured credentials often include a distinctive prefix, length, alphabet, or checksum. Generic secrets may not. Their syntax overlaps with build identifiers, checksums, asset hashes, sample values, and other non-sensitive strings. Context is the deciding signal.

Likely real credential

Likely harmless lookalike

A password assigned beside a production database URL

The same password-shaped value in a test fixture

A connection string in deployment configuration

A localhost connection string in a setup guide

A high-entropy value bound to an API credential

A high-entropy checksum, build ID, or asset hash

These cases are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Adding more rules can suppress some of them, but each exception risks hiding a real secret. A learned classifier can instead use signals such as file path, secret type, variable names, and nearby code or text.

That is why we shipped a new scanner using a two-stage pipeline:

Candidate generation: Regex filters scan content for potential secrets with high recall. This stage is optimized to catch broad families of credential-like patterns quickly and deterministically.

Context-aware classification: A fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier evaluates each candidate and its surrounding context. It is trained to recognize the signals that separate real secrets from false positives, including placeholder values, examples, documentation snippets, generated content, and non-sensitive identifiers. Because the model is small and efficient to run on our inference infrastructure, it costs much less to serve and is simpler to scale than an LLM-based pipeline.

Impact:

11.5% user acceptance improvement, reducing false positives.

86% faster post-push secret detection execution time.

More than 98% cost savings compared with the LLM-based pipeline.

How our pipeline works

As content is scanned, regex patterns cast a wide net and flag anything that looks like a credential, so real secrets aren’t missed at the start. Each candidate then goes to a fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier, which reads the value together with its file path, variable names, and surrounding code. The classifier estimates how likely it is to be a real secret. High-confidence findings become alerts, and lookalikes such as placeholders, test fixtures, and checksums are filtered out before they reach developers.

HOW OUR PIPELINE WORKS

Broad first, careful second

STEP 1

Scan

STEP 2

Generate candidates

Regex patterns identify possible tokens, keys, and credential-like strings.

STEP 3

Classify

Fine-tuned ModernBERT evaluates candidate + context and assigns likelihood of a true secret.

STEP 4

Alert or suppress

High-confidence findings move forward; likely false positives are filtered.

The important design choice is that the model does not replace deterministic scanning. Instead, it complements it. Regexes remain the right tool for finding candidate strings quickly. The classifier is used where machine learning provides the most leverage: distinguishing “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”

The classifier model makes a best effort to distinguish “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”

A hard-negative problem: secrets that almost look real

Most false positives are not random. They are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Examples include documentation placeholders, toy examples in tests, redacted values, non-sensitive IDs, and generated fixtures. These cases are easy for a regex to match and hard for a purely rule-based system to suppress without accidentally losing real secrets.

ModernBERT helps because it can read the candidate together with nearby code and text providing contextual understanding comparable to an LLM without the latency and computational overhead of generating natural-language output. For example, a candidate surrounded by words like “example,” “dummy,” “fake,” or “replace-me” may be lower risk than a candidate assigned to an environment variable in a deployment file. The classifier learns these contextual differences from labeled examples rather than requiring engineers to encode every exception as another rule.

We chose ModernBERT because it provides a strong fit for this workload: it is compact, efficient, and well suited for classification over code-adjacent text. For secret scanning, the model needs to make a calibrated decision over short candidate windows with high throughput and low latency.

That makes a fine-tuned encoder classifier a better serving shape than a general-purpose LLM for this stage of the pipeline. The model can be trained directly on our decision boundary, and evaluated using the same recall and precision metrics that matter to secret scanning quality.

How we trained

The challenge was finding representative data for cases in which syntax alone is misleading. The training and evaluation strategy combines three sources:

Product-derived examples from GitHub repositories, using feedback from the secret detection experience and additional human validation.

High-recall regex candidates from GitHub repository data, including human-annotated examples and weak labels used to expand coverage.

Synthetic examples targeted at sparse and difficult cases, such as documentation secrets, test fixtures, public keys, checksums, structured lookalikes, and near-miss pairs.

Synthetic rows pass deterministic validation and model-based quality review before inclusion. Training emphasizes real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that frequently confuse regex-only approaches. Each model input includes the candidate value, file path, secret type, and a bounded amount of surrounding context. We select thresholds through offline evaluation and then validate behavior on production-like traffic before broader rollout.

Before splitting the data, we grouped rows that share a repository, candidate value, or example so near-duplicates could not appear in both training and evaluation.

Training focused on the cases that matter most for alert quality: real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that regexes frequently match. The input representation includes the candidate secret string, file path, type and a bounded amount of surrounding context. The output is a classification score used by the scanner to decide whether the candidate should proceed.

We optimized for the product tradeoff: preserve or improve recall while reducing false positives and serving cost. In practice, that means the classifier threshold is selected using offline evaluation, then validated against production-like traffic before rollout.

The most important training principle was to make the model see the confusing examples. We included candidates that are syntactically similar to real secrets but semantically different, so the model learns not only what a secret looks like, but also what a false positive looks like in context.

The trained model is exported to ONNX format with 8-bit quantization, enabling fast inference.

Evaluation results

We evaluated the new pipeline’s impact in production in two stages: first against the production baseline on the same public traffic and then through a customer A/B experiment.

Offline evaluation: On post-push scanning, the new pipeline achieved 13% higher precision and 19% higher recall than the previous LLM pipeline when evaluated on the same public traffic.

Online evaluation: We then validated whether these quality improvements translated to customer outcomes through an A/B experiment against the previous LLM pipeline. Repository owner-weighted acceptance increased by 11.5%. We weight acceptance by repository owner to reduce the influence of customers who bulk-resolve large volumes of alerts at once, which can otherwise distort a simple average.

Take this with you

The best security tool is the one developers trust enough to use. Higher precision means fewer distracting alerts. Higher recall means more real secrets are caught. Lower cost means we can keep improving coverage without making scanning prohibitively expensive.

For developers and security teams, this should translate into fewer false positives, and faster feedback in the places where secrets are most likely to be introduced: commits, pull requests, and everyday development workflows.

Hybrid systems are powerful. Regex gives us speed, transparency, and broad candidate coverage. ModernBERT gives us learned context understanding and false-positive reduction. The combination outperforms either approach used alone for this product constraint.

We also learned that model size is not the same as model usefulness. A smaller fine-tuned classifier can be the right answer when the task is narrow, the decision boundary is measurable, and serving efficiency is critical.

This is one step toward making secret scanning more accurate, scalable, and easy to use. Looking ahead, we are focused on two areas:

Building a continuous improvement flywheel. We will use production feedback loops to identify new false negatives and false positives, turning real-world signals into higher-quality training and evaluation data.

Exploring new model architectures. We are investigating approaches that can perform secret detection and extraction in a single step, reducing pipeline complexity while preserving accuracy and scale.

Title: Defenders Reluctant to Deploy Agentic AI as a Cybersecurity Tool
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Companies have invested more resources than ever into agentic AI as a cyber defense tool amid growing AI-enabled cyber threats to enterprise networks from. However, the majority of cybersecurity teams remain reluctant to deploy the technology due to concerns over their effectiveness.

Published on October 13, The Enterprise Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 from Flashpoint suggested that despite the ongoing discussion surrounding the potential cyber risks around offensive agentic AI, just a quarter (25%) of cybersecurity teams are actively using agentic AI tools as part of their active cyber defense strategy.

While three quarters of security teams have yet to fully investigate the potential deployment of AI tools into their security operations, 20% of those surveyed said that they are running a closed pilot scheme, and a further 35% said they are examining the potential of adoption within the next 12 to 24 months. The remaining 20% of respondents said they have no plans to test out agentic AI as part of their cyber defense as things stand.

Of those who are using or are piloting AI agents, tasks these tools are involved in include information retrieval and alert prioritization, as well as more active tasks such as blocking IP addresses, updating blacklists and monitoring suspicious traffic.

Some organizations have also used AI to help with more advanced activity, including taking automated action that can directly affect security operations. However, many remain wary of providing an AI agent with this amount of decision-making authority.

When AI Agents Are ‘Confidently Wrong’

Some cybersecurity professionals expressed concerns about agents making wrong decisions.

“An agent that’s confidently wrong is worse than one that’s slow,” said one respondent.

Other hurdles to deployment of AI agents in cyber defense include concerns about data leakage, auditability, regulatory requirements and cost, as well as the level of control agents should have over security workflows.

While many organizations are toying with the investment in and deployment of agentic AI as a cyber defense tool, many are still reluctant to go all in until they have done more research into whether AI agents can be trusted with tasks.

“The opportunity for agentic AI on the defensive side is significant, and our research shows security leaders are ready to invest. But they aren't swayed by the hype,” said Josh Lefkowitz, founder and CEO of Flashpoint.

“They're holding agentic AI to a high bar, and they want to know where it improves their work, whether they can trust the output, and where human judgment must remain part of the process."

While cybersecurity teams are still testing the waters with agentic AI, the report also suggests that boards and executive funding providers appear keen on the adoption of the technology, with over half expecting a significant budget increase to aid with the investigation of agentic AI for cyber defense.

More than a third (35%) said that over the next 12 months, they expect their budget to rise by over 10%, while a further 15% suggested they expect to see an increase of up to 10%. Zero respondents said they believed their cybersecurity budget is set to decrease.

Title: Why AI Red Teaming Belongs at the Core of Your AI Security Program
Context: Gartner’s 2026–2027 ThreatScape names AI application compromise and prompt injection among four critical threats where attackers hold a significant advantage
Full Text:
Enterprises are putting AI applications and agents to work on sensitive data and business workflows, while attackers look for new ways to manipulate the models and exploit the tools connected to them. Security leaders need to know whether those systems will hold up against a real attack, and AI red teaming gives them that answer by testing AI the way an attacker would.

What AI red teaming is

AI red teaming is the process of proactively testing models, agents, applications, and other AI systems to find the weaknesses an attacker could exploit. It simulates techniques such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, data leakage, and model manipulation to see how a system responds under pressure.

Because AI systems and the attacks against them change all the time, red teaming works best as a continuous loop: test real-world behavior, find what fails, use that evidence to strengthen the protections that guard AI in production, and test again.

Why AI systems need continuous testing

Attack methods keep evolving. Threat actors constantly develop new ways to manipulate models and abuse connected tools and APIs. Because these techniques evolve as fast as AI itself, a system that passed last quarter’s tests may not hold up against this month’s attacks. Security teams need to test continuously for new attack techniques, not just the ones they already know.

Model choices change the risk profile. As token costs shape decisions, teams may switch models to lower-costs, or alternatively, switch to more capable, or different models to better fit their AI application. Each switch can change how a system responds to attacks and which safeguards it needs.

What red teaming achieves

Done well, AI red teaming delivers two outcomes: reduced business risk and proof that your AI controls work.

Red teaming shows which weaknesses matter

Red teaming exposes weaknesses before attackers find them and shows which of those weaknesses matter most.

Not every unexpected model response is a real risk, and testing for weaknesses no attacker could realistically exploit wastes effort. Good red teaming focuses on the attack paths that matter for your applications and data and ranks findings by realistic impact, so teams can choose models and design guardrails that align with real risk.

Red teaming produces the evidence compliance teams need

Governance, risk, and compliance teams increasingly need evidence that safeguards withstand realistic attacks, that AI systems don’t expose sensitive or regulated information, and that each application aligns with internal policy.

Gartner’s 2026–2027 ThreatScape names AI application compromise and prompt injection among four critical threats where attackers hold a significant advantage. To counter them, Gartner recommends testing AI applications early and using the results to improve runtime controls.

Frameworks including the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026), the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, MITRE ATLAS, and the EU AI Act also call for adversarial testing and ongoing evaluation. Red teaming produces the record these frameworks expect: what was tested, what failed, how risks were prioritized, and how the organization responded.

Red teaming shows where your AI can be exploited

Treating red teaming as a prelaunch checkbox leaves a gap between what was tested and what runs in production, because models and connected tools keep changing after launch.

A mature AI security program should include three layers of defense: discovery, posture control, and runtime guardrails. Discovery answers “What AI do we have?” Red teaming sits within posture control and answers the next question: “Where can it be exploited?”

Those results help teams choose models that fit their risk profile and design guardrails around proven attack paths instead of generic assumptions.

What to look for in AI red teaming

A strong AI red teaming approach should include:

Continuous, proactive testing that keeps pace as models and attack techniques change or new models are adopted.

Actionable risk visibility that prioritizes tests by exploitability and impact, so teams focus on the risks that matter when choosing models and designing guardrails.

Audit-ready reporting that maps results to the risk and compliance frameworks governance teams already use.

Integrated remediation that connects findings to the policies and protections that address them, without stitching together disconnected tools.

Research quality matters too. Generic prompt libraries catch generic problems, while testing built on new attack research catches the techniques advanced attackers use.

Cato connects red teaming to runtime protection

At Cato, we believe red teaming delivers the most value when it combines deep attack research with the platform that protects AI in production. That research comes from Cato AI Labs, the team behind EchoLeak, the first reported zero-click AI vulnerability in Microsoft 365 Copilot, and CurXecute, a remote code execution flaw in the Cursor IDE. The team turns discoveries like these into realistic attack scenarios and adds new techniques as threats evolve, so testing reflects how attackers actually operate.

Cato AI Red Teaming puts that research to work. It continuously tests AI models with context-aware adversarial scenarios, prioritizes findings by realistic risk, maps them to leading frameworks, and turns them into policy and model recommendations inside the same AI Security solution that protects AI interactions at runtime.

With testing and protection on one platform, security teams can find AI risk and close the gaps before attackers exploit them.

Title: ClickFix to BEC in 24 Hours: Tragic Quadrant | Huntress
Context: Threats like AI platform abuse and ClickFix-style attacks on their own can feel like small problems
Full Text:
Most cyber threats start out small and unassuming before they turn into the OH $#!T moments that put your whole business at risk. They can creep up fast during a normal day with a website you trust and a habit you don't question. You ask your favorite AI platform for help, follow "fix it" instructions when it hits a snag, and get back to work without thinking twice.

Nothing feels risky on the surface. But underneath, the "normal" AI search result you clicked and the "fix it" instructions you followed just helped an attacker gain access to your Microsoft 365 account. While you move on to the next task in your day, they walk straight into your inbox without a password or MFA prompt, looking just like you. They read through your messages and create hidden inbox rules that hide their tracks. That stealthy intrusion is mailbox manipulation, and in this case, it can escalate into full-blown business email compromise (BEC) within hours.

Threats like AI platform abuse and ClickFix-style attacks on their own can feel like small problems. Chained together, they give an attacker everything they need to set up an OH $#!T moment that no one sees coming until it's too late.

Meet Doris and her ClickFix problem

Principal Product Researcher Truman Kain shows what this looks like in practice and how easily it blends into a normal workflow.

Meet Doris Stewart, a fictional finance employee at a company called Speedway Laundry, owned by Speedway Industries. Doris wants help responding to an email, so she goes to Google and searches for ChatGPT. She clicks what appears to be a normal sponsored result and, unknowingly, lands on a custom attacker-built GPT. But there are no obvious tells that this custom GPT is malicious. And Doris trusts ChatGPT, which is what the attacker was banking on.

Here's where things start to get sketchy. The custom GPT tells her there's a service issue and sends her to a fake verification page. Doris is prompted to press Command+Space, paste a command into Terminal, and press Enter. She doesn't recognize that this is a ClickFix scam, and by following those steps, the attacker has tricked her into compromising her own machine.

Now, the attacker runs a script to retrieve cookies and spots Doris' Microsoft session cookie, the one that keeps her logged in to Outlook without entering a password or MFA code each time she needs access. By dropping that cookie into a fresh browser using a free extension and refreshing the page, the attacker is now sitting in Doris' inbox with full control. There was no password and no MFA prompt to get past. The session was already authenticated, so the stolen cookie did the work.

This is where the attacker turns access into cash. In Doris' inbox, the attacker finds an invoice awaiting approval, creates an inbox rule named ".." so it gets easily overlooked, and sets it to archive any message containing the invoice number. Then the attacker replies to Treasury as Doris, asking them to send the payment to a new routing number, deletes the sent message to hide the evidence, and empties the trash. Doris never sees any of it, and the whole thing unfolds in about 24 hours.

This attack didn't require lots of time, money, or technical know-how. But it worked fast, and Doris will be left cleaning up a financial mess that she didn't even know existed.

How Doris could have avoided trouble

The good news is that knowing where to break links in the attack chain can stop a bigger business disruption from happening. In this case, on the endpoint side, the initial access shows up as a Mac shell running curl output with the attacker's IP address Base64-encoded inside it, the exact command Doris walked through pasting into Terminal a few minutes earlier. That pattern is worth flagging as suspicious on endpoints until proven otherwise.

On the identity side, the tells are just as suspicious. Two browsers are active in one session; there are two different operating systems tied to the same login; traffic is routed through a VPN with no business reason to be there; and that sketchy, almost invisible inbox rule ("..").

This isn't new tradecraft, but it's effective and convenient for attackers to slip in unnoticed without dropping noisy tooling that'll get flagged by managed security tools.

Getting ahead of OH $#!T moments with the Tragic Quadrant

The Huntress Tragic Quadrant plots threats on two axes, including the ones in this exact attack chain. The x-axis (prevalence) shows how often we see them in the environments we monitor, and the y-axis, or as we all call it, "pucker factor" (which, if you've ever been on the receiving end of these attacks, makes perfect sense), shows how much damage they cause when they land. That view helps you tackle the riskiest gaps first, so you don't end up in an OH $#!T moment like Doris.

On the lower quadrants, you see tactics like AI platform abuse and ClickFix that aren't usually catastrophic on their own, even if we see them often in our telemetry. The real risk happens when attackers chain them together, and the arrows move up and to the right into the OH $#!T quadrant, where a hidden inbox rule can turn into much bigger problems like BEC or ransomware.

When you know which corner a tactic falls into, it gets easier to see which threats deserve your focus right now and how to spot them in your environment.

Title: Quantum-resistant signing on AWS, Part 2: Enforce your ML-DSA algorithm policy with SCPs and IAM
Context: Review these controls periodically and pair the deny-list with detection so a variant outside your policy surfaces quickly rather than waiting to be discovered
Full Text:
You want to set a cryptographic algorithm policy and stop non-compliant choices from being made in your Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment. This post shows you how. As you adopt post-quantum cryptography, one of the first decisions you face is which algorithms and parameter sets fit your business needs, balancing security against signature size, key size, and performance. Your cloud environment’s job is to let you express that decision and enforce it consistently, so an approved choice stays fully usable while an excluded one cannot be introduced. This post works through one concrete example on AWS: taking an organization’s cryptographic algorithm policy and turning it into preventive and detective controls. The same patterns apply to whatever your approved set is today and whatever it becomes as standards evolve.

This post is Part 2 of a two-part series on quantum-resistant signing on AWS. Part 1, Build a software supply chain with ML-DSA, is for builders and constructs an end-to-end ML-DSA signing pipeline for binaries, container images, and software bills of materials. This part is for the security, governance, and compliance teams who decide which algorithms that pipeline, and everything else in the organization, is permitted to use, and who need that decision enforced.

AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) supports the ML-DSA digital signature scheme (FIPS 204) through three parameter sets, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87, targeting NIST security categories 2, 3, and 5. All three are strong, standardized choices. Each one trades signature size, key size, and speed against security margin, the amount of cryptographic strength a parameter set holds in reserve above its target security category. ML-DSA-44 is the most compact and fastest. ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 carry a larger security margin, which is what you want for signatures that must stay trustworthy over a long lifetime.

Throughout this post, the examples use the same example policy: an organization that has standardized on ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 and wants ML-DSA-44 kept out of its approved set. That is a standardization decision, not a judgment that ML-DSA-44 is insecure (see the following note). Wherever you see ML-DSA-44 in the controls that follow, read it as the variant your policy doesn’t include; the mechanics are identical for any allow/deny split you choose. The approved set here is also the one the Part 1 architecture deploys: ML-DSA-87 for the root certificate authority (CA) and ML-DSA-65 for the subordinate CA and the code-signing key. Part 1 makes the choice; this post makes it stick.

Note: ML-DSA-44 is a valid choice. ML-DSA-44 is a fully NIST-standardized parameter set (FIPS 204) at NIST security category 2, which targets roughly 128-bit-class classical security (category 2 is benchmarked against the collision resistance of SHA-256). It produces the smallest signatures and public keys of the three variants (a 1312-byte public key and 2420-byte signature) and is the fastest to sign and verify, which makes it a strong fit for constrained devices, high-volume signing, and bandwidth- or storage-sensitive workloads. You would choose ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87 instead to gain extra security margin for long-lived signatures or to align with an internal standard, not because ML-DSA-44 is weak.

What success looks like

The approved variants (ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 in the example) remain fully usable throughout. What you want to rule out is the introduction of a variant outside the policy (here, ML-DSA-44). Concretely, within the AWS service surfaces in scope, principals shouldn’t be able to:

Create ML-DSA-44 key material

Use existing ML-DSA-44 keys for signing or verification

Stand up private certificate authorities (CAs) that would introduce ML-DSA-44.

And any drift from those settings should be detected.

Scope and limitations

These controls operate on AWS service APIs, principally AWS KMS, AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA), and AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). They don’t and can’t govern cryptography that runs on compute you control. For example, OpenSSL or an application might perform ML-DSA-44 signing on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, container, or AWS Lambda function. Protocol-level use, such as OpenSSH’s hybrid ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 public key authentication, is also outside the reach of Service control policies (SCPs) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and isn’t addressed in this post.

Certificate material brought in through acm:ImportCertificate or iam:UploadServerCertificate is also not algorithm-aware (see the Private CA section). Other TLS-terminating or signing services (for example Amazon CloudFront and Amazon API Gateway) and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere aren’t covered in this post and should be assessed separately. (Part 1 of this series uses IAM Roles Anywhere with ML-DSA certificates; controls for that service are out of scope here.)

These controls are intended to be applied as defense in depth. You can apply all of them or only a subset, depending on how prescriptive you want to be:

A blanket SCP at the organization root prevents member accounts from creating or using ML-DSA-44 keys. (SCPs don’t apply to the management account, so workloads there aren’t restricted.)

An SCP at a production organizational unit (OU) restricts keys only in production accounts.

If you need flexibility inside an account, use IAM permission boundaries instead of account-wide settings enforced through an SCP.

Choose the combination that matches your operating model. The policy examples here are written to apply across all AWS Regions. If you need to scope a control to specific Regions, add an aws:RequestedRegion condition.

The policies in this post are illustrative starting points. Authoring, validating, and maintaining the specific SCPs, IAM policies, and permission boundaries for your environment is your responsibility. Test all policies in a non-production environment before deployment and adjust example values (such as policy names and key Amazon Resource Names (ARNs)) to match your organization’s approved standards.

A note on cryptographic agility

Your algorithm policy isn’t fixed forever, and these controls shouldn’t be either. The point of expressing the policy as AWS controls is that you can revise it as your needs and the relevant standards change, tightening, loosening, or swapping the approved set without re-architecting. Treat the examples here as a template you adjust to whatever your current policy is.

A deny-based control that names specific algorithms is, in effect, an allow-list of everything it does not name. The risk is default-allow: any parameter set you have not explicitly denied is permitted, so a newly introduced variant, including one you have not yet evaluated, becomes usable until you notice it and add it to the deny list. Deprecation of an already-approved variant is easy to handle in this model, because you simply add the deprecated variant to the deny list. What the model does not catch on its own is the arrival of something new. Review these controls periodically and pair the deny-list with detection so a variant outside your policy surfaces quickly rather than waiting to be discovered.

The alternative is to write the condition against the approved set rather than the excluded one. A Deny that uses StringNotEquals with a list of approved key specs fires when the request’s key spec matches none of them, so a new or not-yet-evaluated variant is blocked by default until you add it. That closes the default-allow gap, at the cost of a policy update before anyone can use a newly approved variant. The family-level SCP in Part 1 of this series takes this shape: it denies creation of any signing key whose key spec isn’t ML_DSA_*. The examples in this post take the other shape and name the excluded variant, so that approved variants stay usable without a policy change. Both are valid. Choose based on whether you would rather block something new first and approve it later, or notice it first and decide then.

{ "Sid": "OnlyApprovedMlDsaVariants", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_*" }, "StringNotEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": ["ML_DSA_65", "ML_DSA_87"] } } }

The StringLike clause scopes the statement to ML-DSA key specs so it doesn’t affect other key types; the StringNotEquals clause denies any ML-DSA variant outside the approved list.

Just as algorithms and key sizes will be introduced over time, or move from approved to unapproved, so will AWS service operations. The set of operations through which an ML-DSA-44 key can be used today (AWS KMS Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey) reflects current service capabilities and might expand as AWS releases new features. If your policy is to block use in addition to creation, you should periodically review the list of operations you restrict, because services evolve over time.

Background: Key spec compared to signing algorithm

AWS KMS support for ML-DSA introduces three key specs—ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, and ML_DSA_87—that all use a single post-quantum signing algorithm: ML_DSA_SHAKE_256. This distinction drives which controls are effective.

kms:KeySpec: Reflects the KeySpec property of the key. It’s evaluated both on CreateKey (the requested key spec) and on AWS KMS key resource operations that act on a specific key, including Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey. This makes kms:KeySpec a reliable lever for both preventing creation of ML-DSA-44 keys and restricting use of existing ones, because it can single out ML_DSA_44 from ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87.

kms:SigningAlgorithm: Reflects the signing algorithm supplied on Sign and Verify, which is ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 for all three variants. It therefore can’t distinguish ML-DSA-44 from the approved variants and shouldn’t be used for this purpose.

The practical consequence: for keys held in AWS KMS, preventing ML-DSA-44 key material from being created is the most robust single control. If no ML-DSA-44 KMS keys exist, none can be used for signing through AWS KMS and none can become the subject key of a certificate. CA keys and TLS server keys are separate material: AWS Private CA generates and holds a CA’s key pair in its own HSMs, and ACM-issued, imported, or uploaded TLS certificates carry their own keys, so those surfaces are governed by the AWS Private CA and certificate controls later in this post. Where ML-DSA-44 KMS keys already exist, their use can additionally be restricted with kms:KeySpec.

Organization and account-level blocking using SCPs

SCPs can be applied at the organization root or to a specific OU to restrict ML-DSA-44. Placement determines the effective scope: it applies organization-wide when attached at the root; attached to an OU, it applies to the accounts within that OU. An SCP is the broadest-scope preventive control available.

Note that SCPs apply to member accounts and OUs but not to the organization’s management account, so avoid running ML-DSA-44-capable workloads in the management account, where an SCP will not restrict them.

The following example SCP denies both the creation of ML-DSA-44 keys (kms:CreateKey) and their use (kms:Sign, kms:Verify, kms:GetPublicKey), matching on the ML_DSA_44 key spec in each case. The creation deny stops new keys from being created; the usage deny covers keys that already exist, whether created before the SCP was attached or living in an account that later joins the OU, because kms:KeySpec is also evaluated at request time on those usage operations.SCPs are guardrails: a Deny in an SCP can’t be overridden by any IAM policy within member accounts.

Attach the following SCP at the organization root (or relevant OU):

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } }, { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyUsage", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": [ "kms:Sign", "kms:Verify", "kms:GetPublicKey" ], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] }

Scope the usage deny to the three key-spec-aware actions. Limit the use of Deny to kms:Sign, kms:Verify, and kms:GetPublicKey (testing confirmed kms:KeySpec is evaluated on all three). Avoid a blanket kms:*: a wildcard that would also catch management operations such as DescribeKey, DisableKey, and ScheduleKeyDeletion, which you need to inspect or clean up those same keys, effectively locking you out of managing the keys you’re trying to remove. If you use multi-Region keys, also add kms:ReplicateKey to the creation deny: replicating an ML-DSA-44 primary key creates a new ML-DSA-44 key in another Region, and kms:KeySpec is evaluated on ReplicateKey as well.

Combining with a family-level guardrail. This SCP governs which ML-DSA parameter set is allowed; it says nothing about RSA or ECDSA. Part 1 of this series includes a complementary SCP that denies creation of any signing key whose key spec isn’t ML-DSA. Attached together, they require every new signing key to be ML-DSA and to be an approved variant.

Operational considerations. A blanket Deny at the organization root is the strongest control but has trade-offs: it removes any ability to create ML-DSA-44 keys anywhere in scope, with no exception path, which can block legitimate testing and might cause infrastructure as code (IaC) or pipeline runs that attempt ML-DSA-44 creation to fail. To preserve flexibility, consider scoping the Deny to a production OU and using IAM permission boundaries (see the following section) in build and non-production accounts.

What the caller sees. When an SCP denies a request, the caller receives an AccessDenied error indicating an explicit deny in a service control policy. For same-account and same-organization requests, the error includes the type of the denying policy and, as the enhanced error messages roll out across services, its ARN. The error doesn’t expose the SCP policy contents, and the user being blocked often can’t see the SCPs applied to their environment. Document the SCP ARN and its purpose internally so support teams can map an AccessDenied quickly.

Prevent ML-DSA-44 key creation in AWS KMS (principal-level)

The following IAM policy blocks ML-DSA-44 at the principal level. It is the identity-based counterpart to the SCP shown earlier, useful when you want per-account or per-role control rather than an organization-wide guardrail. Attach it to the IAM role or user you want to constrain.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] }

Key points:

The condition value is ML_DSA_44 (underscores, not hyphens).

This policy blocks CreateKey only. To also block use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys at the principal level, add the Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey deny shown in the Restricting use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys section.

For comprehensive, non-overridable coverage, deploy as an SCP rather than relying solely on principal-level policies.

IAM permission boundaries

IAM permission boundaries set the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant to an IAM role or user and can be used as an alternative or complement to using SCPs. The effective permissions are the intersection of the identity-based policy and the boundary, and a Deny in a boundary can’t be overridden by an attached policy. Boundaries are useful where you want per-account or per-role flexibility (for example, in build or non-production accounts) rather than a blanket, multi-account deny.

Operational consideration. A permission boundary only takes effect on principals that have it attached. To rely on boundaries as a control, you need a mechanism to enforce the boundary on all IAM principals programmatically. One example enforcement mechanism would be an SCP that denies iam:CreateRole, iam:CreateUser, iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary, and iam:PutUserPermissionsBoundary unless the approved boundary is set (using the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key), and denies iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary and iam:DeleteUserPermissionsBoundary outright so the boundary can’t be removed after the fact. You would also want to probe for non-conforming principals periodically and respond, perhaps by automatically attaching the PermissionsBoundary. IAM users shouldn’t be used, but the enforcement should account for the possibility that they exist.

Because a boundary only sets a ceiling and does not itself grant anything, it opens with Allow on all actions, then denies ML-DSA-44 key creation specifically. The following permission boundary denies creation of ML-DSA-44 keys:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowAll", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" }, { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] }

To also block use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys for the principals carrying this boundary, add the Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey deny statement shown in the following section (which also uses kms:KeySpec).

Restricting use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys

As described in the Background section, kms:KeySpec is also evaluated on Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey, reflecting the KeySpec of the key being used. You can therefore deny those operations when kms:KeySpec equals ML_DSA_44 while continuing to permit ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87. The IAM policy below, attached to an IAM principal, does exactly that.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyUsage", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": [ "kms:Sign", "kms:Verify", "kms:GetPublicKey" ], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] }

This deny can also live in an AWS KMS key policy. The same kms:KeySpec deny can be placed directly in the key policy of an AWS KMS key. A key policy is a resource policy, so the statement must include a Principal element. Identity policies and SCPs do not name principals to which they apply. A deny in the key policy is a resource-side backstop that protects a specific key, while an SCP gives non-overridable organization-wide coverage. To turn the previous example into an AWS KMS key policy, add a Principal element to the statement (for example "Principal": {"AWS": "*"}, or a more specific principal), and keep the rest of it the same.

Additional approaches

Depending on your goals you might also want to remove the key material itself rather than only deny its use. Remember that it is difficult to know what data has been signed by a specific key, unless you track that somehow. Deleting a key that was used will make signature verification impossible. Take great care to make sure keys are not used before deleting them.

Disable or schedule deletion of the keys. Disabling stops key use immediately and is reversible. Key deletion is definitive but irreversible after the waiting period, so confirm before scheduling.

Deny Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey by specific key ARN. You can target named keys rather than the whole key spec. To do this, you would list the exact key ARNs in the Resource element of the IAM policy (no condition key required). This is effective for targeting a single key specifically, but it is difficult to maintain lists of key ARNs. Use this strategy sparingly. If you’re considering using an IAM policy naming a key ARN, remember that a Deny in the key policy of the target key accomplishes the same goal and is attached to the key itself.

Finding existing keys (only needed if you disable or delete). A Deny in an IAM policy or SCP, based on kms:KeySpec, doesn’t require you to know which keys exist – it applies by key spec at request time. If you want to disable or delete existing ML-DSA-44 keys, you need to locate them. AWS KMS has no server-side filter for key spec, so you must enumerate keys with ListKeys and call DescribeKey and inspect each KeySpec. This client-side filtering pattern is common across AWS APIs and is well supported by pagination in the AWS SDKs. You can also use AWS Config to record and query KMS key resources.

Reference: Choosing a KMS key spec – kms:KeySpec condition key

Approved ML-DSA variants and control of AWS Private CA

AWS Private CA sets a certificate authority’s (CA’s) signing algorithm at creation time, in the CertificateAuthorityConfiguration parameter of CreateCertificateAuthority (valid values include ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, and ML_DSA_87). There is currently no condition key for the algorithm, so an SCP cannot enforce signing algorithm. The approach in this section controls who can create CAs and pins the algorithm in that trusted path, backed by AWS CloudTrail-based detection.

Recommended approach

Restrict who can create CAs. Deny acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority broadly via SCP, and allow it only for a small set of trusted roles or an approved provisioning pipeline. This removes the ability for arbitrary principals to stand up a CA with an unapproved algorithm.

Pin the algorithm in the trusted path. Have that approved pipeline or infrastructure-as-code template hard-code SigningAlgorithm to ML_DSA_65 or ML_DSA_87 in CertificateAuthorityConfiguration. Because AWS Private CA exposes no algorithm condition key, this provisioning path is the enforcement point. Note that the CA’s algorithm pins the signature on the certificates it issues; the subject key in each certificate comes from the CSR, which AWS Private CA copies without validating its algorithm, so pin the CSR key algorithm in the same issuance pipeline.

Control the trust chain. On the PKI side, only add approved CAs to your trust stores and issuance hierarchies, and do not trust or subordinate CAs that could issue ML-DSA-44. This prevents an unapproved CA from being introduced into a trusted path.

Detect drift. Use CloudTrail to capture CreateCertificateAuthority calls and AWS Config to flag any CA whose configuration uses ML_DSA_44, so an unapproved CA is caught quickly.

Part 1 of this series shows what this looks like in practice: it creates an ML-DSA-87 root CA and an ML-DSA-65 subordinate CA with CreateCertificateAuthority, activates them, and distributes the resulting chain to verifiers. In the model described here, those are the calls that only your approved provisioning pipeline is allowed to make.

Setting the ML-DSA value in CertificateAuthorityConfiguration. The same variant goes in both the KeyAlgorithm and SigningAlgorithm fields (for example, KeyAlgorithm=ML_DSA_65 with SigningAlgorithm=ML_DSA_65). Note a difference in signing algorithms between AWS KMS and AWS Private CA. With AWS Private CA, the SigningAlgorithm takes the variant value directly (ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, and ML_DSA_87), and doesn’t accept ML_DSA_SHAKE_256. In contrast, AWS KMS uses ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 as its signing algorithm. Be aware that some older AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) builds omitted descriptions of the ML-DSA variants from the built-in CLI help, so don’t rely on the help in the AWS CLI to determine valid values. For more information, see CertificateAuthorityConfiguration API Reference.

Known limitation. Some surfaces have no algorithm condition key, so you enforce them through provisioning and detection rather than policy. acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority has no condition key for the algorithm, and acm:ImportCertificate and iam:UploadServerCertificate are not algorithm-aware, so a disallowed signature setting on a created, imported, or uploaded certificate cannot be blocked by an IAM policy or SCP condition. Govern these through your provisioning process, restrict who can call them, and deny the import and upload actions entirely where they are not required. The controls above remain the available mitigation.

In particular, iam:UploadServerCertificate doesn’t support any method to prevent use of particular algorithms, and AWS doesn’t recommend using this API to generate and upload certificates. This API predates ACM and exists mainly to cover AWS Regions or partitions where ACM is not yet available. While a new Region or partition is being built out, workloads can still need a TLS server certificate before ACM support has shipped there, and uploading a certificate to IAM gives you a place to store and reference it in the meantime. Once ACM is available in that Region, you should use ACM instead. Outside that narrow case, deny iam:UploadServerCertificate unless it is genuinely required.

ACM-issued leaf certificates. A CA’s own key and signing algorithm are separate from the leaf certificates that ACM issues from it. If you use ACM to request leaf certificates, you can constrain the leaf’s key algorithm with the acm:KeyAlgorithm condition key on acm:RequestCertificate. This lets you allow-list approved algorithms for leaf certificates using SCPs or IAM policies, similar to the AWS KMS examples earlier in this post. Be aware that, at the time of writing, ACM doesn’t offer ML-DSA leaf certificates. So a policy like this is a forward-looking defense-in-depth control rather than an immediate ML-DSA-44 risk. The IAM example below is illustrative (using example approved algorithms). Since this is an evolving part of the service, be sure to validate this in your environment before relying on it.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "RestrictACMLeafKeyAlgorithm", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "acm:RequestCertificate", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringNotEqualsIfExists": { "acm:KeyAlgorithm": [ "EC_secp384r1", "RSA_2048" ] } } } ] }

This example uses StringNotEqualsIfExists so it denies only requests that specify a disallowed algorithm. With plain StringNotEquals, a request that omits acm:KeyAlgorithm would also be denied, because the missing key makes the condition evaluate true. Choose the operator that matches whether you want to block requests that leave the algorithm unspecified.

Prevent ML-DSA-44 usage in TLS for NLB and ALB

Elastic Load Balancing, for both network load balancers (NLB) and application load balancers (ALB), terminates TLS on behalf of your applications. The certificates used by these listeners are requested through or imported into ACM, or uploaded to IAM. A listener’s configured security policy and its certificate determine what’s offered during negotiation. At the time of writing, ACM requests and imports accept RSA and ECDSA keys only, and NLB and ALB listeners accept RSA and ECDSA certificates only, so no ML-DSA certificate can be bound to a listener today. As with the ACM leaf-certificate policy earlier, the controls in this section are forward-looking defense in depth rather than a mitigation of an immediate ML-DSA-44 risk.

Certificate controls (the effective mechanism for ML-DSA-44)

Because the listener API calls reference a certificate only by ARN, you can’t write an SCP on CreateListener, ModifyListener, or AddListenerCertificates that inspects the certificate’s algorithm. IAM conditions can’t reference attributes of a separately-referenced resource. Keeping ML-DSA-44 out of TLS therefore relies on there being no ML-DSA-44 certificate material to associate:

Configure your private CA to issue only ML_DSA_65 or ML_DSA_87 certificates, and control who can create CAs.

Prevent ML-DSA-44 key creation in AWS KMS, so that no KMS-held ML-DSA-44 key can become the subject key of a certificate. TLS server keys for ACM-issued, imported, or uploaded certificates are not KMS keys; those are governed by items 1 and 3.

Control imported and uploaded certificates through your provisioning process or deny the import and upload actions where not required, as described in the AWS Private CA section.

Detective controls

CloudTrail records the certificate and listener API calls in this section: certificate creation and import (acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority, acm:ImportCertificate, iam:UploadServerCertificate) and listener configuration (CreateListener, ModifyListener, AddListenerCertificates). Whether the algorithm shows up in the event depends on what the call itself carries. Creation calls that take the algorithm as an input record it: kms:CreateKey logs the KeySpec, and acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority logs the signing algorithm. That makes CloudTrail effective for catching the creation of ML-DSA-44 key material or a CA. A listener binding references its certificate only by ARN, so the certificate’s algorithm does not appear in that event. To evaluate the algorithm of a bound or imported certificate, use AWS Config resource evaluation as the detective backstop.

Summary for TLS

The primary preventive control is the certificate material itself: with no ML-DSA-44 CA, no ML-DSA-44 KMS key, and certificate import and upload controlled, no ML-DSA-44 certificate can be issued or bound. Where you also operate an allow-list of permitted TLS security policies, the elasticloadbalancing:SecurityPolicy condition key (on CreateListener and ModifyListener) can additionally constrain which TLS policies listeners can use.

Summary of controls

The following table maps the example policy (allow ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87, exclude ML-DSA-44) to the available controls. Modify the controls to limit use to the approved set of algorithms your policies require.

Area

Control

Status

Block ML-DSA-44 key creation (Organization-wide or for all accounts in an organization OU)

SCP on kms:CreateKey using kms:KeySpec

Fully supported via condition key

Block ML-DSA-44 key creation (per account or per role)

IAM policy or permission boundary using kms:KeySpec

Supported; requires programmatic enforcement of boundaries

Block use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys

Deny Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey using kms:KeySpec (key policy, IAM, or SCP); optionally disable and delete keys

Supported using kms:KeySpec (not kms:SigningAlgorithm)

Only allow approved variants in Private CA

Restrict who can create CAs; pin ML_DSA_65 or ML_DSA_87 in provisioning path

No algorithm condition key; enforce using process and detection

Limit variants in imported or uploaded TLS certificates

Process controls, or deny import or upload APIs (prefer ACM over iam:UploadServerCertificate)

APIs aren’t algorithm-aware

Block use of ML-DSA-44 in TLS with network load balancers (NLB) and application load balancers (ALB)

Restrict TLS policy using elasticloadbalancing:SecurityPolicy; control cert material

TLS-policy restriction supported; no per-cert algorithm condition

Detect use of unapproved variants

CloudTrail (API-level) and AWS Config custom rules

Supported using custom AWS Config rules; not managed rules

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to use ML-DSA as an example of turning a cryptographic algorithm policy into enforceable AWS controls. The key lever is the kms:KeySpec condition key: it keeps your approved parameter sets (ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87) fully usable while preventing the creation and use of a parameter set you’ve excluded (ML-DSA-44) on the CreateKey, in addition to the Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey operations, where kms:SigningAlgorithm can’t tell the variants apart. Applied as defense in depth across SCPs, IAM policies, permission boundaries, and KMS key policies, and extended to the surfaces that have no algorithm condition key (AWS Private CA, certificate import, and Elastic Load Balancing TLS) through provisioning controls plus AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config drift detection, these controls give you a consistent way to keep an unapproved variant out of your accounts.

The pattern isn’t specific to ML-DSA-44. Title: The Hidden AI Security Risks Threatening Businesses
Context: Externally, AI accelerates vulnerability exploitation, making faster patching and continuous monitoring critical
Full Text:
getty

As businesses race to adopt artificial intelligence, new security risks are emerging alongside the technology’s benefits. These threats are challenging traditional security practices and introducing vulnerabilities that organizations may not be equipped to recognize or manage. As AI takes on a greater role in daily workflows and decision-making, leaders must understand how their organizations’ exposure is changing.

Protecting business systems and sensitive information requires more than adapting existing cybersecurity defenses; it also means considering the unique risks associated with AI technologies. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council highlight AI security risks business and tech leaders need to understand and share practical ways organizations can address them.

Sensitive Data Exposure Through AI Prompts

AI prompts can silently leak more sensitive information than most tech leaders imagine. For any AI tool, understand what goes into the underlying LLM, who hosts it and what privacy and security measures are provided. The more concentrated your LLM infrastructure or provider, the better your chance to guardrail your business’s sensitive information. - Alekh Jindal, Tursio

AI-Accelerated Zero-Day Exploits

AI makes it very easy to find and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities in an operating system, hypervisor or anywhere in infrastructure. This means that the whack-a-mole game of patching systems as quickly as possible won’t work anymore. What tech leaders need to understand is that the game has shifted to prevention—the key is securing the infrastructure in a way that, even if there’s a zero-day, the data is still safe. - Ayal Yogev, Anjuna Security

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Unchecked AI Agent Authority

The AI security risk leaders should watch is unchecked AI authority. Internally, as AI agents move from recommending to executing, organizations need clear permissions, policy-based authorization, approval thresholds and audit trails. Externally, AI accelerates vulnerability exploitation, making faster patching and continuous monitoring critical. The goal is not to restrict AI autonomy but to ensure it is governed at the point of action. - Shahir Daya, Zafin

Third-Party AI Data Exposure

Sending data, especially PII data and legal and compliance-sensitive data, through a direct API or MCP connection to a third-party model like OpenAI or Anthropic creates a new trust boundary. That data now flows through infrastructure you don’t control. Self-hosted models keep data and inference in one environment, reducing third-party exposure and the number of trust boundaries that can fail. - Julia Penfield, PH.D., VelocityEHS

Unmonitored AI Tools With Data Access

Ask security how many AI tools and agents employees connected to company data last month—most can’t answer, and that blind spot is the real exposure, not the AI itself. Treat every AI tool like a company laptop: Give it an owner, log what it can access and revoke it the day someone leaves. - Siva Samy, ValGenesis, Inc.

Uncontrolled AI Access To Business Data

One of the biggest risks is giving AI access to business data without fully understanding what it can access or how that data will be used. Companies need clear rules around data access, permissions and how AI-generated outputs are used. The goal is to build those safeguards into the technology from the beginning rather than trying to address them later. - Steve Cangiano, CMiC

AI Agents As Insider Threats

AI agents act like humans, but they consume and move data far faster than any person could, often with more permissions than they need. Organizations need to govern them the way they govern insider risk: by understanding intent and behavior, not just access. In practice, that means connecting your AI security strategy to your data security strategy. Treat them as separate, and the gaps become the risk. - Sumit Dhawan, Proofpoint

AI-Generated Identity Fraud

Single-signal identity checks are obsolete. Fraudsters now use injection attacks and AI-generated media to bypass liveness checks, so a face or document that looks real proves nothing on its own. Verification must be continuous rather than a one-time onboarding checkbox, layering device and network signals, behavioral biometrics, and risk-based orchestration that pulls them together to build trust. - Kaarel Kotkas, Veriff

AI-Enabled Hiring Fraud

AI is turning hiring fraud into a real security threat. A fake candidate can now get through multiple stages of a hiring process, seem credible on paper and even ace interviews. If that person is hired, the company may hand an attacker legitimate access to internal systems, customer data, source code or financial information. Before giving candidates access to sensitive systems or data, companies need to verify that they really are who they say they are. - Gergo Vari, Lensa, Inc.

Sensitive Data Leaks Through Shadow AI

A widely underestimated risk is data leakage through shadow AI: employees quietly pasting sensitive customer, financial or IP data into unapproved tools whose retention, security and training practices IT cannot see. Bans can drive usage further underground. Organizations need better visibility to enforce responsible use and risk‑based controls that protect data without slowing innovation. - Neal Bradbury, Barracuda

AI Observability And Compliance Gaps

While the focus is more on AI-based cost savings or productivity, emphasis on observability and compliance needs equal attention; if overlooked, it will lead to regulatory and credibility issues, along with an auditability nightmare. These vital layers decide the distance between a proof of concept and successful production of AI agents. - Shammy Narayanan, Welldoc

Overreliance On AI-Generated Outputs

The biggest risk for me is not that AI will stop obeying humans but that humans will make a habit of trusting AI automatically. Although we are investing in better agentic AI defenses, we should also invest more in the internal architecture of the cyber professional, because the pressure will only increase, and without a zen-like mental clarity, the wrong choices could be made. - Carlo Tortora Brayda, Cyber Eagle Project Inc.

Inadequate AI Data Security

I don’t think enough leaders realize that AI security is fundamentally a data problem, not a model, agent or user one. Regardless of how AI is leveraged, it cannot operate safely unless it’s working with data that is trusted, accurate and high-quality. Teams can ensure their data meets these standards by implementing comprehensive, foundational data security posture management. - Thyaga Vasudevan, Skyhigh Security

Loss Of Granular Data Access Controls

Many product organizations underestimate the challenge of maintaining data access control as they scale AI. AI-augmented search, analytics and content synthesis offer enormous value, but preserving fine-grained access to sensitive IP is complicated if data is extracted into a data lake. Digital thread strategies need governed AI access to operational data and context to preserve access policy integrity. - Leon Lauritsen, Aras

Unmonitored ‘Synthetic Insiders’

One underestimated AI security risk is the rise of the “synthetic insider.” AI agents are given access to systems and permission to act for employees. They are no longer just tools but start to behave like insiders. Their actions should be continuously monitored against the role and task they were intended to perform. In the agentic era, leaders need to know whether an agent’s activity made sense. - Aviv Nahum, Above Security

AI Document Retention And Deletion Gaps

Every doc uploaded to AI is a doc outside your retention policy. Company docs end up all over the place, including staff laptops. Staff upload docs because 1. there is no system with secure doc storage or 2. outside tooling is faster. Provide a fast and secure place for content that LLMs can access. Second, ensure docs are fully deleted. Ask AI vendors what happens to derived artifacts, embeddings, caches and backups when a source document is deleted. - Aaron Rallo, Trovia

Unclear Accountability For Autonomous AI

One underestimated AI security risk is unclear accountability as AI moves from recommending actions to executing them. Organizations should define what AI can access, what it can act on autonomously, what requires human approval, and who owns the outcome. AI governance must address not only what a system can do but also who is accountable when it acts. - Jayasri Ranganathan, Trinity Solar Inc.

AI-Accelerated Attacks Against Static Defenses

AI is collapsing the cost and time required for attackers to experiment. They can automate reconnaissance, generate thousands of attack variations, and continuously adjust based on what gets through. Static rules and known-pattern detection cannot adapt at the same rate. Organizations need behavioral and unsupervised detection to surface novel patterns, paired with real-time decisioning so newly identified risk can immediately inform controls. - Yinglian Xie, DataVisor

AI-Accelerated Post-Breach Exploitation

AI enables attackers to analyze stolen source code and cloud stacks at machine speed, exposing new vulnerabilities on the fly. Believing an attack is contained just by revoking initial access is untenable; block one vector, and attackers find another within hours. Businesses must move faster than feels comfortable, apply same-day patching, and treat self-inflicted downtime as the safer option. - Ryan Ikeler, MOXFIVE

Title: Stopping destructive commands in AI agents
Context: Together, they can take an application offline, erase critical configuration, lock out the employees needed to restore service, and turn a routine task into an expensive incident
Full Text:
An engineer gives a coding agent a routine task: clean up an old test deployment.

The request sounds harmless, and the environment is cluttered with unused cloud resources, stale branches, and temporary credentials that should have been removed weeks ago. The agent gets to work.

It lists resources, identifies old infrastructure, and finds a deployment command. Then it sees a naming pattern that appears to connect the test environment to production. Trying to be helpful, the agent removes what looks unused, resets a repository to a clean state, and revokes access it believes is no longer needed.

None of those steps necessarily looks alarming on its own.

Together, they can take an application offline, erase critical configuration, lock out the employees needed to restore service, and turn a routine task into an expensive incident.

Agents do more than answer questions

That is the challenge of agentic AI: agents are valuable because they can act. They can run commands, change files, and update security controls. But that same ability to act can create real business risk.

Sometimes, the agent makes the wrong move while trying to complete a legitimate task. It follows an unclear instruction, misunderstands its environment, or chooses an efficient path that exceeds what its user intended.

Other times, the intent is malicious. A threat actor who manipulates an agent through a prompt, a tool, or untrusted content can use the same permissions and capabilities to cause damage. What begins as a simple request can become a path to service disruption, data loss, weakened security controls, or costly cloud activity.

Ungoverned agentic behaviors can lead to lost revenue, interrupted operations, exposed data, recovery work across multiple teams, and damaged customer trust.

Access controls do not answer every question

The natural response is to restrict the agent’s access. An agent should only have the permissions it needs. But access controls alone do not answer the full question: should the agent take this action now?

Agents are designed to complete objectives. If one path is blocked, an agent may look for another permitted route to finish the task: using a different command or API, switching to another tool or service, accessing a different file or data source, or asking another agent or user to perform the step. A policy that says “do not use this resource” may still leave the agent able to create the same harmful outcome another way.

Consider an agent that cannot delete a production environment directly. It may still be able to remove the credentials that keep it running, overwrite its configuration, reset its deployment state, or disable the protections around it.

The risk comes from the behavior the agent is about to carry out with its access, and the impact that behavior could have.

Not every destructive action should be blocked

Recognizing a harmful action depends on context. A command such as rm -rf is not automatically destructive. Deleting a temporary build folder may be normal. Deleting a directory that contains customer data is very different.

The same is true for resetting a repository, deleting infrastructure, removing access, or changing a security policy. The command alone does not reveal whether the action is appropriate.

And some high-impact actions are intentionally part of the job.

An IT team may ask an agent to revoke a departing employee’s access. Data teams may ask it to delete records that have reached the end of their retention period, and Cloud teams may ask it to retire infrastructure after a migration.

In these cases, simply blocking the action is not the answer. The organization needs a way to make sure the right person understands and approves the impact before the agent proceeds.

Context turns commands into informed decisions

Cato’s destructive commands detector evaluates the action in context before it is executed.

The detector examines what the agent is trying to do, what it is targeting, where the action is happening, whether it is authorized, how difficult it would be to reverse, and how widely the impact could spread.

This helps Cato distinguish normal automation from actions that create material risk.

Removing temporary files from a test environment can proceed. Deleting customer data from production deserves a different response. Revoking access may be the intended task, but it can still require confirmation from the user who requested it.

That is the difference between treating every delete command as a threat and applying the right level of control to the action at hand.

Put teams in control of agent behavior

When the detector identifies a risky action, teams can define what happens next.

Using destructive commands detection in custom policies allows teams to create rules that reflect their own environments, policies, and risk tolerance. These rules can apply differently to users, teams, and the apps that they use. For one team, deleting temporary test resources may be acceptable, only requiring a user notification before execution, or simply monitoring and logging the behavior. For another, any command targeting production infrastructure, customer data, privileged credentials, or security controls should be blocked immediately.

The goal is to apply contextual control before an action creates an incident, so agents doing routine work are not slowed down at every turn.

Combined with other detectors and runtime protections, destructive commands detection gives teams a more complete way to govern agentic AI. It helps teams see risky behavior and enforce the right response.

Agentic AI can bring real speed and scale to the business when teams let agents act within clear limits on the actions that can cause real harm.

Title: UK and Allies Warn of Cyber Threat from China’s Integrity Technology Group
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The US, UK and several allied countries have issued a joint alert detailing the tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) associated with a sanctioned Chinese organization.

The work of Integrity Technology Group has in the past enabled prolific Beijing-backed groups such as Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda, Red Juliett) according to the advisory, published on October 8.

“Integrity Tech employs individuals who support malicious cyber activity in different ways, including acquiring or building cyber tools for use and sale, acquiring and hosting infrastructure and compromising networks across global victims, which the authoring organizations track as China-based malicious cyber activity,” it continued.

“The services provided by Integrity Tech also contribute to the larger Chinese cyber ecosystem, which aims to exfiltrate sensitive data from victims around the world.”

Read more on Integrity Technology Group: US Sanctions Chinese Cybersecurity Firm for Global Botnet Attacks.

The report highlighted various technical details associated with Integrity Tech TTPs including:

The use of open source scanning tools to find vulnerabilities in networks and web-based applications

The use of the “MicroScan” hacking tool which contains over 1300 pen-testing scripts designed to scan sites for specific flaws

Initial access to networks and cloud services via command line utilities built on exploit codes written in Python and Go

Exploitation of cross-site scripting (XSS) bugs to compromise third-party apps

Use of the EBurst tool for password spraying/guessing to compromise Microsoft 365 email accounts

Persistence by installing VPN clients (eg SoftEther) on victim devices to obfuscate command and control (C2) comms

Staging exfiltration data with different file names to minimize detection of the MySQL email dump

Creation of a bot using the PHP script Curlc4.txt to obtain emails from victims

Use of DC.exe to trick a domain controller into handing over sensitive Active Directory information, including account credentials

Exfiltration of email data from on-premises systems and cloud-based services, with targeted verticals including government, law enforcement, healthcare and religious institutions located in Southeast Asia

Use of command-line utility office-cli to continuously access Microsoft Outlook 365 accounts and steal emails

Next Steps for Network Defenders

The report lists a large number of indicators of compromise (IoCs), additional resources and mitigations, as well as advice for incident responders that think they may already have been compromised.

However, its main advice for mitigating the threat from Integrity Tech can be distilled into the following:

Disable unused services and ports, including automatic configuration, remote access and file sharing protocols

Sanitize user input in web applications to prevent possible XSS payload injection

Implement identity, credential and access management (ICAM) policies, and then require multifactor authentication (MFA) where possible

NCSC director of operations, Paul Chichester, said the extent of Integrity Tech’s activities should be concerning for all security teams.

“The breadth of sectors that have been targeted across the globe demonstrate the extent of the threat and all organizations should take note of this warning and engage with NCSC advice and guidance,” he added.

“We will continue to call out malicious actors and the malevolent ecosystem they operate in.”

Also on October 8, the US announced the seizure of several domains associated with hacking tools Microscan and FishHub, in a bid to disrupt the operations of Integrity Tech and associated threat groups.

Title: AI Training Critical as Governance Challenges Grow
